teile.einleitung: In Switzerland there are two important authorities dealing with money and banks: the **SNB** and **FINMA**. They are often confused, but they have quite different tasks. In short: the SNB conducts monetary policy, FINMA supervises the financial institutions.
wichtigste: SNB stands for Swiss National Bank; FINMA stands for Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority.
The SNB steers interest rates and the amount of money so that prices stay stable.
FINMA licenses and supervises banks, insurance companies and other financial institutions.
Both work independently of the government.
FINMA has existed since 2009, the SNB since 1907.
Both work closely together on the stability of the financial system.

abschnitte.titel: The SNB: in charge of money
abschnitte.text: The **Swiss National Bank** is the central bank. It sets the key interest rate and in this way influences how expensive loans are. Its aim is **price stability**, meaning low inflation. It issues the banknotes and manages the currency reserves. It also watches whether the financial system as a whole is under threat.

**FINMA** has its head office in Bern. It decides who may run a bank or an insurance company in Switzerland. For this it grants a **licence**. After that it constantly checks whether the institutions have enough equity capital and keep to the rules. Anyone who does not can expect measures to be taken, and in the worst case the licence may be withdrawn.

People trust banks with their savings and insurance companies with their premiums. For this trust to be justified, there must be **checks**. In this way FINMA protects customers and makes sure that the financial centre works well. It also takes action against companies that accept people's money without a licence. In a dispute between an individual and their bank, on the other hand, the Banking Ombudsman helps.

With large banks, both are needed. The SNB looks after the **stability** of the whole system, FINMA after the individual institutions. Certain banks are considered **systemically important**, because their collapse would harm the whole economy. Stricter rules apply to them. In crises, the SNB, FINMA and the Confederation coordinate closely.

gewusst: FINMA was formed in 2009 from three earlier authorities, including the Swiss Federal Banking Commission.
A simple way to remember it: SNB stands for money, FINMA for supervision.

teile.einleitung: A railway station is a place where trains stop and people get on and off. Railway lines and stations are important for the whole country, so the Confederation uses tax money to help build and maintain them.
wichtigste: The Confederation pays a lot towards new railway lines, including with tax money.
Since 2016 there has been the Railway Infrastructure Fund for this.
The cantons also contribute to rail transport in their region.
SBB belongs entirely to the Confederation.
The Gotthard Base Tunnel is one of the longest railway tunnels in the world.
Zurich main station is the largest station in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: At a **station** there are **platforms** where the trains stop. Big departure boards show when which train leaves. Larger stations have ticket machines, shops and restaurants. Buses and trams often stop there too, so that it is easy to change. The largest station in Switzerland is **Zurich main station**.

Building and maintaining tracks, tunnels and stations costs a great deal of money. The **Confederation** pays a large part of it, including with **tax money**. Since 2016 there has been the **Railway Infrastructure Fund**, RIF for short, for this. The voters approved it in 2014. Money flows into the fund from various sources, for example from the heavy vehicle fee and from VAT. The **cantons** contribute too.

The **Swiss Federal Railways**, SBB for short, are the largest railway company in Switzerland. They belong entirely to the **Confederation**. There are also many other railways, such as the Rhaetian Railway in the Grisons or the BLS in the canton of Bern. For regional transport, the Confederation and the cantons order the services together. Ticket income covers only part of the costs.

Switzerland has some particularly large railway structures. The **Gotthard Base Tunnel** is about 57 kilometres long and was opened in 2016. It is part of the **NRLA**, the New Rail Link through the Alps. The Lötschberg Base Tunnel and the Ceneri Base Tunnel are also part of it. The voters had a say in such big projects in popular votes.

gewusst: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world.
Swiss railways are known for their regular-interval timetable: many trains leave at the same minute every hour.

teile.einleitung: If you stay overnight in a holiday resort, you often pay a small charge per night. It is called the **tourist tax**, or “Kurtaxe”. With this money, the resort pays for things that mainly serve its guests.
wichtigste: The tourist tax is paid by **holiday guests** per night.
It is set by the **municipality** or the resort.
The hotel or holiday flat usually collects the tourist tax.
The money goes into services for tourists, for example footpaths.
The amount varies from place to place.
Children often pay less or nothing at all.

abschnitte.titel: How does the tourist tax work?
abschnitte.text: The **tourist tax** is a charge that guests pay per person and night. It usually appears on the bill from the hotel, youth hostel or campsite. The host collects the money and passes it on to the municipality or the **tourism organisation**. Each place decides for itself how high it is.

abschnitte.titel: What the money is used for
abschnitte.text: The tourist tax pays for services that mainly benefit guests. These include, for example, **footpaths**, cross-country ski trails, information offices or events. It may not simply be used for the municipality's normal tasks. In this way guests help to pay for what they also use on holiday.

In many holiday resorts, you get a **guest card** for the tourist tax you have paid. With it, you can often travel on buses for free or get reductions, for example for mountain railways, museums or the swimming pool. That way you see directly what the money is used for.

gewusst: The word “Kur” recalls the old days, when many guests travelled to spas and health resorts to recover.
Anyone who owns a holiday flat in a resort often pays the tourist tax as a fixed annual flat rate.

teile.einleitung: If you overdraw your account, you are borrowing money from the bank. For this it charges overdraft interest. It is one of the most expensive kinds of interest there is.
wichtigste: Overdraft interest is calculated on the amount below zero.
It is usually much higher than savings interest.
The bank takes a big risk, because it lends without any security.
The interest is given per year, but only calculated for the days of the overdraft.
If you often go overdrawn, you end up paying a lot of money.

abschnitte.text: If your account slips below zero, the bank lends you the missing money. For this short **loan** it charges **overdraft interest**. It is calculated only on the missing amount and only for the days on which the account is in the minus. But it is given as an interest rate per year. It is often taken from the account at the end of a quarter or a year.

With a **mortgage**, the bank has the house as **security**. With an overdraft there is no such security. If someone does not pay it back, the bank could lose the money. For this **risk** it charges high interest. On your credit balance, on the other hand, it pays little, because it carries no such risk there.

Suppose the overdraft interest is 10 per cent a year. If an account were 1,000 francs in the minus for a whole year, that would cost 100 francs. If it is only in the minus for one month, it is about a twelfth of that. That sounds like little, but it can add up. That is why an overdraft is not a good solution for a longer time.

gewusst: In Switzerland, the Federal Council sets a maximum interest rate for consumer credit. Overdrafts are covered by it too.
The savings interest on an account and the overdraft interest on the same account can differ many times over.

teile.einleitung: In your tax return you may deduct certain costs from your income. These deductions reduce your taxable income, and the tax is then calculated on that.
wichtigste: A deduction is an amount that reduces taxable income.
A deduction of 1,000 francs lowers taxable income by 1,000 francs, not the tax.
How much tax you save depends on the tax rate.
Only costs that the law expressly allows can be deducted.
Rent, food and clothes are living costs and cannot be deducted.
The Confederation and the cantons have their own tax laws with their own amounts.

abschnitte.text: In your **tax return**, you state how much you have earned. From this income you may subtract certain costs, the so-called **deductions**. What is left is your **taxable income**. The tax is calculated on this smaller amount. Deductions are meant to take into account that some people have particular expenses.

A deduction of 1,000 francs lowers taxable income by **1,000 francs**. But the tax itself falls by less. How much you save depends on the **tax rate**. In Switzerland, the tax rate rises with income; this is called **progression**. That is why someone with a high income saves more tax with the same deduction than someone with a low income.

Common deductions are **work-related expenses**, for example for travelling to work or eating out during the working day. Contributions to **pillar 3a**, part of insurance premiums and donations to charitable organisations can also be deducted. Families get a **child deduction**. **Living costs** such as rent, meals at home or clothes cannot be deducted. Only what the law expressly allows can be deducted.

In Switzerland, you pay taxes to the **Confederation**, the **canton** and the **municipality**. The Confederation and the cantons have their own **tax laws**. The kinds of deduction have largely been brought into line; this is called **harmonised**. But the amounts allowed are often different. That is why the tax return often has two columns: one for the canton and one for the Confederation.

gewusst: Today, in almost all cantons you can fill in your tax return on the computer and submit it electronically.
If you have receipts for deductions, you should keep them, because the tax office can ask for them.

teile.einleitung: The **school playground** is the place where children play, run and relax during break. It belongs to the school and is usually built and looked after by the municipality with tax money.
wichtigste: The school playground belongs to the school building.
In Switzerland, compulsory schooling is paid for mainly by municipalities and cantons.
New play equipment such as a climbing frame is usually paid for by the municipality with taxes.
Larger items of spending are often decided by the municipality's voters.
Play equipment must be safe and checked regularly.
Outside school hours, the school playground is often open to all children.

abschnitte.text: During break, children need exercise and fresh air. That is why almost every school building has a **school playground**. There are often climbing frames, swings, table tennis tables or a small football pitch. Trees and benches are part of it too, so that you can sit in the shade. A good school playground has room for play and for quiet.

In Switzerland, the **cantons** regulate compulsory schooling. The **municipality** usually provides the school buildings and playgrounds. The money for this comes from the **taxes** that the people in the municipality pay. Sometimes parents' associations or donations help too, for example for a special piece of play equipment.

Smaller items of spending are decided by the **municipal council** within the budget. Large projects, such as a completely new school playground, often need the approval of the **municipal assembly** or a **vote**. Sometimes the children may also have their say and put forward their wishes. That way the playground is designed so that the children really like it.

Play equipment must be well built so that nobody gets hurt. Under climbing frames there is often soft **impact protection**, for example wood chips, sand or rubber mats. The equipment is checked and repaired regularly. The **BFU**, the Swiss Council for Accident Prevention, gives tips on how to make playgrounds safe.

gewusst: Many school playgrounds are a public playground for the whole neighbourhood in the evenings and at weekends.
More and more municipalities are replacing grey tarmac with grass, trees and water, so that it stays cooler in summer.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, people who have saved money pay a **wealth tax** on it. But not from the very first franc: a certain amount remains tax-free. This amount is called the **tax-free allowance**.
wichtigste: A tax-free allowance is an amount up to which no wealth is taxed.
People with only a little wealth pay no wealth tax.
Wealth tax is charged only by cantons and municipalities, not by the Confederation.
Each canton sets the amount of the tax-free allowance itself.
Married people and families with children often have higher allowances.

abschnitte.text: **Wealth** includes everything someone owns that is worth money. This means, for example, savings in an account, **shares**, a car or a house. **Debts** are subtracted from this. What is left is the net wealth. The tax is calculated on that.

If your wealth is below the **tax-free allowance**, you pay no wealth tax at all. In this way small savings remain tax-free. If it is above, in many cantons you only pay on the part above the allowance. The exact amounts are in the cantons' tax laws and vary greatly.

The **Confederation** does not charge a wealth tax. It is a matter for the **cantons** and **municipalities**. That is why there are big differences in how high the tax is and how much remains tax-free. The term **allowance** also appears with other taxes, for example with deductions for children.

gewusst: Switzerland is one of the few countries in Europe that still has a wealth tax.
Children can also have wealth, for example a savings account. It is usually declared by the parents.

teile.einleitung: **Volatility** shows how strongly the price of an investment goes up and down. A price is the amount at which you can buy or sell, for example, a share. The higher the volatility, the bigger the ups and downs.
wichtigste: Volatility describes how strongly the price of an investment goes up and down.
High volatility means big price swings.
Low volatility means a fairly calm price movement.
It is often used as a measure of the risk of an investment.
Shares usually go up and down more than bonds or a savings account.
People who invest for a long time can usually cope better with swings.

abschnitte.titel: Ups and downs on the stock exchange
abschnitte.text: Share prices change all the time, sometimes several times a minute. With some investments the swings are small, with others huge. **Volatility** measures how big these swings are. You can imagine it like a roller coaster: a gentle ride has small hills, a wild one has steep drops and climbs.

Experts usually calculate volatility using the **standard deviation**. This statistical measure shows how far values on average differ from their mean. Volatility is often given as a percentage per year. But a number on its own does not say whether the price will rise or fall. It only says how restlessly it moves.

High volatility means more **uncertainty**. You know less exactly how much an investment will be worth at a certain time. If you need the money soon, you can make a loss when prices are low. In return, investments that go up and down, such as shares, often offer better chances of a return in the long term. A savings account, by contrast, does not go up and down, but usually earns less.

If you have a long time, for example for your pension, you can more easily **sit out** the swings. If you are planning for the short term, it is better to choose calmer investments. Many people spread their money across different investments; this is called **diversification**. That way the swings partly balance each other out. In unsettled times, for example during crises, volatility on the stock markets often rises sharply.

gewusst: There are even indices that only measure expected volatility; they are sometimes called the stock market's fear gauge.
The word volatile comes from the Latin word for to fly and means fleeting or unstable.

teile.einleitung: **National roads** are the most important roads in Switzerland, above all the motorways. Since 2008 they have belonged to the **Confederation**. It builds and maintains them with money from charges and taxes.
wichtigste: National roads are mainly the **motorways** and expressways.
Since **2008**, the **Confederation** alone has been responsible for them.
They are built and run by the **Federal Roads Office**, FEDRO for short.
Anyone who uses the motorway with a car needs a **vignette**.
They are financed, among other things, by the mineral oil tax and the vignette.
Switzerland's first stretch of motorway was opened near Lucerne in 1955.

abschnitte.text: **National roads** are roads that are important for the whole of Switzerland. They connect the big cities and regions with each other. Most of them are **motorways** with separate carriageways, plus some expressways. You can recognise them by their green signposts.

In the past, the Confederation and the cantons shared the tasks for national roads. That changed with a major reform of the division of tasks between the Confederation and the cantons, the **NFA**. Since **2008**, the national roads have belonged to the Confederation. The **Federal Roads Office**, FEDRO for short, plans, builds and maintains them.

Motorways need a lot of money, for example for new tunnels, bridges or resurfacing work. The money comes from the **National Roads and Urban Transport Fund**, NAF for short. Revenue from the **mineral oil tax** and the **motorway vignette**, among other things, goes into this fund. So anyone who fills up with fuel and buys a vignette helps to pay for the motorways.

gewusst: Switzerland's first stretch of motorway ran from Lucerne to Horw in 1955.
The Gotthard road tunnel on the A2 national road was opened in 1980 and is about 17 kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: **Municipal tax** is the tax you pay to your own municipality. With this money, the municipality pays for things on your doorstep, such as the nursery school, the school building and local roads.
wichtigste: Municipal tax goes to the municipality where you live.
It uses it to pay, for example, for the nursery school and local roads.
Waste water, playgrounds and school buildings are also included.
In many cantons, the amount depends on the municipality's tax rate.
That is why municipal tax is not equally high everywhere.

abschnitte.text: Every municipality has tasks that directly affect the people who live there. It runs **compulsory schooling**, builds **local roads** and provides clean **water**. For this it needs money. It gets most of it from **municipal tax** on residents' income and assets.

In many cantons, a **simple tax** is first calculated according to the canton's rules. The municipality then sets a **tax rate** as a percentage. If it is high, you pay more; if it is low, you pay less. The tax rate is often decided by the voters, for example at the municipal assembly.

Usually you do not get a separate bill for each level. Often the canton or the municipality collects **cantonal and municipal taxes** together. **Companies** also pay municipal taxes on their profits. In some cantons there is also a **church tax** if you are a member of one of the established churches.

gewusst: If you move to a municipality with a lower tax rate, you may pay less tax on the same wage.

teile.einleitung: Dog tax is a charge that dog owners pay every year for their dog. In Switzerland it is usually charged by the municipalities or cantons. The money helps to pay, for example, for Robidog bins and for checks on dogs.
wichtigste: In many Swiss municipalities you pay a dog tax for every dog.
The tax is usually paid yearly.
The amount varies from municipality to municipality.
In Switzerland, dogs must be identified with a microchip.
Every dog is registered in a national database.
There is often no dog tax for guide dogs and other assistance dogs.
Anyone who does not register a dog risks a fine.

abschnitte.text: **Dog tax** is a special tax just for dog owners. It is one of the small taxes that many municipalities charge in addition to income tax. In Switzerland there is no comparable tax for cats, hamsters or horses. The rules are set out in cantonal laws and in municipal regulations.

Anyone who buys or takes on a dog must register it with their municipality. After that you get a bill for the dog tax every year. The amounts are often around 100 to 200 francs a year, sometimes more in towns. Some municipalities charge a higher amount for a second dog.

Since 2007, every dog in Switzerland must be identified with a **microchip** under its skin. The chip is about the size of a grain of rice and is inserted by the vet. The data is stored in the national dog database **AMICUS**. In some municipalities, after paying the tax you also get a **dog tag** for the collar.

abschnitte.titel: What is the money used for?
abschnitte.text: Dogs cause the municipality extra costs. These include the Robidog bins with bags for dog mess and emptying them. Cleaning paths and meadows and checking how dogs are kept also cost money. But the dog tax usually goes into the general municipal funds and is not always set aside specifically for dogs.

Many municipalities exempt **assistance dogs** such as guide dogs, rescue dogs or police dogs from the tax. Dog owners also have other duties, for example picking up dog mess. In some cantons, certain breeds must be kept on a lead or even need a permit. Anyone who does not register their dog or does not pay the tax can be fined.

begriffe.erklaerung: A yearly charge paid to the municipality for a dog.
A tiny memory chip with a number, placed under the dog's skin.
The national database in which all dogs in Switzerland are registered.
A specially trained dog that helps people with a disability.

gewusst: About half a million dogs live in Switzerland (as of 2023).
For a small chihuahua you normally pay the same dog tax as for a big St Bernard.
The name Robidog for the green dog bag bins comes from Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Before a bank grants a **mortgage** for a house or a flat, it checks **affordability**. It wants to know whether the buyer can afford the housing costs in the long term. As a rule of thumb, these costs should make up no more than about a third of income.
wichtigste: Affordability means: can you afford the housing costs in the long term?
Housing costs should be no more than about a third of gross income.
The bank calculates with a cautious interest rate that is higher than the current one.
On top of that come additional costs for maintenance and repayment.
The bank also requires enough of your own money, usually at least 20% of the purchase price.

abschnitte.titel: Why the bank does the sums
abschnitte.text: A house or a flat costs a great deal of money. Most buyers borrow a large part of it from the bank. This loan is called a **mortgage**. The bank wants to be sure that the interest can be paid even in more difficult times. That is why it checks affordability before saying yes.

The bank does not calculate with the current interest rate but with a higher, cautious **imputed interest rate**. This is often about 5%. On top of that come **additional costs** for maintenance and repairs, often about 1% of the property's value per year. And finally the **amortisation**, meaning paying back part of the mortgage step by step. The total of these costs should not be more than about a third of gross income.

Besides affordability, the bank requires **equity**. In Switzerland this is normally at least 20% of the purchase price. Part of it must come from your own money, for example from savings. In some circumstances, the rest can also be taken from the pension fund or pillar 3a. The larger part of the price is then financed through the mortgage.

The strict rules do not only protect the bank. They also stop families from taking on too much when buying a house. If interest rates rose sharply, the costs could otherwise suddenly become too high. Anyone who does not meet the affordability test may have to save for longer or look for a cheaper property.

gewusst: The imputed interest rate is often much higher than the interest you actually pay.
Amortisation can also be done indirectly, by paying money into pillar 3a instead of reducing the mortgage directly.

teile.einleitung: For most children in Switzerland, school life begins at nursery school, called “Kindergarten”. The public nursery school is free for families. It is paid for with tax money from the municipality and canton.
wichtigste: The public nursery school is part of **compulsory schooling**.
In most cantons, nursery school lasts two years.
Attending costs the parents no school fees.
The teachers are paid by the municipality and canton.
The money for this comes from **taxes**.
Buildings, toys and materials are also paid for with tax money.

abschnitte.text: Nursery school is the first part of **compulsory schooling**. It is followed by primary school and lower secondary school. In most cantons, nursery school is now compulsory and lasts two years. There the children learn through play to live together with others, to listen and to solve tasks.

The teacher at a public nursery school receives their **wages** from tax money. Depending on the canton, the **municipality** and the **canton** share the costs in different ways. The municipality often provides the building, the garden and the materials. Families pay no school fees for it.

People without children also pay taxes that go into nursery schools. The idea behind it: education is important for the whole of society. Well-educated children later become adults who work, have a say and pay taxes themselves. So in the end everyone benefits.

Besides public nursery schools, there are also **private** options. These usually charge school fees, because they are supported with little or no tax money. But most children in Switzerland attend the public nursery school in the municipality where they live.

gewusst: With the **HarmoS agreement**, many cantons agreed that compulsory schooling begins with nursery school.
The word Kindergarten was coined in the 19th century by the German Friedrich Fröbel and is even used in English today.

teile.einleitung: The accommodation rate is one of Switzerland's three VAT rates. It applies to overnight stays in hotels, holiday flats and similar accommodation.
wichtigste: Since 2024 the accommodation rate has been 3.8 per cent.
It applies to overnight stays with breakfast.
Hotels, guesthouses and holiday flats can use it.
Food and drinks other than breakfast have the standard rate.
The rate is meant to strengthen tourism.

abschnitte.text: **Value added tax**, VAT for short, has three rates in Switzerland. The **standard rate** of 8.1 per cent applies to most goods and services. The **reduced rate** of 2.6 per cent applies, for example, to food, books and medicines. In between is the **accommodation rate** of 3.8 per cent. All three rates have applied since 2024.

The accommodation rate applies to an **overnight stay**. Breakfast that comes with the room is included. Besides hotels, holiday flats, guesthouses or youth hostels can also use the rate. What matters is that guests stay and sleep there in return for payment. Anyone who rents a flat on a permanent basis for a longer time, on the other hand, pays no VAT on the rent.

With the low rate, the Confederation wants to support **tourism**. Switzerland has high wages and prices. But guests from abroad compare what holidays cost here and elsewhere. A lower tax rate makes a night a little cheaper. This is especially important for **mountain regions**, which depend heavily on tourism.

abschnitte.titel: An exception with an expiry date
abschnitte.text: The accommodation rate was introduced in the 1990s as a **temporary** measure. Parliament has extended it several times since then. Supporters say it secures jobs in hotels. Critics think exceptions make the tax complicated. In the end such questions are decided by politicians, and sometimes by the people.

gewusst: The accommodation rate was originally meant only for a short time and has been extended again and again.
A youth hostel can use the same tax rate as a luxury hotel.

teile.einleitung: If you get a bill, you do not have to pay it straight away. The payment deadline says by when the money must reach the recipient. With credit cards, it decides whether interest is charged or not.
wichtigste: The payment deadline is the time within which a bill must be paid.
Many bills in Switzerland have a deadline of 30 days.
The credit card company sends a statement once a month.
If you pay the whole statement within the deadline, you normally pay no interest.
If you pay only part of it, you usually pay high interest on the rest.
After the deadline has passed, a reminder with fees may arrive.

abschnitte.text: A **deadline** is a period within which something must be done. A bill often says “payable within 30 days”. This is the **payment deadline**. It gives you time to check the bill and get the money ready. What matters is that the money reaches the recipient by the last day. A transfer can take one or two working days.

With a **credit card**, you buy first and pay later. Once a month the credit card company sends a **statement** with all your purchases. It shows the total amount and the payment deadline. If you pay the whole amount on time, there is normally no interest to pay. If you pay only part of it, the rest counts as a **loan**, and the company charges high interest for it.

If a bill is not paid on time, the creditor often sends a **reminder**. The creditor is the person or company that is owed money. Fees may be charged for reminders if this has been agreed. In addition, **default interest** can be added. If the bill stays unpaid for a long time, the creditor can start **debt enforcement proceedings**. This is a procedure for collecting debts.

It is best to enter payment deadlines in a calendar. In online banking, you can set up a payment in advance for a particular date. With credit cards, a **direct debit** helps: the amount is taken from your account automatically. But there must be enough money in the account. If you realise that you cannot pay, it is best to contact the creditor early.

gewusst: The Swiss Code of Obligations sets default interest at 5 per cent a year, unless something else has been agreed.
Some companies give a small discount, known as a cash discount, if you pay particularly quickly.

teile.einleitung: The **ZEK** is the Central Office for Credit Information in Switzerland. It collects details about loans, leasing contracts and card accounts. Banks check there before giving someone a new loan.
wichtigste: ZEK stands for the Swiss Central Office for Credit Information.
It collects details about loans, leasing contracts and card accounts.
Missed payments are also stored there.
Banks and credit companies check with the ZEK before giving a loan.
Anyone can ask the ZEK which data about them is stored.

abschnitte.text: The ZEK is an **association** whose members are banks, credit card companies and leasing companies. These members report to the ZEK who has a loan, a leasing contract or a credit card with them. On top of that come details if someone stops paying. This creates an overview of a person's existing **obligations**.

abschnitte.titel: What the data is used for
abschnitte.text: Before a bank gives a new loan, it wants to know whether someone already has other debts. That is why it checks with the ZEK. If someone already has several loans or unpaid **missed payments**, a new loan is often refused. This protects the lenders. But it is also meant to stop people getting **too deeply into debt**.

Anyone may ask the ZEK for a **personal information report**. Then you can see which details about you are stored. If something is wrong, you can ask for it to be corrected. Stored entries are deleted again after a certain time. If you pay your bills on time, you normally have no problems with the ZEK.

gewusst: Besides the ZEK, Switzerland has the Consumer Credit Information Office, IKO for short, which is required by the Consumer Credit Act.
An entry with the ZEK is not automatically a bad thing: a loan that is running normally is stored there too.

teile.einleitung: **Progression** means: those who earn more pay a higher share of their income in tax. But the higher rate only applies to the additional part. That is why you always have more money left after a pay rise.
wichtigste: With progression, the tax rate rises with income.
The higher rate only applies to the part of income that is added.
A pay rise therefore always leads to more money after tax.
A distinction is made between the marginal tax rate and the average tax rate.
Direct federal tax and cantonal taxes are progressive.
The idea: those who have more can contribute a bigger share.

abschnitte.text: The word **progression** comes from Latin and means “moving forward”. With taxes it means: the higher the income, the higher the **tax rate**. Those who earn little pay a small share or nothing at all. Those who earn a lot pay a bigger share. In this way everyone should contribute to the state according to what they can afford.

You can imagine progression like a **staircase**. Income is divided into steps. A low rate applies to the bottom step, a slightly higher one to the next. If your wage rises, only the new part goes onto a higher step. The money on the lower steps continues to be taxed in the same way as before.

The **marginal tax rate** says how much tax is due on the next franc earned. The **average tax rate** says what percentage of the whole income goes in tax. The average rate is always lower than the marginal rate. Since the marginal rate never reaches 100 per cent, something from every pay rise stays in your pocket.

In Switzerland, the **income taxes** of the Confederation, cantons and municipalities are progressive. For **direct federal tax**, the highest rate is 11.5 per cent. Each canton has its own scale, which is why the burden varies from place to place. VAT, on the other hand, is not progressive; it applies equally to everyone.

gewusst: The mistaken idea “With a higher wage I end up with less” is not true with progression.
Because the cantons have their own scales, you pay different amounts of tax on the same income depending on where you live.

teile.einleitung: Church tax is a tax with which members of a recognised established church finance their church. In most cantons it is charged together with the other taxes. Anyone who leaves the church no longer has to pay church tax.
wichtigste: Church tax is paid by members of the recognised established churches.
In most cantons it is collected together with the municipal tax.
Anyone who leaves the church no longer pays church tax.
The established churches are mainly the Reformed and the Roman Catholic Church.
In many cantons, companies also pay a church tax.
The rules are slightly different in every canton.
The money pays for pastoral care, buildings and social services.

abschnitte.text: **Church tax** is a tax that benefits not the state but the churches. It is charged by the so-called **established churches**, meaning religious communities that a canton has officially recognised. Usually these are the Protestant Reformed, the Roman Catholic and the Christian Catholic Church. Some cantons such as Bern, Zurich or Basel-Stadt have also recognised Jewish communities.

In Switzerland, each canton itself decides how the state and the church work together. In most cantons there is a church tax, which is calculated together with the other taxes. In Geneva and Neuchâtel it is voluntary, and you only pay if you want to. In the canton of Vaud, the churches are supported directly from the general state funds.

Church tax is usually calculated as a percentage of the simple cantonal tax, similar to the municipality's **tax rate**. Those who earn more therefore also pay more church tax. The exact rate is set by the local **parish**. So it can even differ between neighbouring municipalities.

In Switzerland there is **freedom of religion**; nobody has to be a member of a church. Anyone who wants to leave writes a letter to the parish. From the date of leaving, you no longer have to pay church tax. From the age of 16, young people in Switzerland may decide about their religion themselves.

abschnitte.titel: What is the money used for?
abschnitte.text: With church tax, the churches pay their ministers, priests and other employees. They also use it to maintain church buildings, many of which are listed historic monuments. A large part goes into social tasks, such as youth work, help for poor people or pastoral care in hospitals and prisons. These services are often open to everyone, including non-members.

begriffe.erklaerung: A religious community that a canton officially recognises.
The church in a municipality, together with its members.
The right to choose for yourself whether you belong to a religion, and which one.
A figure with which a municipality sets how high its tax is.

gewusst: In many cantons, even companies pay church tax, although a company does not belong to any religion.
In Switzerland, the links between church and state vary greatly from canton to canton.
In Switzerland, you are considered old enough to decide about your religion at 16.

teile.einleitung: People who work often have costs because of their work, for example for getting to their workplace. Such costs are called work-related expenses. You may deduct them from your wages in your tax return.
wichtigste: Work-related expenses are costs that are necessary in order to earn your income.
They include commuting, meals away from home and tools for your job.
Work-related expenses are deducted from wages and lower your tax.
There are flat rates for many expenses.
The deductions are partly limited by the Confederation and the cantons.

abschnitte.text: **Work-related expenses** are costs you only have because you work. Without them, you could not earn your wages at all. One example is a train season ticket for getting to the office. Special work clothes or tools also count. Private spending such as holidays or clothes for your free time does not count.

A common deduction is for **commuting**, for example by train, bus or bike. If you cannot go home at lunchtime, you may deduct the cost of **meals away from home**. On top of that come **other work-related expenses**, such as specialist books, tools or a computer for work. Further training can also be deductible. There are separate rules for each kind.

For many expenses there is a **flat rate**. This is a fixed amount that you may deduct without receipts. If you have higher costs, you can prove them with receipts. For commuting, the Confederation and many cantons have set an **upper limit**. The exact amounts vary from canton to canton.

The idea behind it: you should only pay tax on the money you really have left. If you have to spend a lot for your work, you have less left over. That is why these costs are deducted from **income**. The **taxable income** becomes smaller, and so does the tax.

gewusst: Apprentices can also deduct work-related expenses, for example for getting to their training company.
If you cycle to work, in many cantons you can also make a deduction for it.

teile.einleitung: After you submit your tax return, the tax office sends an assessment notice. It states how much tax you have to pay. If it is wrong, you can challenge it by lodging an objection.
wichtigste: The assessment notice shows how the tax office has calculated the tax.
You can lodge an objection against a mistake.
The time limit for this is 30 days.
The objection must be in writing and must give reasons.
If you do not agree with the decision, you can take it further.

abschnitte.text: After you have submitted your **tax return**, the tax office checks the details. Then it sends the **assessment notice**. It shows the taxable income, the taxable assets and the amount of tax. Sometimes the tax office departs from your own figures. Then it is worth reading the notice carefully.

If you find a mistake, you can lodge an **objection**. This means you ask the tax office to review its decision again. The objection must be submitted to the tax office **in writing**. You must **explain** what is wrong and what would be correct. Receipts and records help to show your point of view.

You have **30 days** to lodge an objection. The time limit begins when you receive the notice. If you miss it, you normally can no longer challenge the decision. The notice then becomes **legally binding**, meaning final. That is why you should not leave post from the tax office lying around for long.

The tax office examines the objection and makes a **decision on the objection**. If it agrees with the taxpayer, the tax is corrected. If you still do not agree, you can take the decision to a **court**. What exactly this is called and how it works is regulated slightly differently in each canton. But often a mistake can already be cleared up with a phone call to the tax office.

gewusst: The objection procedure at the tax office is normally free of charge.
An objection can also lead the tax office to discover another mistake, which results in a higher tax.

teile.einleitung: The exact tax bill often only arrives long after the tax year. So that you do not have to pay everything at once, the tax office sends a **provisional bill** beforehand. It is an estimate; the exact accounts are settled later.
wichtigste: Provisional means temporary.
The provisional bill is usually based on the figures from the previous year.
It helps you pay your taxes spread over the year.
Later comes the final assessment with the final settlement.
Anyone who has paid too much gets money back; anyone who has paid too little pays the rest.
Many cantons allow payment in several instalments.

abschnitte.text: You only fill in the tax return for a year in the following year. After that, the tax office needs time to check everything. This check is called the **assessment**. So that the state still receives money regularly, it sends out a **provisional tax bill**. It is usually based on the last tax return.

With the provisional bill, you can pay your taxes **in instalments**, for example a part every month. That way you do not get a huge bill all at once at the end. Many cantons send payment slips or QR-bills for several instalments with it. In some cantons, if you pay early you are credited with a little **interest**.

When the assessment is finished, the **final bill** arrives. It compares what you have already paid with what you really owe. If you have paid too much, you get a **refund**. If you have paid too little, you must **pay the rest**. That is why it is worth taking a pay rise into account when saving for your taxes.

It is wise to put a fixed amount aside for your taxes every month. If your income changes a lot, you can ask the tax office to adjust the provisional bill. That way the estimate fits better, and there is no nasty surprise at the end.

gewusst: For employees with a Swiss passport, tax is usually not deducted from their wages; they pay it themselves. That is why the provisional bill is important.
Foreign employees without a permanent residence permit often pay tax at source, which is deducted directly from their wages.

teile.einleitung: A **price** tells you how much money you have to pay for goods or a service. In Switzerland, VAT is already included in the price shown. At the till you pay exactly the amount on the label.
wichtigste: The price is the amount you pay for something.
In Switzerland, prices must be shown in francs.
VAT is already included in the price shown.
In 2024 the standard VAT rate is 8.1 per cent.
A lower rate applies to food and books.
In some other countries, the tax is only added at the till.

abschnitte.text: When you buy something in a shop, a **price label** shows how much it costs. The price depends on what it costs to make, how many people want the goods and how much of them there is. If something is in demand and scarce, the price often rises. If there is a lot of it, it tends to fall.

In Switzerland, almost every price includes **VAT**. The shop collects this tax and passes it on to the **Confederation**. The till receipt often shows how much of it was tax. For the customer it makes no difference: the price on the label is the price she pays.

Not everything is taxed equally heavily. In 2024 the **standard rate** of 8.1 per cent applies, for example to toys or clothes. For everyday necessities such as **food**, medicines and books, there is a **reduced rate** of 2.6 per cent. For overnight stays in hotels, a special rate of 3.8 per cent applies.

In Switzerland there is a rule that prices must be shown as you will really pay them. This is called **price disclosure**. In the USA, on the other hand, the label often shows the price without tax. The **sales tax** is only added at the till, which is why you pay a little more there than the price shown.

gewusst: VAT is one of the Confederation's most important sources of income.
Part of VAT goes to the AVS.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, VAT has different **rates**, meaning percentages. How high they may be at most is written in the **Federal Constitution**. That is why the standard rate can only be raised with a popular vote.
wichtigste: Since 2024 the **standard rate** has been 8.1 per cent.
The **reduced rate** of 2.6 per cent applies, for example, to food and books.
For overnight stays a **special rate** of 3.8 per cent applies.
The maximum rates are written in the **Federal Constitution**.
An increase needs the approval of the **people and the cantons**.
The last increase was to finance the **AVS**.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland has three VAT rates. The **standard rate** of 8.1 per cent applies to most goods, such as clothes, toys or electronics. The **reduced rate** of 2.6 per cent applies to everyday necessities such as food, books and medicines. For hotel stays there is a **special rate** of 3.8 per cent.

How high VAT may be at most is written in the **Federal Constitution**. Every change to the Constitution must be put to the people. This is called a **mandatory referendum**. For an increase to be accepted, it needs a **popular majority** and a **majority of the cantons**, meaning a majority of the voters and of the cantons.

In 2022 the people and the cantons approved an increase to secure the **AVS**. That is why since 1 January 2024 the standard rate has been 8.1 per cent instead of 7.7 per cent. The other two rates were also raised slightly. The extra revenue goes to the AVS.

gewusst: Because the people have a say, VAT in Switzerland is much lower than in neighbouring countries.
When VAT was introduced in 1995, the standard rate was 6.5 per cent.

teile.einleitung: **Recycling** means collecting used materials and making something new from them. In Switzerland, municipalities often provide collection points for glass, aluminium and paper. This saves raw materials and energy.
wichtigste: With recycling, waste is processed into new raw materials.
Many municipalities run collection points for glass, aluminium, paper and cardboard.
Glass is sorted by colour: clear, green and brown.
You take PET bottles back to the shop.
Many municipalities charge a fee for the rubbish bag.
Electrical devices can be returned to the shop free of charge.

abschnitte.text: The word **recycling** comes from English and means “bringing back into the cycle”. Instead of throwing things away, you collect them separately. Then they are processed in factories. Old bottles become new bottles, waste paper becomes new paper. This means fewer **raw materials** are needed, and often less **energy** too.

Many municipalities have **collection points**. There you find containers for **glass**, sorted into clear, green and brown. Next to them there are often containers for **aluminium** and tin cans. In many places, paper and cardboard are collected from outside the house on certain days. The municipality organises this and pays part of it with fees or taxes.

Some things you take straight to the shop. You can put **PET bottles** into collection containers in almost all shops. Shops also take back **batteries** and **electrical devices**. For electrical devices, you already pay an **advance recycling fee** when you buy them. That is why returning them later costs nothing.

In many municipalities, every **rubbish bag** costs extra; this is called the **bag fee**. Anyone who recycles a lot needs fewer bags and saves money. Behind this is the **polluter pays principle**: whoever produces rubbish pays for it. The remaining rubbish is burned in a **waste incineration plant**, which uses it to produce electricity and heat.

gewusst: Glass can be melted down again and again without getting worse.
Making aluminium from scrap metal takes much less energy than making new aluminium from ore.

teile.einleitung: A **capital gain** happens when you sell something for more than you bought it for, for example shares. In Switzerland, such gains are in principle **tax-free** for private individuals. But there are important exceptions.
wichtigste: A capital gain is the profit from selling assets.
In Switzerland, gains on private shares are in principle tax-free.
Dividends, on the other hand, count as income and are taxed.
People who trade in securities professionally are treated differently.
Gains from selling land are charged with a separate tax.

abschnitte.text: If someone buys a **share** for 100 francs and later sells it for 150 francs, the **capital gain** is 50 francs. If you sell for less, there is a **capital loss**. For private individuals with private **movable assets** such as shares, this gain is tax-free. In return, losses cannot be deducted either.

A public limited company can pay out part of its profit to its shareholders as a **dividend**. This dividend is **income** and must be taxed. **Interest** on a savings account also counts as income. So only the gain from a rise in price when selling is tax-free.

Anyone who trades very often and on a large scale can be treated as a **professional securities dealer**. Then the gains are taxable. If you sell a **house** or a piece of land at a profit, the cantons charge a **property gains tax**. The taxation of capital gains is debated again and again in politics.

gewusst: The popular initiative that wanted to tax capital income more heavily was rejected at the ballot box in 2021.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who leaves a car in a public parking space often has to pay for it. This money is called a **parking fee**. It is the price for using space that belongs to everyone.
wichtigste: You pay a parking fee for parking on public land.
You pay at the parking machine, the parking meter or with an app.
A fee is paid for a particular service, here for the parking space.
In the blue zone you may park free of charge for a limited time with a parking disc.
Anyone who does not pay or parks for too long can get a fine.
The municipality or town decides how much parking costs.

abschnitte.text: Streets and squares usually belong to the municipality, the canton or the Confederation. Anyone who leaves their car there takes up space that others could otherwise use. That is why many towns charge a **parking fee**. It is not a tax but a **fee**: you only pay it if you really use the service. If you do not park, you pay nothing.

In the past there were mainly **parking meters** that took coins. Today there are often **parking machines** at the roadside that also accept cards. Many towns also allow you to pay with an **app** on your mobile phone. You state how long you want to stay and pay for that. If you stay longer, you have to pay more or move your car.

In Switzerland, colours on the ground show how you may park. In the **blue zone** you need a **parking disc**. There you may park for a limited time without paying any money. **White spaces** are often subject to a fee; a sign or the machine will say so. **Yellow markings** are usually reserved for special purposes, for example for delivery vans.

In towns there is little space and there are lots of cars. If parking costs something, cars do not stay parked all day. That way more people find a space, for example for a quick shopping trip. The income also helps the municipality to build, check and maintain parking spaces. Anyone who does not pay risks a **fixed penalty**.

gewusst: Multi-storey car parks often belong to private companies; they then charge a price rather than a fee.
In Switzerland, the parking disc for the blue zone is blue and shows your time of arrival.

teile.einleitung: Value added tax, VAT for short, is a tax that is included in the price of almost all goods and services. Every time you buy something, you pay it without noticing. Since 2024 the standard rate in Switzerland has been 8.1 per cent.
wichtigste: VAT is included in the price of many goods and services.
Since 2024 the standard rate has been 8.1 per cent.
For food, books and medicines, a reduced rate of 2.6 per cent applies.
For overnight stays in hotels, a special rate of 3.8 per cent applies.
VAT is the Confederation's most important source of income.
Children also pay VAT when they buy something.
VAT has existed in Switzerland since 1995.

abschnitte.text: **Value added tax** is a tax on consumption, meaning on shopping. It is one of the **indirect taxes**, because you do not pay it directly to the tax office but through the price. If you buy a chocolate bar, it contains a small amount of tax that the shop passes on to the state. A till receipt often shows how much VAT you have paid.

In Switzerland there are three rates. The **standard rate** of 8.1 per cent applies, for example, to clothes, toys, mobile phones and eating in restaurants. The reduced rate of 2.6 per cent applies to everyday necessities such as food, newspapers, books and medicines. For hotel stays there is a special rate of 3.8 per cent, to strengthen tourism.

The name comes from the fact that at each stage only the newly created value, the **value added**, is taxed. A farmer sells milk to a cheese dairy, the cheese dairy sells cheese to a shop, and the shop sells it to you. Each company pays VAT on its sales, but may deduct the VAT it paid itself when buying; this is called **input tax deduction**. In the end, the consumer bears the whole tax.

VAT brings the Confederation more than 20 billion francs every year. That makes it its largest source of income, ahead even of direct federal tax. Part of the money is set aside for particular tasks, for example the AVS. The increase from 7.7 to 8.1 per cent in 2024 was for precisely this purpose, financing the AVS.

Before VAT, Switzerland had the **turnover tax on goods**. The people voted in 1993 to introduce VAT, and it has applied since 1 January 1995. The rates may only be raised if the people and the cantons agree. Compared with neighbouring countries, Swiss VAT is very low; in Germany the standard rate is 19 per cent.

abschnitte.titel: Who has to account for it?
abschnitte.text: Companies must register with the Federal Tax Administration if they have a turnover of at least 100,000 francs a year. Smaller businesses can have themselves exempted. Certain services are exempt from the tax, such as visits to the doctor, school lessons and flat rents. Anyone who orders goods from abroad often pays import tax at the border, which is the same as VAT.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tax that is hidden in the price of goods.
The ordinary tax rate of 8.1 per cent.
The value that a company newly adds to a product.
VAT that a company pays when buying and is allowed to deduct.

gewusst: A croissant to take away has 2.6 per cent VAT; if you eat it in the café, the standard rate of 8.1 per cent applies.
Switzerland has one of the lowest VAT rates in Europe.
Tourists from abroad can, under certain conditions, have the VAT on larger purchases refunded.

teile.einleitung: The employment contract states how much someone earns. But less arrives in the bank account. The reason is **deductions**, for example for the AVS. Most people in Switzerland pay their taxes separately later.
wichtigste: The wage in the contract is called the **gross wage**.
What arrives in the account is called the **net wage**.
Contributions to the **AVS**, IV and EO, to unemployment insurance and usually to the **pension fund** are deducted from the wage.
For the AVS, the employer pays in the same amount as the employee.
Most people pay their taxes later with a bill from the **tax office**.
For some foreign workers, the tax is deducted directly from their wages.

abschnitte.text: The **gross wage** is the wage written in the employment contract. The employer deducts various contributions from it. What is left afterwards and transferred to the account is the **net wage**. On the monthly **payslip**, you can see exactly which amounts have been deducted.

A large deduction goes to the **AVS**, the old-age and survivors' insurance. On top of that come the disability insurance **IV** and the income compensation scheme **EO**. Money is also deducted for **unemployment insurance** and the **pension fund**. Usually insurance against accidents in your free time is added too. These contributions protect you when you get old, ill or unemployed.

In Switzerland, for most employees taxes are **not** deducted from their wages. You fill in a **tax return** every year and then get a bill from the tax office. Many people pay their taxes in instalments, so that it is not so much all at once. One exception is **tax at source**: for some people from abroad, the employer deducts the tax directly from their wages.

gewusst: For the AVS, the employer pays in the same amount as the employee.
Many companies pay a **13th month's salary**, usually in December.

teile.einleitung: In a **park** you can play, have a picnic or simply rest on a bench. To keep it nice, flowers have to be planted, grass mowed and benches repaired. This is usually paid for by the **municipality** with tax money.
wichtigste: Public parks belong to everyone and are usually **free**.
The **municipality** is usually responsible for looking after them.
This is paid for with **tax money**.
In towns, the **municipal parks department** often looks after parks and green spaces.
Parks are important for relaxation, play and for nature in the town.
Taking care helps to save costs.

abschnitte.text: A public **park** is open to everyone, no matter how old they are or how much money they have. You do not have to pay to get in. Many parks have playgrounds, fountains, lawns and benches. For people who live in a flat without a garden, parks are especially valuable.

Parks are usually looked after by **municipal** employees. In larger towns the department responsible is often called the **municipal parks department**. The gardeners plant flowers, prune trees, mow the grass and empty the bins. Craftspeople repair broken benches and play equipment.

Wages, tools, plants and materials cost money. Because the park belongs to everyone, the municipality pays for its upkeep with **tax money**. If people make the park dirty or damage things, more money has to be spent on repairs and clearing up. So anyone who takes care helps to make sure there is enough money for new things.

abschnitte.titel: Nature in the middle of town
abschnitte.text: Parks are not only there for people. Trees provide **shade** and cool the air on hot days. Birds, hedgehogs and insects find food and shelter there. That is why some municipalities let parts of the meadows grow longer, so that flowers can bloom for **bees**.

gewusst: On a hot summer's day, a big tree can evaporate a great deal of water and in this way cools its surroundings like a natural air conditioner.

teile.einleitung: A **cantonal hospital** is a large hospital that belongs to the canton or is run by it. In Switzerland, the **cantons** are mainly responsible for hospitals. They pay part of the costs with tax money.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, hospitals are mainly the task of the cantons.
The cantons pay part of the hospital costs with tax money.
For a stay in hospital, the canton pays at least 55 per cent.
The health insurance covers the rest.
Each canton keeps a hospital list.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, **health care** is largely the task of the cantons. They make sure there are enough **hospitals**. Many cantons have one or more **cantonal hospitals**. Today these are often independent companies, but they belong to the canton.

If someone has to stay overnight in hospital, this is called **inpatient treatment**. The costs are shared between the canton and the **health insurance**. The canton of residence pays at least **55 per cent**, the health insurance at most 45 per cent. The canton's share comes from **tax money**.

Each canton keeps a **hospital list**. It shows the hospitals whose treatments are paid for by basic health insurance. Private hospitals can also be on it. For very specialised treatments, the cantons work together, for example with the **university hospitals**.

gewusst: Switzerland has five university hospitals: in Basel, Bern, Geneva, Lausanne and Zurich.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who simply throws rubbish on the ground is **littering**. The German language has borrowed this English word. Clearing up costs municipalities a lot of money, and this money often comes from taxes.
wichtigste: **Littering** means carelessly throwing away rubbish or leaving it lying around.
Typical items are cigarette ends, drinks cans and packaging.
The **municipality** has to have the rubbish cleared away.
That costs money, which often comes from **taxes**.
In many cantons and municipalities you can get a **fine** for littering.
Rubbish belongs in the bin or in recycling.

abschnitte.text: With **littering**, rubbish is left where it does not belong: in the park, on the street, by the lake or in the woods. Often it is small things such as cigarette ends, chewing gum or takeaway packaging. On their own they seem harmless. But when many people do it, a big problem soon arises.

The rubbish that has been left behind is usually collected by **municipal** employees, for example from the **works depot** or street cleaning. This takes staff, vehicles and time. The municipality often pays these costs with **tax money**. Money that is needed for clearing up is then missing for other things such as playgrounds.

Rubbish in the countryside can harm animals. Animals mistake plastic for food or injure themselves on cans and broken glass. Some things take a very long time to break down. Cigarette ends contain toxic substances that can get into the water.

The easiest thing is to throw rubbish into the **bin** or take it home again. Many things such as PET bottles, aluminium cans or glass can be taken to **recycling**. Some municipalities have clean-up days on which school classes and clubs help. Anyone who helps saves the municipality money and keeps the place clean.

gewusst: In Switzerland, a large share of PET bottles and aluminium cans are collected and recycled.
In many municipalities you pay a **bag fee** for household rubbish: those who produce less rubbish pay less.

teile.einleitung: If you order from a foreign online shop, you often have to pay something when the goods are imported into Switzerland. The most important charge is import tax. It is the same as Swiss VAT.
wichtigste: Swiss VAT is also due on goods from abroad.
On import it is called import tax.
The Federal Office for Customs and Border Security collects it.
Very small tax amounts are not charged.
There are often also fees from the parcel service for customs clearance.

abschnitte.text: Many people order clothes, games or electronics from **foreign online shops**. When the parcel comes into Switzerland, it is declared at the border. **Import tax** may then be due. It is the same as the **VAT** that you also pay in Swiss shops. This way Swiss and foreign sellers are treated equally.

The **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security**, FOCBS for short, is responsible. The tax is calculated on the value of the goods, including transport costs. For most goods the standard rate of 8.1 per cent applies; for books, for example, the reduced rate. Very **small amounts** are exempt: if the tax is less than 5 francs, it is not charged. That is why you often pay nothing for cheap orders.

The **parcel service** often charges an extra **fee** for customs clearance. It deals with the customs declaration and pays the tax first itself. It then gets the money back from the recipient. This fee can sometimes be higher than the tax itself. That is why it is worth thinking about the total cost before ordering from abroad.

Since 2019, large foreign mail-order companies that sell a lot to Switzerland have had to charge **Swiss VAT** themselves. Then the tax is already included in the price. Switzerland abolished customs duties on industrial goods such as clothes in 2024. But there are still customs duties on many foods. Import tax remains in any case.

gewusst: Since 2024 there have been no customs duties in Switzerland on industrial products such as clothes, bikes or toys.
With a cheap order, the parcel service's fee can be higher than the tax itself.

teile.einleitung: Ticket tax is a tax on admission tickets, for example for the cinema, concerts or sports events. Some municipalities and cantons charge it, but many have abolished it.
wichtigste: Ticket tax is a tax on admission tickets.
It applies, for example, to cinema, concerts, theatre or sports events.
Municipalities or cantons charge it, not the Confederation.
It is usually included in the ticket price.
Many places have abolished ticket tax.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, a **Billett** is a travel ticket or an admission ticket. **Ticket tax** is a tax charged when you buy an admission ticket. It applies to events such as the **cinema**, **concerts**, theatre or football matches. It is usually a small percentage of the price. Sometimes it is also called an entertainment tax.

Ticket tax is not a federal tax. **Municipalities** or **cantons** can introduce it if their laws allow it. That is why it does not exist everywhere. In one town, a cinema ticket may include ticket tax, in the next town it may not. The money stays in the municipality or the canton.

If you buy a ticket, you usually do not notice the tax at all. The **organiser** adds it to the price and passes it on to the municipality. So the tax is included in the **ticket price**. Anyone who buys a concert ticket pays it at the same time. The organiser must then account exactly for how many tickets were sold.

In recent decades, many municipalities have **abolished** ticket tax. Critics say it makes culture and sport more expensive and causes a lot of work. Supporters think it brings in money for public tasks, for example for culture. Whether it exists is decided by the municipalities and cantons, sometimes by the voters too.

gewusst: The word “Billett” comes from French and originally meant a small slip of paper.
Whether a cinema ticket includes ticket tax can vary from place to place.

teile.einleitung: A savings account is a bank account intended for putting money aside for a longer time. Unlike an everyday account, you do not use it to pay in shops; you leave the money alone. In return you often get slightly higher interest.
wichtigste: A savings account is intended for putting money aside for a longer time.
The bank pays interest on your savings.
Savings accounts often have limits on how much you can withdraw at once.
The money is protected up to 100,000 francs per bank by the deposit protection scheme.
Many banks offer youth savings accounts with better interest rates.
With a standing order you can save automatically every month.
For goals such as a bike, a moped or a trip, a separate savings account helps.

abschnitte.text: A **savings account** is like a digital piggy bank at the bank. You pay money in and leave it there so that you can buy something bigger later or have a reserve. You do not normally pay bills or shopping with a savings account. In return the money is not always at hand, which helps with **saving**.

The bank pays **interest** on the money in the savings account. The interest is usually credited once a year, at the end of the year. How high it is depends strongly on the National Bank's key interest rate. In the years of negative interest rates there was almost no interest; today it is usually low, but higher than on a personal account.

With many savings accounts you may only withdraw a certain amount per month or year without giving notice; this is called the **withdrawal limit**. If you want more, you have to tell the bank a few weeks in advance. If you still withdraw more straight away, the bank may charge a fee. This way the money is more likely to stay put, and the bank can plan better.

Many Swiss banks offer **youth savings accounts**, often with a preferential interest rate and no fees. Parents, grandparents or godparents sometimes pay money into them on birthdays. With a **standing order**, you can automatically send a fixed amount every month from your personal account to your savings account. If you have a savings goal, you can see step by step how the amount grows.

Money in savings accounts is protected up to 100,000 francs per person and bank by the **deposit protection scheme**. On interest of more than 200 francs a year, banks in Switzerland deduct a **withholding tax** of 35 per cent, which you get back through your tax return. People who want to save for old age in the long term often also use pillar 3a. A savings account is safe, but the money grows only slowly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bank account for keeping money for a longer time and earning interest.
The maximum amount you may withdraw without giving notice.
A particularly good interest rate, for example for young people.
A tax that is deducted directly from the interest and paid back later.

gewusst: In the past, many children in Switzerland were given a little savings book in which every deposit was entered.
World Savings Day is celebrated every year at the end of October.
Because of inflation, money in a savings account can lose purchasing power if the interest is lower than inflation.

teile.einleitung: Many things are far too expensive for a single family, for example a school, a bridge or a hospital. But if everyone contributes something **together**, there is enough money. That is exactly how taxes work.
wichtigste: With taxes, many people together pay for expensive things for everyone.
A family on its own could not pay for a hospital or a school.
Taxes are like a big class kitty.
Everyone uses something that is paid for with taxes.
Thanks to taxes, all children can go to school.

abschnitte.text: Imagine your class is collecting for a **school trip**. Every child puts something into the **class kitty**. Nobody could pay for the coach on their own, but together it works. With **taxes** it is similar: each person gives a share, and something for everyone is paid for with it.

abschnitte.titel: Far too expensive on your own
abschnitte.text: A **hospital**, a **motorway** or a **school building** costs millions of francs. No family could pay for that. But if thousands or millions of people contribute something, enough comes together. Many small contributions add up to a large amount.

Some people think: “I never go to the swimming pool, so I don't need taxes.” But taxes pay for many different things. Even people who do not swim drive on **roads**, go to **school** or need a hospital at some point. And the **police** and the fire service are there for everyone.

In Switzerland, **compulsory schooling** is free for all children. That is only possible because it is paid for with taxes. Without taxes, families would have to pay for school themselves, and many could not afford it. In this way taxes make sure that **all children are allowed to learn**.

gewusst: According to the Federal Constitution, primary schooling in Switzerland is free of charge.
Children already pay taxes when they buy something: VAT is included in the price.

teile.einleitung: An agricultural tariff is a charge on farm products that are imported into Switzerland from abroad. It makes imported food such as meat more expensive and so protects Swiss farming.
wichtigste: A customs duty is a charge on goods brought in across the border.
There are still customs duties on many farm products such as meat.
The duties are meant to protect Swiss farming.
Since 2024, Switzerland no longer charges customs duties on industrial goods.
For some products there are quotas with a lower duty.
The duties are collected by the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security.

abschnitte.text: A **customs duty**, or tariff, is a charge you pay when goods are brought into a country across the border. In Switzerland, the **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security**, FOCBS for short, is responsible for this. The money from customs duties goes to the **Confederation**. But duties can also have another purpose: they make foreign goods more expensive. In this way they protect products from your own country.

In Switzerland, wages, land and many regulations are more expensive than in other countries. That is why Swiss meat, milk or vegetables often cost more to produce. Without protection, **farms** could hardly compete with cheap goods from abroad. **Agricultural tariffs** make imported farm products more expensive. This protection at the border is called **border protection**.

For many products such as meat there are so-called **tariff quotas**. A certain quantity may be imported at a lower duty. If more is imported, a much higher duty applies. This way enough goods come into the country when home production is not enough. At the same time, Swiss farming stays protected.

Agricultural tariffs are debated again and again in Switzerland. Supporters say they secure home **food production** and the work of farming families. Critics say they make food more expensive for consumers and make **free trade agreements** harder. Switzerland abolished customs duties on **industrial goods** such as bikes or clothes at the start of 2024. On agricultural products they still exist.

gewusst: Switzerland has free trade agreements with many countries, but farm products are often covered by special rules in them.
For shopping abroad, travellers have duty-free allowances, for example for meat.

teile.einleitung: The federal financial system sets out which taxes the Confederation may charge. One special feature: direct federal tax and VAT are only permitted for a limited time, currently until the end of 2035.
wichtigste: The federal financial system sets out which taxes the Confederation may charge.
It is laid down in the Federal Constitution.
Direct federal tax and VAT are time-limited.
The current time limit runs until the end of 2035.
The people and the cantons vote on an extension.

abschnitte.text: The Confederation cannot simply introduce any tax it wants. Which taxes it may charge is written in the **Federal Constitution**. These rules are called the **financial system**. It also sets **maximum rates**, meaning how high a tax may be at most. In this way the Confederation's power over taxes remains limited.

A special Swiss feature is the **time limit**. The Confederation may only charge **direct federal tax** and **VAT** for a certain period. At present, the permission runs until the **end of 2035**. After that, new permission is needed. These two taxes are the Confederation's most important sources of income.

For an extension, the Constitution has to be changed. That is why the **people and the cantons** vote on it. The last extension was accepted in 2018 by a large majority. The vote was also about continuing to allow the taxes without changing the maximum rates. In this way the people keep control over the most important federal taxes.

The time limit has **historical reasons**. In the past, the Confederation lived mainly on customs duties. Direct federal tax grew out of emergency measures in times of crisis. The cantons wanted to protect their own right to tax. That is why the Confederation was given this tax only for a limited time, and this idea still applies today.

gewusst: Without a new vote, from 2036 the Confederation would be allowed to charge neither VAT nor direct federal tax.
Only a few countries let their people vote on extending such important taxes.

teile.einleitung: Your teacher works at school every day and receives a wage for it. This wage comes from **tax money**. That way public school can be free for all children.
wichtigste: Teachers at public schools are paid with **tax money**.
The **cantons** and **municipalities** are responsible for compulsory schooling.
Lessons at public primary school are free for families.
This is written in the **Federal Constitution**.
Teachers also pay taxes themselves on their wages.

abschnitte.titel: Where do the wages come from?
abschnitte.text: Public school is organised by the **canton** and the **municipality**. They also pay teachers' wages. How the costs are divided between canton and municipality is slightly different in every canton. The money for this comes from the taxes paid by people and companies.

In Switzerland, every child has the right to adequate primary schooling that is **free of charge**. Free of charge means: families do not have to pay any school fees. That is why the general public pays for the teachers, the school buildings and many schoolbooks. Education should not depend on how much money a family has.

Teachers receive wages from tax money and in turn pay **taxes** themselves on these wages. These taxes pay for other things, such as roads, hospitals or the police. In this way many things are connected. Everyone contributes something and benefits from the services of the state.

gewusst: In Switzerland, teachers are trained at **universities of teacher education**.
Because the cantons are responsible for schools, Switzerland has 26 different school systems.

teile.einleitung: Fines and taxes are both money that you pay to the state. Even so, they are something quite different: a fine is a punishment, a tax is a normal contribution to shared tasks.
wichtigste: A fine is a punishment for doing something forbidden.
A tax is paid as a matter of course for shared tasks.
One example of a fine is for parking in the wrong place.
If you keep to the rules, you do not have to pay a fine.
Everyone pays taxes according to what they can afford.

abschnitte.text: A **fine** is a **punishment** in the form of money. You get one if you break a rule. Typical examples are **parking in the wrong place**, driving too fast or travelling on the train without a ticket. For minor offences there is often a **fixed penalty** with a set amount. If you keep to the rules, you pay no fine.
