A **tax** is not a punishment. Everyone who has income, buys something or owns assets pays it. With taxes, the state pays for **shared tasks**, for example schools, roads and hospitals. How much you pay usually depends on how much you earn or own. You do not get anything directly in return, but everyone benefits.

The most important difference lies in the **purpose**. A fine is meant to stop people from breaking rules. So it ensures **order** and safety. A tax is meant to give the state the **money** it needs for its tasks. The state would prefer it if nobody had to pay a fine.

Besides fines and taxes, there are also **fees**. You pay a fee for a particular service, for example for a new passport. You can challenge a fine if you think it is wrong. By the way, if you do not declare your taxes correctly, you can get a fine yourself. Then the fine is the punishment for the mistake with your taxes.

gewusst: The money from fines goes into the funds of the canton or municipality that imposed them.
In Switzerland people say “Busse” for a fine; in Germany they usually say “Bussgeld”.

teile.einleitung: A **money box**, called a “Sparkässeli” in Swiss German, is a small tin or figure in which you collect money at home. At the top it has a slot for coins and notes. The best-known money box is the piggy bank.
wichtigste: A money box is a container for collecting money at home.
It is often shaped like a pig; then it is called a piggy bank.
You put coins and notes in through the slot at the top.
Taking money out is harder, which helps you save.
When the money box is full, you can take the money to the bank.

abschnitte.text: Money boxes come in many shapes: as a tin, a house, an animal or a figure. But the best known is the **piggy bank**. In many places the pig is seen as a symbol of luck and wealth. Think of the German expression “Schwein haben”, which means “to be lucky”. That is why it goes well with saving.

Every money box has a **slot** at the top. Through it you put coins and folded notes. Getting them out is not so easy. Some money boxes have a lid at the bottom, others a key. With old clay piggy banks you even had to break the pig. Because you cannot get at the money quickly, you are less likely to spend it.

When the money box is full, you can take the money to the **bank** with your parents. There it is counted and paid into your **savings account**. At the bank it is safer than at home and earns interest. Many banks especially invite children to do this on **World Savings Day** at the end of October. Afterwards you can start filling the empty money box again.

gewusst: More than 2000 years ago there were already clay pots with a slot for collecting money.
“Sparkässeli” is a typically Swiss word; it comes from “Kasse”, meaning till or cash box.

teile.einleitung: **Rega** is the Swiss Air-Rescue service. It rescues people with helicopters and ambulance jets. You can reach it on the emergency number **1414**.
wichtigste: Rega rescues people from the air, mainly with helicopters.
Its emergency number in Switzerland is 1414.
Rega was founded in 1952.
It is a non-profit foundation.
It is financed mainly by its patrons.
With ambulance jets, it brings sick or injured people back from abroad.

abschnitte.text: Sometimes an accident happens in a place where no ambulance can get to, for example in the **mountains**. Then **Rega** helps with its **helicopter**. It quickly brings a doctor to the injured person. Then it flies the person to hospital. Rega is also called out for serious road accidents or emergencies at hospitals.

You can reach Rega on **1414**. In the operations centre, experts take the call and send the right helicopter. From abroad you dial a separate number that begins with the Swiss country code +41. There is also a **Rega app**, which sends your exact location when you raise the alarm.

Rega has several **bases** throughout Switzerland. This means a helicopter can reach almost any place in the country quickly. The crews are ready day and night. In the mountains they often work with a **rescue winch**: a rescuer is lowered on a cable when the helicopter cannot land.

Rega is a non-profit **foundation**. It receives hardly any money from the state but is supported mainly by its **patrons**. These are millions of people who pay a contribution every year. As a thank you, Rega can waive the costs of a mission for them if no insurance pays. In this way Rega belongs to some extent to the whole population.

gewusst: With its own ambulance jets, Rega brings patients back to Switzerland from all over the world.
Rega also helps farmers when an animal is injured in the mountains and has to be recovered.

teile.einleitung: A **safe** is a particularly thick and strong cabinet for money and valuables. It has strong steel walls and a secure lock. Banks often have whole vaults.
wichtigste: A safe is a very strong steel cabinet for valuables.
It protects against burglary and often against fire too.
Safes have strong locks with a key, a combination or an electronic code.
Banks have large vaults, often in the basement.
The German word “Tresor” means the same as “safe”.

abschnitte.text: A safe has **thick walls** made of steel, often with layers of concrete or other hard materials in between. The door is heavy and is locked with several bolts. It is opened with a key, a **combination** or an electronic code. Many safes are firmly fixed to the floor or the wall so that nobody can carry them away.

Banks often have a whole **vault**. It is frequently in the basement and has a huge round or rectangular steel door. Cash and valuables are stored inside, and the customers' **safe deposit boxes** are there too. Some vault doors have a **time lock**: they can only be opened at certain times, even if you know the code.

There are also smaller safes for the home. People keep jewellery, cash or important documents in them. Safes are divided into **security levels**, which show how well protected they are. The higher the level, the longer it takes burglars to break it open. Some models also protect against fire.

gewusst: The German word “Tresor” comes from French and means treasure.
Part of the Swiss National Bank's gold reserves is stored in well-protected vaults in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Direct federal tax is a tax charged by the Confederation on the income of people and on the profits of companies. But it is collected by the cantons, which may keep part of it for doing so.
wichtigste: Direct federal tax is charged on income and profits.
The cantons assess and collect it.
The cantons keep a share of the revenue.
Since 2020 this share has been 21.2 per cent.
The tax is progressive: those who earn more pay a higher rate.

abschnitte.text: Along with VAT, **direct federal tax** is the Confederation's most important source of income. It is charged on people's **income**. Companies pay it on their **profits**. It applies according to the same rules throughout Switzerland. Cantonal and municipal taxes, by contrast, differ from place to place.

The Confederation does not have its own tax office in every canton. That is why the cantons **assess** and **collect** direct federal tax. Assessing means calculating how much someone has to pay. Collecting means asking for the money. So you only fill in one tax return, for the municipality, canton and Confederation together.

For their work, the **cantons** may keep a **share** of the revenue. Since 2020 it has been **21.2 per cent**. Before that it was 17 per cent. The rest goes to the **Confederation**. With their share, the cantons also help to pay for fiscal equalisation between the cantons.

Direct federal tax is **progressive**. Those who earn little pay little or nothing at all. Those who earn more pay a higher percentage. For individuals, the **maximum rate** is 11.5 per cent. This limit is written in the **Federal Constitution**.

gewusst: Many people on low incomes pay no direct federal tax at all.
The Confederation may only charge direct federal tax for a limited time, currently until the end of 2035.

teile.einleitung: The alcohol tenth is part of the income from the tax on distilled drinks such as schnapps. The cantons receive it and must use it against addiction.
wichtigste: The Confederation charges a tax on spirits, meaning distilled drinks.
Ten per cent of the revenue goes to the cantons.
This share is called the alcohol tenth.
The cantons must use it against alcohol abuse and addiction.
Most of the revenue goes to the AVS and the disability insurance (IV).

abschnitte.text: **Spirits** are drinks with a lot of alcohol that are made by distilling, for example schnapps. The **Confederation** charges a special tax on such drinks. It is calculated per litre of pure alcohol. The tax makes strong alcoholic drinks more expensive. Beer and wine are not affected by this tax.

**Ten per cent** of the revenue from the tax on spirits goes to the **cantons**. Because this is a tenth, the share is called the **alcohol tenth**. The cantons cannot spend it as they wish. The Constitution states that they must use the money against the causes and effects of **addiction problems**. The largest part, 90 per cent, goes to the **AVS** and the **IV**.

abschnitte.titel: What the money is used for
abschnitte.text: With the alcohol tenth, the cantons support, for example, **prevention projects** in schools. They pay for advice centres that help people with addiction problems and their families. Leisure activities for young people can also be supported with it. The cantons report to the Confederation on what they have spent the money on. This is meant to make sure it really is used against **addiction**.

gewusst: The rule that one tenth goes to the cantons and must be used against addiction is written directly in the Federal Constitution.

teile.einleitung: Bern is the place where Switzerland's government and parliament work. But officially Bern is not called the capital, but the federal city.
wichtigste: Switzerland's government, the Federal Council, works in Bern.
Parliament also meets in Bern, in the Federal Palace.
Bern is officially called the federal city, not the capital.
Bern was chosen as the seat of government and parliament in 1848.
Bern is also the capital of the canton of Bern.

abschnitte.text: In **Bern**, the **Federal Council**, which is the government, and **Parliament** work. Many federal offices also have their headquarters there. Even so, Switzerland does not call Bern its capital but its **federal city**. The Federal Constitution does not name a capital. The idea was not to put one city above the others.

When the modern **federal state** was created in 1848, it needed a seat. Zurich and Lucerne were also possibilities. Parliament chose **Bern**. The city lay conveniently between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland. Other cities received other federal institutions instead; Zurich, for example, got the ETH.

At the heart of it is the **Federal Palace** with its great dome. The **National Council** and the **Council of States** meet inside. The Federal Council also has its rooms there. In front of the Federal Palace is the **Bundesplatz**, where children play in the water fountains in summer. The building can be visited on guided tours.

Bern is also the capital of the **canton of Bern**. The **old town** with its long arcades is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Its landmarks are the **Zytglogge**, an old clock tower, and the bear park by the River Aare. The bear is also on the city's coat of arms. The **River Aare** flows through the city, and many people swim in it in summer.

gewusst: Bern's old town has about six kilometres of arcades, so you can go shopping almost without getting wet when it rains.
The Federal Constitution does not name a capital; Bern became the seat of the federal authorities in 1848 through a decision of Parliament.

teile.einleitung: The **marginal tax rate** shows how much tax is due on the next franc you earn. It helps you understand how progression works. It is usually higher than the average tax rate.
wichtigste: The marginal tax rate is the tax rate on the last franc earned.
With progression, the rate rises in steps with income.
The marginal tax rate is higher than the average rate.
It shows how much of a pay rise goes in tax.
Even so, earning more almost always pays off.

abschnitte.text: Income tax in Switzerland follows the principle of **progression**. Income is divided into **bands**. For the lowest band you pay little or nothing, for higher bands a higher rate. The rate of the highest band you have just reached is the **marginal tax rate**.

The **average tax rate** shows what percentage of your whole income you pay in tax overall. Because the lower bands are cheaper, it is lower than the marginal tax rate. An example with made-up numbers: someone pays 12 per cent on average, but 25 centimes on every additional franc. Then the marginal tax rate is 25 per cent.

The marginal tax rate is useful when you are thinking about what a **pay rise** will bring. It also shows how much a **deduction** saves, for example a payment into pillar 3a. A common mistake: if you slip into a higher band, you only pay the higher rate on the additional part, not on your whole income.

gewusst: Because the Confederation, canton and municipality all charge tax, the marginal tax rate is made up of several parts.

teile.einleitung: Buses, trams, trains and postbuses are part of **public transport** (ÖV in German). It is there for everyone who buys a ticket. Because tickets do not cover all the costs, the Confederation, cantons and municipalities pay towards it with tax money.
wichtigste: Public transport includes buses, trams, trains, postbuses, boats and mountain railways.
Passengers pay part of the costs with their ticket.
The Confederation, cantons and municipalities pay the rest with tax money.
That is why a ticket is cheaper than the journey really costs.
Switzerland has one of the densest rail networks in the world.
Travelcards such as the Half Fare Travelcard or the GA make many journeys cheaper.

abschnitte.text: **Public transport** includes all means of transport that run to a **timetable** and can be used by everyone. These are **trains**, **trams**, **buses**, **postbuses**, **boats** and many **mountain railways**. In Switzerland they run even to small mountain villages. Without a car, you can get almost anywhere this way.

A train or bus costs a lot: vehicles, tracks, electricity, diesel and wages for the staff. With their **ticket**, passengers pay only part of this. Especially on lines with few passengers, for example in the countryside, the money is not enough. The **public sector** pays the rest with **tax money**.

In Switzerland, the **Confederation**, **cantons** and **municipalities** share the costs. The Confederation pays a large part of the **railway infrastructure**, meaning tracks, tunnels and stations. Cantons and municipalities order and help to pay for many regional bus and rail lines. In this way people in remote places can also travel cheaply.

Since 1982, trains in Switzerland have run on a **regular-interval timetable**. This means they leave at the same minute every hour, and the connections fit together. With the **Half Fare Travelcard** you pay only half the price on many routes. The **general travelcard**, **GA** for short, is valid on almost all routes in the country.

A full train or bus uses much less energy per person than lots of individual cars. That is why public transport is considered **environmentally friendly**. It also takes pressure off the roads and avoids traffic jams. That is one reason why the state supports it with tax money.

gewusst: People in Switzerland are among the keenest train travellers in Europe.
At 57 kilometres, the Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world. It was opened in 2016.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who is employed receives an important document from their employer every year: the **salary statement**. It shows how much you have earned in the whole year. You attach it to your tax return.
wichtigste: The salary statement is issued by the **employer**.
It is issued every year, usually at the beginning of the new year.
It shows the **gross wage**, the contributions deducted and the **net wage**.
The contributions include AVS, IV, EO, unemployment insurance and the pension fund.
Expenses and other benefits are also shown on it.
You attach the salary statement to your **tax return**.

abschnitte.text: The **salary statement** is a certificate of the wages for a whole year. Every employer must issue one for all employees, including apprentices and part-time staff. It has the same form throughout Switzerland. That way the tax office can easily check the details.

First comes the **gross wage**, meaning the full wage before deductions. Then come the contributions to **AVS, IV, EO and unemployment insurance** and to **occupational pension provision**, meaning the pension fund. This gives the **net wage**. Expenses, a company car or contributions to further training may also be noted.

You copy the figures from the salary statement into your **tax return**. Then you attach the salary statement or upload it online. Anyone who has had several jobs receives a separate salary statement from each employer. You should keep them all safe.

gewusst: The salary statement also has a box showing whether the employer offers a canteen or free meals, because this affects the deduction for meals.
When you look for a job or want to rent a flat, you are sometimes asked for your salary statement.

teile.einleitung: Inheritance tax is a tax on money or property that someone inherits after a person has died. In Switzerland, the cantons decide for themselves whether and how much inheritance tax is charged. That is why there are big differences depending on where the person who died lived.
wichtigste: Inheritance tax is charged on assets that are inherited after a death.
In Switzerland it is a cantonal tax; the Confederation does not charge one.
Spouses pay no inheritance tax in any canton.
In most cantons, children also pay no inheritance tax when they inherit from their parents.
Distant relatives and unrelated people usually pay the highest rates.
What normally counts is the canton in which the person who died last lived.
A similar tax on gifts made during a person's lifetime is called gift tax.

abschnitte.text: When a person dies, their assets pass to other people; this is called an **inheritance**. It includes, for example, money in accounts, a house, jewellery or shares. Who receives something is set out by law or in a **will**. The people who receive something are called heirs.

In Switzerland, each canton may decide for itself whether to charge inheritance tax. The canton of Schwyz has no inheritance or gift tax at all, and the canton of Obwalden has also abolished it. The other cantons tax inheritances, but with very different rules. Usually the canton where the person who died lived is responsible; for land, it is the canton in which the land is located.

How high the tax is depends mainly on how closely you were related to the person who died. Spouses are exempt everywhere, and children are too in most cantons. Brothers and sisters, nieces, friends or neighbours, on the other hand, often pay a high percentage. There is also often a **tax-free allowance**, meaning an amount that remains free of tax.

Anyone who gives away large sums during their lifetime often has to pay **gift tax**. In most cantons it works according to the same rules as inheritance tax. So you cannot simply avoid inheritance tax by giving everything away before you die. Small presents such as birthday money are of course not affected.

Inheritance tax is debated again and again in Switzerland. Supporters think that large fortunes can be distributed more fairly in this way. Opponents fear that rich families and companies will move abroad. Proposals for a national inheritance tax on very large fortunes have so far been rejected in **popular votes**, for example in 2015.

begriffe.erklaerung: Assets that pass to other people after a person's death.
A written statement in which someone sets out who will get what after their death.
An amount on which you do not have to pay tax.
A tax on large gifts received during the giver's lifetime.

gewusst: Anyone who dies in the canton of Schwyz leaves their heirs no inheritance tax, however large the fortune.
In some cantons, unrelated heirs pay more than a third of the inheritance in tax.
Clubs and charitable organisations can also inherit and are then usually exempt from the tax.

teile.einleitung: With a **signature** you show that you agree to something. You write your name in your own personal way. At the bank, signatures are needed, for example, to open an account or for contracts.
wichtigste: A signature is your own name, written in a personal way.
Anyone who signs confirms that they want something and agree to it.
At the bank you sign, for example, when you open an account.
A signature can be legally binding.
You only sign what you have read and understood.
Today there are also electronic signatures.

abschnitte.text: For a signature, you write your name **by hand** and always as similarly as possible. Over time, every person develops their own way of signing. That is why a signature is very personal. It shows that this particular person is confirming something. Nobody may copy another person's signature.

When you **open an account**, you sign a contract with the bank. It contains the rules for the account. In the past you also left a **specimen signature**. The bank could use it later to compare whether an instruction really came from the right person. Signatures are also needed for a power of attorney or a loan.

If you sign something, you are often **bound** by it. A signed contract can be enforced by law. That is why you read a document carefully before signing it. If you do not understand something, you ask. For children and teenagers, the parents usually sign important contracts as well.

Today a lot is done online. For this there is the **electronic signature**. In Switzerland, a qualified electronic signature is in principle treated the same as a handwritten signature. For many banking transactions, a confirmation in the app is also enough, for example with a code or a fingerprint.

gewusst: The signature of a famous person is called an autograph, and some people collect them.
Swiss banknotes carry the signatures of people in charge at the National Bank.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who owns a car or a motorbike with a number plate pays a tax to the canton every year. It is called the **motor vehicle tax** or road tax. How high it is depends on the canton and the vehicle.
wichtigste: The **motor vehicle tax** is a **cantonal** tax.
It is charged every year for vehicles with a **number plate**.
It must be paid by the vehicle's **registered keeper**.
Each canton has its own rules and rates.
The amount depends, for example, on weight, engine capacity or power.
Some cantons give discounts for environmentally friendly vehicles.

abschnitte.text: The **motor vehicle tax** belongs to the **cantons**. Anyone who wants to register a car, a motorbike or a lorry must register it with the **road traffic office** and receives a **number plate**. After that, the registered keeper gets a bill for the tax every year. Without a number plate, it is not due.

Each canton decides for itself how it calculates the tax. Some base it on the vehicle's **weight**, others on the engine's **capacity** or on its **power**. Some also take CO2 emissions into account. That is why the same car can cost very different amounts in two cantons.

Several cantons give discounts for economical or **electric** vehicles. In this way they want to encourage environmentally friendly cars. The cantons often use the money from the motor vehicle tax to build and maintain their **roads**.

gewusst: The motor vehicle tax is not the same as the motorway vignette: the vignette goes to the Confederation.
Anyone who hands in their number plate to the road traffic office for a while usually pays no tax during that time.

teile.einleitung: Pillar 3a is a voluntary savings account for old age. Anyone with earned income can pay in an amount every year and deduct it from their taxes. That way you save for later and save tax at the same time.
wichtigste: Pillar 3a is part of the third pillar of pension provision.
Only people with earned income on which AVS contributions are due can pay in.
Apprentices with a wage can already pay in too.
The payments can be deducted from taxable income.
There is a yearly maximum amount.
When you draw it, the money is taxed separately at a lower rate.

abschnitte.text: Pension provision in Switzerland stands on **three pillars**. The first pillar is the **AVS**. The second is the **pension fund** through your employer. The third is **private saving**. **Pillar 3a** is part of this: a restricted savings account that the state supports with tax advantages.

Only people with **earned income** that is subject to the AVS may pay into pillar 3a. So **apprentices** with a wage can already pay in too. Without earned income it is not possible. There is a **maximum amount** per year. In 2025 it was 7258 francs for employees with a pension fund.

Whatever you pay in can be deducted from your **taxable income**. Because of **progression**, this is especially worthwhile with a high income. The deduction lowers income at the point where the tax rate is highest. The higher the income, the bigger the saving per franc paid in.

The money is **tied up**. You can draw it at the earliest five years before the AVS age. There are exceptions, for example for buying your own home, for becoming self-employed or when emigrating. When you draw it, the money is taxed **separately** from your other income and at a **reduced rate**. All in all, you usually still save tax.

gewusst: You can have several 3a accounts and draw them at different times, which can save tax.
The money in pillar 3a can also be invested in funds instead of just being kept in an account.

teile.einleitung: At the **municipal assembly**, the voters of a municipality meet. There they decide together what the municipality's money will be spent on. This is direct democracy right on your doorstep.
wichtigste: In many small municipalities, adults have their say at the municipal assembly.
The voters of the municipality may take part.
Decisions are made there, for example, on a new school building.
The budget and the tax rate are also often decided at the assembly.
Larger towns have a municipal parliament instead of an assembly.

abschnitte.text: The **municipal assembly** usually takes place a few times a year, often in the evening in a sports hall or a hall. All the **voters** of the municipality may come. They can ask questions, make proposals and join in the discussion. At the end there is a vote, often by **raising hands**.

An important item is the **budget**, meaning the plan for income and spending in the following year. The **tax rate** is often set too. Other topics are large items of spending, for example a new **school building**, a road or a fire engine. The **annual accounts** are also approved.

It is mainly small and medium-sized municipalities that have a municipal assembly. In big cities there would be too many people for one hall. There the voters elect a **municipal parliament**, which makes the decisions. Important questions then go to a **ballot vote**. At cantonal level, the **Landsgemeinde** in Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden works in a similar way.

gewusst: Often only a small share of the voters take part in the municipal assembly.
In many municipalities there are drinks and snacks after the assembly, where people can carry on the discussion.

teile.einleitung: Tax at source is a tax that is deducted directly from wages before the money arrives in the account. It mainly affects foreign employees without a permanent residence permit. The employer then transfers the tax to the tax office itself.
wichtigste: With tax at source, the tax is deducted directly from wages.
It applies mainly to foreign employees without a permanent residence permit C.
Many cross-border commuters also pay tax at source.
The employer calculates the tax and transfers it to the canton.
The tax rate depends on the wage, marital status and number of children.
Anyone who earns more than 120,000 francs a year must also fill in a tax return.
Swiss citizens, by contrast, pay their income tax through the tax return.

abschnitte.text: The word **source** here means the place where the income arises, in other words the wages from the employer. With **tax at source**, the tax is already deducted there, before you receive the money. On the payslip you can see the deduction next to the AVS and other contributions. Tax at source replaces the federal, cantonal and municipal tax on these wages.

Tax at source is paid mainly by foreign people who work in Switzerland and do not yet have a **permanent residence permit** C. This includes many people with a B residence permit. **Cross-border commuters**, who live abroad and travel to work in Switzerland every day, also often pay tax at source. If someone is married to a Swiss citizen or has the C permit, the normal procedure applies.

The canton sets **scales** that depend on the wage, marital status and number of children. The employer looks up the right scale and deducts the amount every month. Then it transfers the money to the cantonal tax office. This is work for the employer, but it receives a small payment for it.

New rules have applied since 2021. Anyone who is liable to tax at source and earns more than 120,000 francs a year must also fill in a tax return; this is called a **subsequent ordinary assessment**. People who earn less can apply for it voluntarily, for example to claim deductions for pillar 3a. The tax at source already paid is then credited.

Tax at source makes sure that people who may only stay in Switzerland for a short time also pay tax. Without it, someone could leave the country before the tax bill arrived. Tax at source is also charged on artists, sportspeople or speakers from abroad who only come for one appearance. Switzerland has agreements with many neighbouring countries so that nobody has to pay tax twice.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tax that is deducted directly from wages.
Permit C, which allows foreigners to stay in Switzerland permanently.
A person who lives in a neighbouring country and works in Switzerland.
A treaty between states so that people do not pay tax twice.

gewusst: More than 300,000 cross-border commuters work in Switzerland, mainly in Ticino, Geneva and Basel (as of 2023).
Prize money won by foreign sportspeople at tournaments in Switzerland can also be subject to tax at source.
A special agreement applies to cross-border commuters from Italy; it was renewed in 2024.

teile.einleitung: The **police** make sure that everyone keeps to the law and can live safely. They help with accidents, in traffic and when someone is in danger. They are paid for by the state with tax money.
wichtigste: The police protect safety and order for everyone.
Their wages are paid by the state with tax money.
In Switzerland, the police are mainly a matter for the cantons.
Many cities also have their own city police.
You can reach the police emergency number on 117.
Anyone who needs help does not normally have to pay for it.

abschnitte.text: The police have many tasks. They direct **traffic**, record **accidents** and check whether everyone is keeping to the rules. They help people who are in danger and solve **crimes**, for example a theft. Police officers also visit schools and explain how to cross the road safely.

In Switzerland, the police are mainly the task of the **cantons**. Each canton has its own **cantonal police**. Big cities such as Zurich or Bern often also have **city police**. The Confederation has the **Federal Office of Police**, fedpol for short. It deals with cases that involve several cantons or other countries.

The police are there for everyone, including people who have little money. That is why they are paid for with **tax money**. If everyone only paid when they needed help, some people could not afford it. So everyone pays a little, and everyone is protected. This is called a **public task**.

If someone is in danger or a crime is happening, you dial **117**. The call is free and works even without credit on your mobile phone. It is important to say calmly **who** is calling, **where** something has happened and **what** has happened. You must never call the emergency number for fun, because then help might be missing for someone who urgently needs it.

gewusst: The European emergency number 112 also works in Switzerland.
In Switzerland, police officers do a training course of about two years and finish with a federal professional certificate.

teile.einleitung: Taxes are divided into **direct** and **indirect taxes**. Indirect taxes are included in the price of goods and services. You often pay them without noticing.
wichtigste: Indirect taxes are included in the price of goods.
Examples are VAT, tobacco tax and the mineral oil tax on petrol.
Direct taxes are charged on income or assets.
In Switzerland, indirect taxes are charged mainly by the Confederation.
VAT is the Confederation's most important source of income.

abschnitte.text: With a **direct tax**, you pay directly to the tax office, calculated according to your own **income** or **assets**. With an **indirect tax**, the company that sells something pays first. It adds the tax to the price. So in the end it is the customer who pays.

The best-known indirect tax is **value added tax**, VAT for short. It is included in almost everything you buy. In 2024 the standard rate was **8.1 per cent**. A lower rate applies to food, books and medicines. There is a separate rate for overnight stays in hotels.

On **petrol** and diesel, the Confederation charges the **mineral oil tax**. Part of it is used for roads. There are also special taxes on **tobacco**, beer and distilled drinks. These are also meant to help people smoke and drink less. When goods are imported, **customs duties** are sometimes added too.

Indirect taxes are easy to collect, because the companies account for them. But they affect everyone equally, no matter how much someone earns. For people with little money, this takes up a bigger share of their income. That is why a **reduced rate** applies to everyday necessities such as food.

gewusst: VAT has existed in Switzerland since 1995; before that there was a turnover tax on goods.
Part of VAT goes to the AVS.

teile.einleitung: In a library you can borrow books, comics, films and games. For children this is often free or very cheap. This is possible because municipalities and cantons support libraries with tax money.
wichtigste: Many libraries are supported by the municipality with tax money.
That is why borrowing is often free or very cheap for children.
There are municipal, school, cantonal and university libraries.
The Swiss National Library in Bern belongs to the Confederation.
Libraries are an example of how taxes benefit everyone.

abschnitte.text: A **library** collects books and other media. You can read them there or **borrow** them for a few weeks. Today, besides books, there are also audiobooks, films, games and e-books. Many libraries also offer places to study and events such as story times. Everyone may use them, no matter how much money they have.

A library costs money: for rooms, books, computers and staff. The fees paid by readers cover only a small part. Most of it is usually paid by the **municipality** out of its **taxes**. Sometimes the canton, associations or donations help too. In this way everyone pays together for something that is open to everyone.

Besides the **municipal library**, there are **school libraries** in many school buildings. The cantons often run a **cantonal library**. Universities and colleges have their own libraries for research. The Confederation runs the **Swiss National Library** in Bern. It collects works that have been published in Switzerland or about Switzerland.

Taxes are often invisible, because you do not see directly what happens to them. The library is a good example where you can see it. With taxes, people pay for things that one person alone could hardly buy. Thousands of books for yourself alone would be far too expensive. But paid for together, everyone can benefit from them.

gewusst: The Swiss National Library was founded in 1895.
Many libraries lend e-books, which you read on a tablet and which disappear by themselves after the loan period.

teile.einleitung: The **final bill** is the definitive tax bill for a year. Before that, you usually pay according to a provisional bill. If that was too high, you get back what you paid too much, often even with interest.
wichtigste: The tax office usually sends a provisional bill first.
It is often based on the figures from the previous year.
After the tax return has been checked, the assessment follows.
After that you receive the definitive final bill.
Anything paid too much is refunded or credited.
Many cantons pay credit interest on amounts paid too much.

abschnitte.text: The taxes for a year are only fixed once the year is over and the **tax return** has been checked. So that people do not have to pay everything at once, many cantons send a **provisional bill** beforehand. It is usually based on the figures from the **previous year**. You can pay in instalments; these are also called **payments on account**.

After you submit it, the **tax office** checks the tax return. It decides how high the taxable income and assets are. This decision is called the **assessment**. If you do not agree, you can lodge an **objection** within 30 days. After that comes the definitive **final bill**.

In the final bill, the amounts already paid are compared with the real tax. If you have paid **too little**, you must pay the rest. If you have paid **too much**, the money is **refunded** or **offset** against the next bill. In this way everything adds up to the exact franc in the end.

Many cantons pay **credit interest** on taxes paid too much. So paying early is rewarded. On the other hand, they often charge **equalisation interest** or **default interest** if you have paid too late or too little. The exact rules and interest rates vary from canton to canton.

gewusst: Some cantons give a small discount if you pay your taxes early in one go.
If your situation changes a lot, for example with a new wage, you can have the provisional bill adjusted.

teile.einleitung: The **school building** is the building where you learn. In Switzerland, compulsory schooling is paid for with tax money. Usually the municipality takes care of building and maintaining the school building.
wichtigste: Compulsory schooling in Switzerland is free of charge.
This is written in the Federal Constitution.
The cantons regulate compulsory schooling.
The municipalities usually build and maintain the school buildings.
The voters often vote on a large new building.
A school building includes a sports hall, a playground and often a library.

abschnitte.text: A school building does not only have **classrooms**. It often also has a **sports hall**, a **playground**, rooms for crafts and music and sometimes a **library**. A **caretaker** makes sure that everything is clean and in good order. Many school buildings are also used by clubs in the evening.

The **Federal Constitution** states that all children are entitled to **adequate primary schooling that is free of charge**. Free of charge means: parents do not have to pay school fees. The costs are borne by the **municipalities** and **cantons** with tax money. In this way all children can go to school, no matter how much money their family has.

When more children live in a municipality, more space is needed. Then the municipality plans a **new building** or an extension. There is often an **architectural competition**, in which the best project is chosen. Because a school building can cost many millions of francs, the voters usually vote on the **building loan**.

A school building should last for many decades. That is why it has to be **renovated** regularly, for example with new windows or a new roof. Children can help too, by treating tables, walls and equipment carefully. Every repair costs money that everyone pays with their taxes.

gewusst: Many new school buildings in Switzerland are built of wood and produce their own electricity with solar panels.
Some school buildings are more than a hundred years old and are listed historic monuments.

teile.einleitung: The **rubbish fee** is the amount you pay for getting rid of your rubbish. In many municipalities it is included in the price of the official rubbish bags. Those who produce more rubbish pay more.
wichtigste: With the official rubbish bags, you pay a fee for disposal.
Those who produce more rubbish pay more.
This is called the polluter pays principle.
Often there is also a basic charge per household.
In Switzerland, rubbish is burned, and energy is produced in the process.

abschnitte.text: The Huber family buys their municipality's **official rubbish bags** in the shop. Other bags are not collected. The **rubbish fee** is included in the price. Instead of bags, some municipalities use **tags** to stick on or weigh the rubbish containers.

The **polluter pays principle** means: whoever causes costs should pay for them. It is written in the Swiss **Environmental Protection Act**. If you throw away a lot, you need more bags and pay more. If you sort **paper, glass, PET and compost**, you need fewer bags. So it pays to avoid rubbish.

The rubbish is picked up by the **rubbish collection** and taken to a **waste incineration plant**. There it is burned. The heat is used to produce **electricity** and district heating for homes. The fees pay for collection, incineration and collection points. Many municipalities also charge a **basic charge** per household.

gewusst: Since 2000, combustible rubbish may no longer be dumped in landfill sites in Switzerland; it must be burned.

teile.einleitung: Some taxes you pay without noticing. They are included in the **price** of goods and services. These are **indirect taxes**; the most important example is VAT.
wichtigste: With indirect taxes, you do not get your own tax bill.
The tax is included in the price.
The seller collects the tax and passes it on to the state.
VAT is the most important indirect tax in Switzerland.
Other examples are tobacco tax and the mineral oil tax on petrol.
Everyone pays the same rate when buying, no matter how much they earn.

abschnitte.text: When you buy something in a shop, a tax is already included in the price. You pay it at the till, but you do not get a separate bill from the tax office. That is why it is called **indirect**. The shop collects the money and passes it on to the state. The receipt often shows how much of it was tax.

**Value added tax**, **VAT** for short, is the most important indirect tax in Switzerland. Since 2024 the **standard rate** has been 8.1 per cent. For food, books and medicines the **reduced rate** of 2.6 per cent applies. For overnight stays in hotels there is a special rate of 3.8 per cent. VAT goes to the Confederation.

On **petrol and diesel** there is the **mineral oil tax**. Cigarettes are charged with **tobacco tax**, and schnapps with a tax on alcohol. Such taxes are also meant to help people buy less of unhealthy things. Customs duties on imported goods also count as indirect charges.

With a **direct tax** such as income tax, you get your own bill, and those who earn more pay more. With indirect taxes, everyone pays the same rate when buying. Those who buy a lot pay more tax. The state needs both kinds to pay for its tasks.

gewusst: VAT has existed in Switzerland since 1995. Before that there was a turnover tax on goods.
Compared with EU countries, VAT in Switzerland is very low.

teile.einleitung: **Customs duties**, or tariffs, are charges on goods brought into a country across the border. Since 1 January 2024, Switzerland no longer charges customs duties on **industrial goods** such as bikes, clothes or toys. But VAT on imports still exists.
wichtigste: A customs duty is a charge on goods imported into a country.
Since 1 January 2024 there have been no more industrial tariffs in Switzerland.
This affects, for example, bikes, clothes, cars and electronics.
There are still customs duties on many agricultural products.
VAT on imports remains.

abschnitte.text: When goods come into Switzerland from abroad, they are **cleared through customs** at the border. In the past, a **customs duty** had to be paid on many goods. Customs duties make foreign goods more expensive. In this way they can protect home-grown products, but they also make shopping more expensive.

Parliament decided to abolish **industrial tariffs**. This has applied since **1 January 2024**. It affects industrial products such as **bikes**, clothes, shoes, furniture or household appliances. Companies are meant to be able to buy more cheaply as a result, and some goods may also become cheaper for consumers.

There are still customs duties on many **agricultural products** such as meat, dairy products or vegetables. This is meant to protect Swiss farming. In addition, **VAT** is almost always due on imports. That is why anyone who shops abroad still has to pay something at the border for larger amounts.

gewusst: For shopping abroad there is a value-free limit: up to a certain amount per person you do not have to pay any VAT.
The customs authority is now called the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security.

teile.einleitung: In parks, on squares and at bus stops there are litter bins. The municipality puts them up and has them emptied regularly so that public spaces stay clean.
wichtigste: Litter bins in the park are emptied by municipal staff.
This is paid for, among other things, with taxes.
Anyone who simply leaves rubbish lying around is littering.
In many places, littering can be punished with a fine.
Things that can be sorted are better taken to a collection point.

abschnitte.text: In the park, by the playground or at the railway station there are **litter bins**. The **municipality** puts them where lots of people pass by. Staff from the **municipal works depot** or road maintenance empty them regularly. In good weather, when lots of people are out having picnics, they fill up especially quickly. Then they have to be emptied more often.

Putting up and emptying litter bins costs money. The municipality pays for staff, vehicles and disposal. This money comes, among other things, from the **taxes** paid by the residents. In this way everyone benefits from clean streets and parks. Clean squares are nicer and safer, for animals too.

When someone simply throws rubbish on the ground or leaves it lying around, this is called **littering**. Clearing it up costs municipalities a lot of money and work. Rubbish in the countryside can harm animals, for example if they eat plastic. In many cantons and municipalities you can get a **fine** for littering. If a bin is full, it is better to take your rubbish home with you.

In some places there are litter bins with separate openings, for example for **PET** and aluminium cans. Anything that can be recycled belongs in the right opening or at a **collection point**. Large amounts of household rubbish do not belong in public bins. They go into the fee bag for rubbish collection. That way the system stays fair for everyone.

gewusst: In many Swiss municipalities there are clean-up days every year, when school classes and clubs collect rubbish in the countryside.

teile.einleitung: With a bank transfer, you send money from one bank account to another without any cash changing hands. This is how you pay bills or the rent, or send money to family and friends. For the money to arrive correctly, you need the recipient's IBAN.
wichtigste: With a bank transfer, you send money from one account to another.
For this you need the recipient's IBAN and name.
Transfers are usually made in online banking or in the banking app.
Within Switzerland, the money usually arrives on the same or the next bank working day.
Since 2024, Switzerland has also had instant payments that take a few seconds.
Once a transfer has been carried out, it can hardly be reversed.
Regular transfers can be set up as a standing order.

abschnitte.text: A **bank transfer** is an instruction to the bank to send an amount of money from your own account to another account. The money is only moved as a number; no cash changes hands. A **debit** appears in your own account and a credit in the recipient's. Today, transfers are the most common way of paying bills.

abschnitte.titel: What do you need for it?
abschnitte.text: For a transfer you need the recipient's **IBAN**, their name and the amount. Often you also add a message, such as the invoice number. With a QR-bill you do not have to type anything in, because the app reads all the details from the code. Before you confirm the payment, you should **check** everything carefully.

Within Switzerland, the money usually reaches the recipient on the same or the next **bank working day**. Behind the scenes, this runs through the SIC payment system, which the National Bank operates together with the company SIX. Since August 2024 there have been **instant payments** in Switzerland: the money arrives within seconds, even at the weekend. Transfers abroad can take longer and sometimes cost fees.

For transfers within Europe there is the **SEPA area**, which Switzerland also takes part in. Payments in euros go through quickly and cheaply this way. For countries further away, the worldwide network **SWIFT** is often used, through which banks exchange messages. Part of the amount can be lost in fees and exchange rates.

Once a transfer has been carried out, you usually cannot get it back. That is why fraudsters often use tricks, such as fake bills or messages from supposed friends in trouble. Paying **in advance** by transfer when buying online from strangers is also risky. If in doubt, you call the person or company on a number you know before sending money.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sending money from one account to another.
The international account number that you need for transfers.
A day on which banks process payments, usually Monday to Friday.
A transfer that arrives within a few seconds.

gewusst: The Swiss payment system SIC processes payments worth many billions of francs in a single day.
A Swiss IBAN has 21 characters and always begins with CH.
In the past, you filled in a paper form for a transfer and took it to the bank or post office.

teile.einleitung: Beer tax is a federal tax on beer. Breweries in Switzerland and companies that import beer pay it. In the end it is included in the price of every beer.
wichtigste: Beer tax is a federal tax.
Breweries and importers pay it.
It is included in the price of every beer.
The amount depends on the strength of the beer.
The Federal Office for Customs and Border Security collects the tax.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are taxes on certain goods, which are called **excise taxes**. One of them is **beer tax**. It is not charged separately in the shop. The **brewery** pays it to the Confederation and includes it in the price. So anyone who buys a beer pays it indirectly.

The tax depends on the quantity and the **strength** of the beer. What is measured is the content of the wort from which the beer is brewed. Strong beer is taxed more highly than light beer. Small breweries get a **reduction**. This is meant to give small businesses a good chance too.

The **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security**, FOCBS for short, is responsible. Beer from Switzerland is taxed at the brewery. Beer from abroad is taxed on **import**. In this way all beer is treated the same, wherever it comes from. The money goes into the Confederation's funds.

Beer contains **alcohol**. That is why in Switzerland it may only be sold to people aged 16 and over. For spirits such as schnapps, the **alcohol tax** applies, and there the age limit is 18. Taxes on alcohol also aim to make people drink less of it. In Switzerland, on the other hand, there is no separate tax on wine.

gewusst: There are hundreds of breweries in Switzerland, many of them very small.

teile.einleitung: A **property** is a piece of land, often with a house or a flat on it. For taxes, an important rule applies to properties: they are taxed where they are located. This is especially interesting when someone owns a holiday flat in another canton.
wichtigste: A property is a piece of land with or without a building.
Land is taxed in the canton where it is **located**.
Anyone who has a holiday flat in another canton pays part of their taxes there.
The division between the cantons is called **tax allocation**.
Nobody should have to pay tax twice on the same thing.

abschnitte.text: **Property** means a piece of land that belongs to someone. There is often a house on it. A flat that you own also counts. Anyone who owns a property must declare it in their **tax return**, because it is part of their assets. If it is rented out, the rent is also income.

You cannot take a house with you when you move. That is why the rule is: land is taxed in the canton and municipality where it is **located**. If a family lives in the canton of Zurich and has a holiday flat in the canton of the Grisons, they pay tax for the holiday flat in the Grisons.

So that nobody pays twice, the cantons involved divide the tax between them. This is called **tax allocation**. The canton of residence taxes the rest of the income and assets; the canton of the holiday flat taxes the part relating to the flat. In Switzerland, **double taxation** between cantons is forbidden.

Anyone who sells a property at a profit pays a special tax on it, the **property gains tax**. It too is charged by the canton in which the land is located. In many cantons, the longer you have owned the property, the lower this tax is.

gewusst: All land in Switzerland is entered in the **land register**, where you can see who owns it.
Some cantons and municipalities also charge a yearly **property tax**.

teile.einleitung: **Smishing** is a scam using fake text messages. The word is made up of SMS and phishing. The fraudsters want you to tap a link and give away data or money there.
wichtigste: Smishing means phishing by SMS or text message.
The messages often pretend to come from the post office, a parcel service, a bank or an authority.
They usually contain a link to a fake website.
There you are supposed to enter passwords, card details or codes.
Time pressure and small amounts are typical, for example a supposed customs fee.
You do not open suspicious links; you delete the message.

abschnitte.text: With **phishing**, fraudsters fish for data, rather like an angler fishing for fish. With smishing, this happens by **SMS** or through messenger apps. A message claims, for example, that a parcel cannot be delivered. You are told to pay a small fee via a link. The linked website looks real but belongs to the fraudsters.

Many smishing messages create **pressure**: you must act immediately, or an account will be blocked. They often come from unknown or foreign numbers. The link leads to an address that only looks similar to the real one. Sometimes the text has mistakes in it. Real companies do not ask for passwords or card details by text message.

With a suspicious message, you do **not** tap the link and you do not reply. If you are unsure, open the official app yourself or call the company on the number you know. In Switzerland you can report such messages to the **Federal Office for Cyber Security**. If you did enter data, you should inform the bank immediately and change your passwords.

gewusst: Smishing messages often use the names of well-known companies, because many people happen to be waiting for a parcel.
A similar trick by phone call is called vishing, from voice.

teile.einleitung: Anyone in Switzerland who wants to drive a car or ride a motorbike on the motorway needs a motorway vignette. It costs 40 francs and is the charge for using the national roads.
wichtigste: The motorway vignette costs 40 francs.
It is valid from 1 December of the previous year until 31 January of the following year, so 14 months.
Cars and motorbikes up to 3.5 tonnes need it for the motorway.
Heavy lorries pay the HVF instead.
The vignette is a charge, because the money is earmarked for the national roads.
Today the vignette is also available electronically as an e-vignette.

abschnitte.text: The **motorway vignette** is proof that you have paid the charge for using the motorways. It used to always be a sticker on the windscreen. Since 2023 you can also buy it online as an **e-vignette**; it is then linked to the number plate. It costs **40 francs**. Anyone who drives on the motorway without a valid vignette has to pay a **fine**.

A vignette shows a **year**. But it is already valid from **1 December** of the previous year. And it remains valid until **31 January** of the following year. So altogether you can use it for **14 months**. There is no vignette for just a few days; tourists also buy the full annual vignette.

**Cars** and **motorbikes** up to **3.5 tonnes** that use motorways and expressways need a vignette. Trailers and caravans also need their own vignette. Heavy **lorries** over 3.5 tonnes pay the **HVF**, the performance-related heavy vehicle fee, instead. It depends on weight, distance driven and pollutant emissions. If you only drive on cantonal and municipal roads, you do not need a vignette.

The vignette is officially called the **national road charge**. An ordinary **tax** goes into the general funds and can be used for all sorts of things. With a **charge** such as the vignette, the money is earmarked for a particular purpose. It is used to build, maintain and run the **national roads**. That is why the vignette counts as a charge and not as an ordinary tax.

gewusst: The motorway vignette was introduced in Switzerland in 1985, after the voters had approved it.
The colour of the sticker vignette changes every year, so that the police can see at once whether it is valid.

teile.einleitung: A **safe deposit box** is a small lockable box in a specially secure room at the bank. You can keep valuables and important papers in it. You rent the box and pay a fee for it.
wichtigste: A safe deposit box is in a well-protected room at the bank, often in the basement.
You can keep jewellery, important documents or keepsakes in it.
The box is rented, usually for a yearly fee.
The bank normally does not know what is in the box.
Opening it often needs two keys: one belonging to the customer and one belonging to the bank.

abschnitte.titel: How a safe deposit box works
abschnitte.text: The safe deposit boxes are built into a long metal wall. Each box has a number and its own lock. Often the **two-key principle** applies: the person renting it has one key, the bank has the other. Only with both together does the box open. Today there are also systems that you open with a card, a code or a fingerprint.

Typical things are **jewellery**, coins, wills, contracts or certificates. Some people also put photos or storage devices with copies of important files in the box. These things are better protected there against burglary, fire and water than at home. Forbidden or dangerous items are not allowed in it; that is written in the rental contract.

The bank does not open the box and does not look inside. When you want to use it, you are taken to the **vault** and can then look on your own. The rent depends on the size of the box. Because the bank does not know what is inside, the contents are not automatically insured. For very valuable things, people therefore often take out their own insurance.

gewusst: Many banks offer fewer safe deposit boxes today than in the past, because important documents are more and more often stored digitally.
You can also give another person power of attorney for a safe deposit box, so that they may open it too.

teile.einleitung: It is not only people who pay taxes, but **companies** too. A company that makes a profit gives part of it to the state. This applies to large corporations just as much as to the village bakery.
wichtigste: Companies pay tax on their profits.
This tax is called profit tax.
Small shops such as bakeries also pay taxes.
Companies also pass on the VAT that customers pay.
With a sole proprietorship, the owner pays the tax with their own income.

abschnitte.text: A **company** or **business** makes goods or offers services. It might be a bakery, a car garage or a big bank. Common forms in Switzerland are the **public limited company (AG)**, the **limited liability company (GmbH)** and the **sole proprietorship**.

The bakery sells bread and croissants. From this it pays for flour, electricity, rent and wages. What is left is the **profit**. An AG or GmbH pays **profit tax** on it to the Confederation, canton and municipality. If the bakery belongs to a single person as a sole proprietorship, the profit counts as that person's **income**.

Many companies have to account for **VAT**. It is included in the price the customers pay, and the company passes it on to the Confederation. AGs and GmbHs also pay a **capital tax** on their equity in the cantons. In addition, companies deduct contributions for the **AVS** from wages.

The cantons set their own tax rates for companies. That is why taxes are not equally high everywhere. Some cantons try to attract companies with low taxes. Since 2024, a **minimum tax** of 15 per cent has applied to very large international corporations.

gewusst: If a company makes a loss, it pays no profit tax.
Companies with very low turnover do not have to account for VAT.

teile.einleitung: If you are ill or need to go to the dentist, you often pay part of the bill yourself. Such **medical costs** can be deducted in the tax return under certain conditions. For direct federal tax, a limit of 5 per cent applies.
wichtigste: Only costs that you have **paid yourself** are deductible.
These include, for example, the deductible, the co-payment and dentist's bills.
For direct federal tax, only the part above **5 per cent** of net income counts.
Health insurance premiums do not count here but belong to the insurance deduction.
The cantons have their own rules, which may be similar or different.
You should keep records such as bills and statements from the health insurance.

abschnitte.text: **Medical costs** include treatments that you pay for out of your own pocket. These are, for example, the **deductible** (franchise) and the **co-payment** for health insurance. Dentist's bills also count, because basic insurance usually does not cover them. What the insurance pays cannot be deducted.

For **direct federal tax**, you may only deduct the part that exceeds **5 per cent of net income**. An example: with a net income of 60,000 francs, the limit is 3,000 francs. If you have paid 4,000 francs yourself, you may deduct 1,000 francs. So small amounts often make no difference at all.

The monthly health insurance **premiums** are not medical costs. They are entered under the **insurance deduction**, which has its own maximum. You may not deduct the same costs twice. That is why the tax return keeps the two deductions strictly separate.

Besides federal tax, you also pay **cantonal and municipal taxes**. The cantons set their own rules for the medical costs deduction, and many also have a percentage limit. The exact rules are in the **guidance notes** for the canton's tax return.

gewusst: Costs arising from a **disability** may be deducted at federal level without the 5 per cent limit.
Glasses or contact lenses can also count as deductible costs if you pay for them yourself.

teile.einleitung: An account is overdrawn when more money goes out than there is in it. Some banks allow this up to a limit, others do not. Both can have consequences and often cost money.
wichtigste: With an overdraft, the account balance is below zero.
Some accounts have an overdraft limit; many youth accounts do not.
The bank usually charges high interest for an overdraft.
If there is not enough money for a standing order, the payment is often not made.
Then the bill stays unpaid, and reminder fees may be charged.

abschnitte.text: An account holds a **credit balance**. If you spend more than there is, the balance slips below zero. This is called an **overdraft**. The bank then lends you the missing money for a short time. How far you may overdraw an account is set by the bank with an **overdraft limit**. With many youth accounts, an overdraft is not possible at all.

With a **standing order**, the bank regularly pays a fixed amount, for example the rent. If there is too little money in the account, the bank often does not carry out the order. Then the bill is not paid. The recipient may send a **reminder**, and reminder fees may be charged. Some banks also charge a fee of their own.

It is best to keep an eye on your balance, for example in online banking or in the bank's app. Many banks will send a message on request when your balance is low. You plan larger payments so that they come after your wages or pocket money. If you often go overdrawn, you should make a **budget**. That way you can see where the money is going.

gewusst: For the overdrawn money, the bank charges overdraft interest, which is much higher than savings interest.
In Germany the permitted overdraft is often called “Dispo”; in Switzerland people usually speak of a current account credit or an overdraft limit.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is made up of **26 cantons**. Each canton has its own laws, its own government and its own parliament. Cantons look after things such as the police, upper secondary schools and hospitals.
wichtigste: Switzerland has 26 cantons.
Many cantons have the same name as their capital, for example Lucerne.
The police are largely a matter for the cantons.
Upper secondary schools (Gymnasien and cantonal schools) usually belong to the canton.
The cantons pay for their tasks with their own taxes.

abschnitte.text: Each canton has a **capital**. Often the canton and its capital have the same name: the city of **Lucerne** is in the canton of Lucerne, the city of Bern in the canton of Bern. But there are also exceptions; for example, Liestal is the capital of Basel-Landschaft. Each canton also has its own **coat of arms**.

Each canton has its own **constitution**. The government is usually called the **Executive Council** and the parliament the **Cantonal Council** or **Grand Council**. Both are elected by the people. In Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden, the voters even decide important questions in the open air at the **Landsgemeinde**.

The **police** are mainly a matter for the cantons. That is why there is the Bern cantonal police, the Zurich cantonal police and many more. The cantons also run the **Gymnasien** and **cantonal schools** and are responsible for hospitals. They also decide how compulsory schooling is organised.

For these tasks, the cantons charge **taxes** on income and assets and on companies' profits. Each canton sets its own rates. That is why taxes are not equally high everywhere. Through **fiscal equalisation**, financially weak cantons receive money from financially strong cantons and from the Confederation.

gewusst: The youngest canton is the canton of Jura; it was founded in 1979.
Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Innerrhoden, and Obwalden and Nidwalden used to be called half-cantons.

teile.einleitung: Apprentices earn their own money with their apprentice's wage. That is why they also have to fill in a **tax return**. But thanks to various **deductions**, many of them pay little or no tax.
wichtigste: The apprentice's wage is **taxable income**.
Apprentices must submit a tax return, even if they earn little.
Typical deductions are **travel costs** to work and to vocational school.
**Meals** away from home can also be deducted.
After the deductions, there is often only a little taxable income left.
You need the salary statement from your training company for the tax return.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who works and receives wages has an **income**. This also applies to apprentices. Their apprentice's wage is taxed separately, meaning it is not added to their parents' income. That is why the tax office sends them their own **tax return**, in some cantons even before their 18th birthday.

Anyone who travels to work or to **vocational school** has costs, for example for a season ticket. These **travel costs** can be deducted. If you have to eat lunch away from home, you can make a deduction for **meals**. Such costs are called **work-related expenses**. They lower your taxable income.

The apprentice's wage is fairly low. If you subtract the social insurance contributions and the work-related expenses, often only a small amount is left. For low incomes, the **tax rate** is very low or zero. Even so, you must fill in and submit the return on time.

gewusst: In many cantons you can now fill in the tax return online.
If you cannot meet the deadline, you can ask the tax office for an **extension**.

teile.einleitung: Bridges, roads and school buildings cost a lot of money. A single person could never pay for something like that. That is why the municipality, the canton or the Confederation takes on such structures, and the money for them comes from taxes.
wichtigste: The state pays for large structures such as bridges.
The money for them comes from taxes.
Depending on the road, the municipality, the canton or the Confederation is responsible.
The Confederation is responsible for motorway bridges.
For large spending, the voters can often have a say.

abschnitte.text: A **bridge** is useful to everyone who uses it: drivers, cyclists, pedestrians and the bus. But building it is very expensive. That is why the **state** pays for such structures jointly for everyone. For this it needs **taxes**. Such structures are also called **infrastructure**.

In Switzerland it depends on which road the bridge belongs to. Bridges on **municipal roads** are paid for by the municipality. The canton is responsible for **cantonal roads**. The **motorways**, also called national roads, belong to the **Confederation**. With railway bridges, the railways and the Confederation are involved.

Large spending is decided democratically. In many municipalities, the **municipal assembly** votes on a loan. For very expensive projects there is often a **popular vote**. In this way people can have a say in what their tax money is spent on. Beforehand, experts check how the bridge should be built and what it will cost.

Building it is not the end of the story. Bridges must be **inspected** and repaired regularly. Wind, weather, frost and heavy lorries take their toll on them. This **maintenance** is also paid for with tax money. A well-maintained bridge can last for many decades.

gewusst: Because of its mountains and rivers, Switzerland has particularly many bridges and tunnels.
There is a separate federal fund for the motorways, into which money from the vignette flows, for example.

teile.einleitung: With a **power of attorney**, an account holder allows another person to use her bank account as well. This person may then, for example, make payments. But the money still belongs to the account holder.
wichtigste: A power of attorney allows another person to act on someone's behalf.
With a bank account, the authorised person can make payments or withdraw money.
The money still belongs to the account holder.
You give a power of attorney in writing, usually with a form from the bank.
The account holder can withdraw the power of attorney at any time.
You only give a power of attorney to people you trust completely.

abschnitte.titel: What a power of attorney is
abschnitte.text: A **power of attorney** is permission to act in another person's name. At the bank, you fill in and sign a **form** for this. It states who is authorised and what this person may do. The account holder remains the owner of the account and the money. The authorised person acts only on her behalf.

Powers of attorney are practical when someone cannot go to the bank themselves. Older people often give their children a power of attorney so that they can pay bills. It can also help during long stays abroad or in hospital. With children's accounts, the parents often have access. In a company, certain employees are given a power of attorney for the company account.

The account holder can **withdraw** a power of attorney **at any time**. To do this, she informs the bank, preferably in writing. A power of attorney can also be limited, for example to one particular account. Because the authorised person may do a lot, great **trust** is needed. For cases where someone can no longer make decisions themselves, Switzerland also has the **advance care directive**.

gewusst: A power of attorney can remain valid after death, if this has been agreed.
The bank checks the identity of the authorised person just as carefully as that of the account holder.

teile.einleitung: Income is the money you receive in a year, for example as wages. In principle, all income must be taxed, including wages from a side job.
wichtigste: In principle, all income is taxable.
This includes wages, side jobs, bonuses and tips.
Pensions and interest also count as income.
Gifts and inheritances are not income.
Gifts and inheritances are covered by separate cantonal rules.

abschnitte.text: **Income** is all the money you receive in a year for work or from assets. The most important is usually your **wages**. On top of that come, for example, a **bonus**, a 13th month's salary or **tips**. Anyone with a **side job** also earns income. Apprentices also earn income with their apprentice's wage.

It is not only work that brings in income. Anyone who receives a **pension**, for example from the AVS, also has income. **Interest** on a savings account or earnings from securities also count. Anyone who rents out a flat has income from rent. All this belongs in the **tax return**.

**Gifts** and **inheritances** are not income. Separate rules apply to them. The cantons can charge a **gift tax** or **inheritance tax** on them. In most cantons, children and spouses are exempt. Pocket money from your parents is not taxable income either.

In the tax return, you first add up all your income. Then you may make certain **deductions**, for example for travelling to work. What is left is your **taxable income**. The tax is calculated on this. Because the tax is progressive, people with a low income pay little or nothing.

gewusst: In Switzerland, tips also count as income and are taxable.
In Switzerland, lottery winnings are tax-free up to a certain amount.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss National Bank, SNB for short, is the central bank of Switzerland. It issues the Swiss banknotes and makes sure that the franc stays stable. Its head offices are in Bern and Zurich.
wichtigste: The Swiss National Bank is the central bank of Switzerland.
It issues the Swiss banknotes.
Its most important aim is price stability.
To achieve this, it sets the key interest rate.
The SNB started work in 1907.
It has two head offices, in Bern and in Zurich.
The SNB is independent; the Confederation and the cantons receive part of its profit.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss National Bank** is the **central bank** of Switzerland, in other words the bank of the banks. Private individuals cannot open an account with it. Instead it supplies the commercial banks with money and steers the amount of money in the country. Its building in Bern stands right on the Bundesplatz, next to the Federal Palace.

The SNB issues all the **banknotes** of the Swiss franc. The current ninth series came into circulation between 2016 and 2019 and was designed by the graphic designer Manuela Pfrunder. Each note shows a typical side of Switzerland, for example time, light, wind, water, matter and language. The **coins**, on the other hand, are minted by Swissmint on behalf of the Confederation.

The SNB's most important aim is **price stability**: inflation should be below 2 per cent a year. To achieve this it sets the key interest rate and can buy or sell foreign currencies. It also makes sure that payments between banks work. In addition, it manages Switzerland's **currency reserves**, including around 1040 tonnes of gold.

Until the beginning of the 20th century, many different banks in Switzerland issued their own banknotes. To bring order, the National Bank was founded and started work on 20 June 1907. From 2011 to 2015 it set a **minimum exchange rate** of 1.20 francs to the euro, in order to protect the export industry from a franc that was too strong. Its removal in January 2015 caused a stir around the world.

The SNB is a special **public limited company** whose shares are traded on the stock exchange, but most of them belong to cantons and cantonal banks. It is run by a three-member **Governing Board**, with Martin Schlegel as chairman since October 2024. The SNB is independent of the Federal Council, but must account for its actions to Parliament and the public. If it makes a profit, part of it is paid out to the Confederation and the cantons.

begriffe.erklaerung: A country's highest bank, which issues the money and watches over the currency.
Gold and foreign currencies that the National Bank holds as a reserve.
When prices rise or fall only a little.
The management of the National Bank.

gewusst: Part of Switzerland's gold reserves is stored in Switzerland, part in Great Britain and Canada.
The 1000-franc note is one of the most valuable banknotes in the world.
The banknotes of the ninth series are designed to be looked at upright, in portrait format.

teile.einleitung: A **fee** is money you pay for a particular service from the state. This is different from a tax, for which you get nothing directly in return. You pay fees, for example, for a passport or for rubbish bags.
wichtigste: For a fee, you get a particular service.
Taxes are paid without anything directly in return.
The price of a new passport is a fee.
In many municipalities, rubbish bags include a fee for the collection.
If you produce less rubbish, you pay less.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who orders a **passport** or an **identity card** pays a fee for it. You get exactly one service: the document. **Taxes**, by contrast, are paid for all the state's tasks, for example schools and roads. Whether you use these yourself does not matter.

In many municipalities, you may only put rubbish out on the street in official **fee bags** or with a **fee tag**. That is why these bags are more expensive than ordinary ones. With the price, you pay for part of the collection and incineration. If you **sort and recycle**, you need fewer bags and save money.

There are rules for fees. They should not bring in more than the service costs the state overall. This is called the **cost recovery principle**. In addition, the price must be in reasonable proportion to the service. So the state may not make a big profit from fees.
