There are fees in many places: for a **driving licence**, for planning permission, for waste water or for an entry in the land register. A **library card** or entry to the indoor swimming pool can also cost a fee. The amount is set by the Confederation, the cantons or the municipalities.

gewusst: Experts also call fees and similar charges “causal charges”, because they have a particular cause.
Since rubbish bags started to cost something, many people sort their rubbish much more carefully.

teile.einleitung: **Saving** means not spending money straight away but keeping it for later. That way you can make bigger wishes come true or have a reserve for the unexpected. A good trick is to stop and think briefly before every purchase.
wichtigste: Saving means putting part of your money aside for later.
Before buying something, it helps to ask: do I really need this?
If you have a savings goal, saving is easier.
It is best to save as soon as you get money, not just whatever is left over.
In a savings account at the bank you get interest.
Even small amounts grow into a big sum over time.

abschnitte.text: Many purchases happen on impulse, because something is tempting at that moment. The question **“Do I really need this?”** helps you avoid such purchases. You can also sleep on it. If you still want something the next day, it is probably a real wish. But often you notice that you do not need it so urgently after all.

abschnitte.titel: It is easier with a goal
abschnitte.text: If you know what you are saving for, you are more likely to keep going. A **savings goal** can be a bike, a game or a day trip. You work out how much you need to put aside each week. Then you can see how long it will take. It also helps to write down or draw your progress.

A tried and tested trick: you save **right at the start**, as soon as you get pocket money or wages. You put the amount you want to save straight into your money box or account. Whatever is left over you may spend. If you only save at the end, you often find there is nothing left.

Larger amounts are safer in a **savings account** than at home. The bank pays **interest** on them. If the interest stays in the account, the next year you also get interest on that interest. This is called **compound interest**. How high the interest is depends on the bank and on interest rates in general.

gewusst: If you save 2 francs every week, you will have 104 francs after a year.
Many Swiss banks offer special youth savings accounts.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is a **federal** state. This means that power is shared between the **Confederation, cantons and municipalities**. That is also why there are taxes at three levels.
wichtigste: Federalism means that tasks and power are spread over several levels.
The three levels are the Confederation, cantons and municipalities.
Each level has its own tasks and needs its own money for them.
That is why all three levels may charge taxes.
As a result, taxes are not equally high in every canton and every municipality.

abschnitte.text: The **Confederation** is the whole of Switzerland, with the Federal Council and Parliament in Bern. Below it are **26 cantons**, each with its own constitution, government and parliament. The smallest level is the more than 2,000 **municipalities**. Each level looks after what it can do best.

The Confederation is responsible, for example, for the **army**, the national roads and relations with other countries. The cantons provide, for example, the **police**, hospitals and upper secondary schools. The municipalities look after **compulsory schooling**, water, rubbish and playgrounds. In this way many things are organised close to the people.

Each level needs money for these tasks. The Confederation charges **direct federal tax** and **VAT**. Cantons and municipalities mainly charge **income and wealth taxes**. The municipality often sets its **tax rate** every year. That is why you pay more in one village than in another.

Because taxes vary in height, people speak of **tax competition**. Some think it keeps taxes low. Others fear that poorer cantons are put at a disadvantage. That is why there is **fiscal equalisation**: financially strong cantons and the Confederation give money to financially weaker cantons.

gewusst: The Confederation's right to charge VAT and direct federal tax is time-limited in the Constitution and has to be extended by the people again and again.
The number of municipalities is falling, because municipalities keep merging.

teile.einleitung: After shopping you get a **till receipt**, also simply called a receipt. It shows what you bought and how much you paid. Often it also shows, in small print, how much **VAT** is included in the price.
wichtigste: On the till receipt you can see how much VAT is included in the price.
The German abbreviation for VAT is MWST.
A lower tax rate applies to food than to other goods.
The till receipt is a record that you need for an exchange or a guarantee.
Companies keep their records in order to account for VAT.

abschnitte.text: A **till receipt** shows the name of the shop, the date, the goods bought and the prices. At the bottom is the **total amount**. There is usually also a small table with the **VAT**, marked **MWST** in German. It shows how much of the price goes to the Confederation.

The same rate does not apply to everything. In 2024 the **standard rate** was 8.1 per cent, for example for toys or clothes. For **food**, books and medicines a **reduced rate** of 2.6 per cent applied. That is why you often see two different lines with tax rates on a till receipt.

The till receipt is a **record**. If you want to exchange something or a device breaks, you often need it for the **guarantee**. For companies it is even more important: they use the records to account for VAT with the Confederation. Many shops now also offer the till receipt in digital form.

gewusst: VAT is already included in the price on the price tag; it is not added on top at the till.

teile.einleitung: There is a **deadline** for the tax return. This is a date by which you must submit it to the tax office. If you cannot manage it in time, you can usually have the deadline extended.
wichtigste: In many cantons, the regular deadline is 31 March of the following year.
The exact deadline is on the form and may differ from canton to canton.
If you need more time, you can apply for an extension.
This can often be done easily online.
It is important to act before the deadline runs out.

abschnitte.text: A **deadline** is a period within which something must be done. With the tax return, the rule is: in the new year, you report your income and assets for the **previous year**. Many cantons send out the documents at the beginning of the year and want them back by the **end of March**.

If you do not yet have your receipts or are ill, you can apply for an **extension**. Most cantons grant this on **request**, often using a form on the internet. Some charge a small **fee** for a longer extension. You should make the request before the deadline has passed.

If you do not submit your tax return, you receive a **reminder**. If you still do not react, a **fine** may follow. The tax office can then also **estimate** your income. This estimate often does not turn out in favour of the taxpayer.

gewusst: Many cantons offer programs with which you can fill in your tax return on the computer.
A fiduciary adviser can also apply for extensions on behalf of clients.

teile.einleitung: Banks are companies that keep money for people and companies, grant loans and handle payments. Almost all adults in Switzerland have an account, and many children get a youth or savings account early on. Switzerland is famous around the world for its large and well-known financial centre.
wichtigste: Money is kept more safely in a bank account than at home.
Interest is money the bank pays you for keeping your money with it.
A debit card takes the amount directly from your account; a credit card bills you later.
A Swiss IBAN begins with CH and identifies every account clearly.
Banks lend money, for example for a house, and charge interest for it.
A real bank never asks for your password by email.
The Swiss National Bank makes sure the franc is stable.

abschnitte.text: A bank accepts money from customers and manages it in **accounts**. It lends part of this money to other people or companies as a **loan**, for example as a mortgage for a house. For this it charges interest that is higher than the interest it pays savers. The bank earns a large part of its money from this difference.

There are several kinds of bank in Switzerland. The largest is UBS, which took over Credit Suisse in 2023. Then there are the **cantonal banks**, which belong to the cantons, the Raiffeisen banks, PostFinance and many regional and private banks. Above them all stands the **Swiss National Bank**, which issues the franc and ensures stable prices.

With an account you can receive wages, pay bills and save. Every account has an **IBAN**, which in Switzerland begins with CH and is 21 characters long. With a **debit card**, a purchase is taken from the account straight away. With a credit card, the bank pays first and you settle the bill later, usually once a month.

If you put money into a savings account, you receive **interest** for it. At an interest rate of 1 per cent, 100 francs earn 1 extra franc after one year. If interest is also paid on the interest every year, the money grows faster and faster; this is called compound interest. How high interest rates are depends strongly on the National Bank's decisions.

Today many people do their banking with **online banking** on a computer or with an app. Fraudsters send fake emails that look as if they come from the bank. If you get such a message, you do not reply, do not open any link and contact the bank directly. In addition, balances of up to 100,000 francs per customer and bank are protected by the deposit protection scheme if a bank becomes insolvent.

Banks in Switzerland must follow strict rules. The financial market supervisory authority **FINMA** checks whether they have enough of their own money and keep to the law. When opening an account, you must prove your identity so that no money from crimes can be hidden. For children under 18, the parents' consent is usually needed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A kind of cash box at the bank in which your balance is stored.
The price of borrowed money, which the bank pays you or which you pay the bank.
The international account number, beginning with CH in Switzerland.
Money you borrow from the bank and later pay back with interest.
The central bank of Switzerland, which issues banknotes and keeps the franc stable.

gewusst: The word bank comes from the Italian “banco”, the table at which money changers sat in the Middle Ages.
Most francs do not exist as coins or notes at all, but only as numbers in accounts.
Almost every canton has its own cantonal bank; the oldest was founded in the 19th century.

teile.einleitung: The **premium reduction** helps people with little money to pay for their health insurance. The Confederation and the cantons cover part of the premiums. In the tax return, you may only deduct the premiums you have paid yourself.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, everyone must have basic insurance with a health insurance company.
The premiums are a heavy burden for some households.
The Confederation and the cantons pay a premium reduction to people of modest means.
The cantons decide who is entitled, with their own rules.
The money usually goes directly to the health insurance company.
For the insurance deduction, only the premiums you have paid yourself count.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, **basic insurance** is compulsory. Everyone pays a **premium** for it every month. The premium does not depend on income. That is why it is often hard for families with little money to pay. This is where the **premium reduction** helps, also called the individual premium reduction, or IPV for short.

The premium reduction is for people of **modest economic means**. The Confederation and the **cantons** pay for it together. Each canton decides for itself who is entitled and how much they get. To do this, the canton often looks at the details in the **tax return**. Special rules apply to children and young adults in education.

In most cantons, the premium reduction is paid directly to the **health insurance company**. The insured person then gets a lower bill. In some cantons you have to apply; in others you are informed automatically. It is worth knowing the rules in your own canton.

In the tax return, you may deduct insurance premiums up to a maximum amount. This is the **insurance deduction**. But you may only deduct what you have **paid yourself**. If you receive a premium reduction, you first subtract it from the premiums. Only the rest counts for the deduction.

gewusst: The premium reduction has existed since the Health Insurance Act, which came into force in 1996.
A considerable share of the population receives a premium reduction.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes there is not enough time for the tax return. Then you can ask the tax office for an **extension**. If you do nothing at all, on the other hand, you risk a reminder and a fine.
wichtigste: You can usually ask the tax office for an extension.
You should apply for it before the deadline runs out.
This can often be done online or with a short letter.
If you submit nothing at all, you receive a reminder.
After that, there is the threat of a fine and an estimate by the tax office.

abschnitte.text: In many cantons, the **tax office** website has a form for an **extension**. You enter your tax number and choose a new date. Some cantons grant a first extension free of charge and charge a small **fee** for further ones. The rules vary from canton to canton.

If you neither submit nor ask for an extension, you receive a **reminder** with a final deadline. If you miss that too, you can receive a **fixed penalty**. The tax office may then set the taxes **at its discretion**, meaning estimate them. It is hard to challenge such an estimate.

It helps to collect all your **records** in a folder during the year: salary statement, bank statements, receipts for deductions. Then filling in the return goes faster. Even if you extend the deadline, the tax office can send a **provisional bill**, which you have to pay.

gewusst: An extension only postpones the submission, not necessarily the payment of the taxes.

teile.einleitung: Every day, households produce a lot of rubbish. In Switzerland, the municipality makes sure that it is collected regularly and disposed of or recycled properly.
wichtigste: The municipality organises rubbish collection.
It is paid for with fees, for example for rubbish bags, and partly with taxes.
If you produce more rubbish, you also pay more through the bag fee.
Glass, PET, paper and aluminium are collected separately for recycling.
Combustible rubbish is burned in waste incineration plants.
The heat from this is often used for electricity and heating.

abschnitte.text: In every municipality, a **dustcart** regularly drives through the streets and collects the rubbish. The **municipality** organises this **rubbish collection**, sometimes together with other municipalities. The collection calendar shows on which days which rubbish is collected. You only put the bags out at the roadside on collection day. That way the streets stay clean and animals do not tear the bags open.

In most Swiss municipalities you buy special **fee bags** or stick a tag on the bag. This **bag fee** pays for the disposal. Behind it is the **polluter pays principle**: if you produce more rubbish, you pay more. This is meant to encourage people to produce less rubbish and to sort more. Part of the costs is also covered through basic charges or **taxes**.

Many things do not belong in the rubbish bag. **Glass**, **PET** bottles, **paper**, cardboard and **aluminium** are collected separately. New products are made from them; this is called **recycling**. Green waste such as vegetable peelings and grass cuttings can be composted or fermented. Batteries and electrical devices are taken back to the shop or to a collection point.

The combustible rubbish goes to a **waste incineration plant**. Since 2000, combustible rubbish may no longer simply be dumped in landfill sites in Switzerland. Burning it produces heat. Many plants use this to generate **electricity** and **district heating** for heating homes. Modern filters clean the smoke before it leaves the chimney.

gewusst: Switzerland is one of the countries that produce particularly large amounts of rubbish per person, but it also recycles a great deal of it.
Old PET bottles can be made into new PET bottles.

teile.einleitung: In the past, many children were given a **savings book** at the bank. Every deposit and withdrawal was entered in it by hand or with a printer. That way you could always see how much money was in the savings account.
wichtigste: A savings book is a small booklet that belongs to a savings account.
It contains all deposits, withdrawals and the current balance.
The bank entered the transactions at the counter each time.
The interest was also recorded in the savings book.
Today you usually see your balance in an app or in online banking.

abschnitte.titel: What a savings book looked like
abschnitte.text: The savings book was small and fitted easily into a pocket. On the front were the name and the **account number**. Inside there were lines for the date, deposit, withdrawal and **balance**, meaning the current amount in the account. Anyone bringing money handed the book over at the counter. The bank entered the amount; later a machine printed the line straight into it.

The savings book was **proof** of how much money you had. Every year the interest was added and entered as well. For children it was exciting to see the number grow. They often took their money box to the bank, for example on World Savings Day, and had the contents entered in the book.

Most banks have replaced the savings book with **bank statements** and **online banking**. Today you see every transaction straight away in an app. This is convenient and always up to date. But some people keep their old savings book as a souvenir.

gewusst: In Germany and Austria, people usually say “Sparbuch” rather than the Swiss “Sparheft”.
With some savings books, you had to show the book before you were allowed to withdraw any money at all.

teile.einleitung: If you stay overnight in a hotel, the room price also includes VAT. For such overnight stays, known as accommodation, Switzerland has its own low tax rate.
wichtigste: Accommodation means guests get a place to stay overnight in return for money.
Since 2024, a VAT rate of 3.8 per cent has applied to it.
Breakfast is part of the accommodation and has the same rate.
The standard rate, at 8.1 per cent, is more than twice as high.
The lower rate is meant to support tourism in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: **Accommodation** means offering guests somewhere to stay. This includes hotels, guesthouses, holiday flats and similar offers. The guest pays to be allowed to stay one or more nights. **Breakfast** is included too if it comes with the overnight stay. This matters for taxes, because this service is treated in a special way.

**VAT** is a tax on almost everything you buy. Since 2024 a **special rate** of **3.8 per cent** has applied to accommodation. Before that it was 3.7 per cent. The rate was adjusted because VAT was raised slightly in 2024 for the AVS. The hotel includes the tax in the price and passes it on to the Confederation.

Not everything in a hotel counts as accommodation. Dinner in the hotel restaurant or drinks at the bar have the **standard rate** of 8.1 per cent. The same applies, for example, to a massage in the hotel. Only the overnight stay with breakfast gets the low rate. That is why a hotel bill often shows more than one tax rate.

Switzerland is a popular holiday country, but also an expensive one. Hotels compete with hotels in neighbouring countries. The lower rate is meant to make overnight stays a little cheaper and strengthen **tourism**. Many mountain regions depend heavily on guests. The special rate keeps coming up in politics: some think it is necessary, others consider it an unnecessary exception.

gewusst: Switzerland has three VAT rates: 8.1, 2.6 and 3.8 per cent.
A single hotel bill can show two different tax rates.

teile.einleitung: A **savings goal** is something you put money aside for on purpose. With a goal in mind, saving is easier. With a simple calculation you can work out how long it will take.
wichtigste: A savings goal is a wish you save money for.
For this you need the price and the amount you save regularly.
The price divided by the amount saved gives the number of weeks or months.
Example: 30 francs divided by 5 francs a week is 6 weeks.
Patience is part of saving.

abschnitte.text: First you think about what you would like and what it **costs**. It could be a game, a book or a day trip. Then you decide how much you can save regularly, for example from your pocket money. A goal should be achievable. If it is very expensive, you can divide it into smaller stages.

To work out how long it will take, you **divide** the price by the amount you save. Noah would like a game costing 30 francs and saves 5 francs every week. 30 divided by 5 is 6. So Noah needs **6 weeks**. To check, you work it out the other way round: 5 francs times 6 weeks is 30 francs.

It helps to make your **progress** visible. You can draw a sheet with boxes and colour one in each week. If you are given some money as a present, you reach the goal faster. If you buy something else in between, it takes longer. If you keep at it, you will be all the happier at the end.

gewusst: Many adults also save with goals, for example for a holiday or a flat of their own.
Some banks offer a function in their app with which you can create and track savings goals.

teile.einleitung: A budget is a plan for money. It shows how much money you expect to take in and what you will spend it on. Not only families make a budget, but also municipalities, cantons and the Confederation.
wichtigste: A budget is a plan for income and spending.
Every year, municipalities make a budget for the following year.
A municipality's most important income is taxes.
The municipal assembly or municipal parliament approves the budget.
After the year, the accounts show what really happened.

abschnitte.text: A **budget** is a plan. On one side it shows the **income**, meaning the money that comes in. On the other side is the **spending**, meaning the money you need. You can budget pocket money too. That way you can see in advance whether the money will be enough.

Every year, each **municipality** plans how much money it will spend the following year. This includes schools, roads, water, the fire service and much more. Its most important income is the **taxes** paid by residents and companies. On top of that come fees and contributions from the canton. The **municipal council** draws up the budget.

The budget must be **approved**. In smaller municipalities this is done by the **municipal assembly**, where all voters can have their say. Larger municipalities have a **municipal parliament**. The **tax rate** is often set together with the budget. It determines how high the municipal tax is.

A budget is an estimate. At the end of the year, the **accounts** show how much was really taken in and spent. If spending is higher than income, there is a **deficit**. In the opposite case, people speak of a **surplus**. The Confederation also has rules so that it does not permanently spend more than it takes in.

gewusst: Since 2003 the Confederation has had a debt brake, which the people had previously accepted.
The word “budget” originally comes from the French word for a small purse.

teile.einleitung: A password alone is often not secure enough. With a two-factor log-in, you also need a second proof. Banks almost always use this method in online banking.
wichtigste: With a two-factor log-in, you need two different proofs.
There are three kinds: something you know, something you have, something you are.
A password and a PIN are knowledge; a mobile phone is possession.
A fingerprint and your face belong to “something you are”.
You reject an unexpected log-in request and inform the bank.

abschnitte.text: A **factor** is proof that you really are you. There are three kinds. **Knowledge**: something you know, for example a password or a PIN. **Possession**: something you have, for example your mobile phone. **Being**: something you are, for example your **fingerprint** or your face. Such body features are called **biometric**.

First you enter your username and password. Then the bank asks for a second factor. Often a message appears on your phone in an app, which you confirm. Sometimes you get a code by text message. Only when both factors are correct does online banking open. If a fraudster knows only your password, they still cannot get in.

If you get a log-in confirmation even though you are not logging in at all, you need to be careful. Someone may know your password. Then you reject the request, change your password and inform the bank. Never pass on codes on the phone or by email. Real banks never ask for your password. Fraudulent messages that try to steal data are called **phishing**.

gewusst: Many email services, games and social networks also offer a two-factor log-in.
Two passwords one after the other are not a real two-factor log-in, because both belong to the same kind: knowledge.

teile.einleitung: Receipts and records are papers or files that show that you have paid or received something. They are very important for the tax return, because if you claim a deduction, you must be able to prove it.
wichtigste: Records include, for example, receipts, invoices and certificates.
With records you prove the deductions in your tax return.
The tax office may ask for records.
If a record is missing, a deduction can be struck out.
Companies must keep their accounts and records for 10 years.

abschnitte.text: A **record** is proof about money. It can be a **receipt** from a shop, an **invoice** or a bank statement. The **salary statement** from your employer is also a record. It shows how much you earned in a year. Today many records are digital, for example as a PDF.

In your **tax return** you state your income and your assets. You may also **deduct** certain costs, for example for travelling to work or for further training. This lowers your tax. So that the tax office can check the details, records are needed. Some must be sent in directly, for example the salary statement.

The **tax office** may ask for proof if it wants to check a detail. Then you must be able to show the right records. If they are missing, the office can **strike out** the deduction. The tax then becomes higher. That is why it is worth not throwing records away but collecting them in an orderly way.

The simplest way is a file or folder for the whole year. If you collect records digitally, it is best to create a separate folder on the computer. Many people keep their tax documents for several years. For **companies** there is a clear rule: they must keep their accounts and records for **10 years**.

gewusst: A donation receipt is also a record: donations to charitable organisations can be deducted from taxes.
Till receipts on thermal paper can fade over time, which is why some people photograph them.

teile.einleitung: **Profit** is the money a company has left after all its costs. It shows whether a business is successful. The company pays tax on its profit.
wichtigste: Profit is what is left after all costs have been deducted.
If the costs are greater than the income, there is a loss.
A company pays tax on its profit.
With its profit, a company can invest or pay its owners.

abschnitte.text: A company takes in money when it sells something. This is called **revenue** or income. At the same time it has costs, its **expenses**: materials, rent, electricity and wages. If you calculate revenue minus expenses, you get the **profit**. If the result is negative, the company has made a **loss**.

On a market day, Lena sells lemonade for 50 francs. Lemons, sugar and cups cost 20 francs. So her **profit** is 30 francs. With a real company the calculation is bigger, but the principle is the same. All the figures are in the **income statement**.

Part of the profit goes as **profit tax** to the Confederation, canton and municipality. The company can keep the rest, to buy new machines or to save for bad times. A public limited company can pay part of it out to its shareholders as a **dividend**.

gewusst: In Switzerland, a company may offset losses from earlier years against later profits for seven years.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, **VAT** is added to almost everything you buy. But a lower rate applies to everyday necessities: the **reduced rate**. Since 2024 it has been 2.6 per cent.
wichtigste: Since 2024, the reduced VAT rate has been 2.6 per cent.
It applies to food bought in shops, books, newspapers and medicines.
The standard rate for most other things is 8.1 per cent.
For overnight stays in hotels, a special rate of 3.8 per cent applies.
In this way things that everyone needs are taxed less heavily.
The rates were raised in 2024 to strengthen the AVS.

abschnitte.text: The **reduced rate** applies to **everyday necessities**. These include **food** and soft drinks bought in shops, **books**, **newspapers** and **medicines**. Seeds, plants and animal feed are also included. For all these things you pay 2.6 per cent VAT.

Since 2024 Switzerland has had three VAT rates. The **standard rate** of 8.1 per cent applies to most goods, for example clothes, toys or mobile phones. The **special rate** of 3.8 per cent applies to overnight stays in hotels. The **reduced rate** of 2.6 per cent is the lowest.

A sandwich bought in a shop has less tax than the same sandwich eaten at a table in a restaurant. That is because the **standard rate** applies in a **restaurant**, since you also get a service: being served, a table and the washing-up. If you take the food away, you usually pay the reduced rate. Alcoholic drinks are always taxed at the standard rate.

Everyone has to eat and sometimes needs medicines. Low-income families spend a large part of their money on such things. The **lower rate** places less of a burden on them. Books and newspapers are also cheaper, so that education and information remain affordable for everyone.

gewusst: Until the end of 2023, the reduced rate was 2.5 per cent and the standard rate 7.7 per cent.
The increase in VAT in 2024 goes to the AVS.

teile.einleitung: In your tax return you must declare all your income and assets. If the tax office later discovers that something was missing, it demands the missing tax afterwards. This is called **back tax**.
wichtigste: **Back tax** is tax charged afterwards on income or assets that were not declared.
The tax office demands it when it discovers untaxed values.
**Default interest** is added to the back tax.
Anyone who has deliberately evaded tax also pays a **fine**.
Anyone who reports themselves before the office knows anything can escape a fine once in their life.

abschnitte.text: Sometimes something is missing from the tax return, for example a forgotten bank account. Then too little tax was calculated. If the tax office finds out, it demands the missing amount afterwards. This is called **back tax**. On top of that comes **default interest**, because the money is paid too late.

If someone has hidden income or assets **deliberately** or through negligence, this is called **tax evasion**. Then it does not stop at the back tax and the interest. You also have to pay a **fine**, which can be high depending on the case. The tax office can go back several years for this.

Anyone who notices themselves that they have not declared something can report it to the tax office. This is called **voluntary disclosure**. If the office did not yet know about it, once in your life you only have to pay the back tax and the default interest, but no fine. So honesty pays.

gewusst: Heirs can also be asked to pay afterwards if the person who died had hidden assets, but simplified rules apply for this.

teile.einleitung: The **ambulance service** is the rescue service with the ambulance. If someone is seriously injured or suddenly seriously ill, you dial the emergency number **144**. Experts then come as quickly as possible.
wichtigste: In Switzerland you can reach the ambulance service on 144.
It comes with an ambulance and helps on the spot.
Paramedics have a long training.
The police have the number 117, the fire service the number 118.
In cases of poisoning, Tox Info Suisse helps on 145.
Until the ambulance arrives, first aid can make a big difference.

abschnitte.titel: What does the ambulance service do?
abschnitte.text: The **ambulance service**, or **rescue service**, helps in emergencies. It might be a serious accident, a fall or a sudden illness such as a heart problem. The experts take care of the person straight away and, if necessary, take them to **hospital**. In the ambulance they have lots of equipment and medicines with them.

In an emergency you dial **144**. The call costs nothing. You say calmly **who** is calling, **where** you are, **what** has happened and **how many** people are injured. Then you stay on the phone until the professional ends the call. They often give you tips on what to do until help arrives.

There are several emergency numbers in Switzerland. You can reach the **police** on **117** and the **fire service** on **118**. In cases of poisoning, **Tox Info Suisse** helps on **145**. In the mountains you call Rega on **1414**. The European number **112** also works. Emergency calls are important for everyone, which is why you must never dial them for fun.

Until the ambulance arrives, people without medical training can also help. This is called **first aid**. The first important thing is not to put yourself in danger. Then you call for help and look after the injured person. Anyone in Switzerland who wants to get a **driving licence** must attend a **first aid course**. There you learn the most important things to do.

gewusst: In Switzerland, training to become a paramedic takes three years at a college of higher education.
Rescue services are organised by cantons, municipalities and hospitals and are also supported with tax money.

teile.einleitung: Not everything you would like to have is something you really need. That is why people distinguish between **needs** and **wants**. If you know the difference, you can decide better what to spend your money on.
wichtigste: A need is something you really require in order to live.
Food, drink, clothing and a roof over your head are basic needs.
A want is something that would be nice, but that you can live without.
Toys, sweets or a new mobile phone are usually wants.
You cover your needs first, then you fulfil your wants.
What counts as a need for someone can depend on their situation in life.

abschnitte.text: A **need** is something a person cannot live well without. This includes **food and drink**, warm clothing, a home and sleep. Health and safety are also important needs. Such things are called **basic needs**, because every human being has them. In a family, money must be there for these first.

A **want** is something you would like to have but do not necessarily need. A new toy, an ice cream or a video game bring joy. But you can still live well without them. Wants are not bad; they are part of life. You just do not have to fulfil every one of them straight away.

Sometimes the line is **blurred**. You need shoes, but expensive designer shoes are more of a want. A bike may be necessary for getting to school, but a particularly expensive model is a want. Time plays a part too: a mobile phone used to be a luxury, but today many people need one for school or work. It is worth thinking honestly about it each time.

If you know what is a need and what is a want, you can **plan** your money better. What you really need comes first. Whatever is left over can be spent on wants or saved. Many adults make a **budget** for this. It shows how much money is set aside for what.

gewusst: Advertising often tries to turn a want into the feeling “I absolutely need this”.
Drinking water is one of the most important needs of all: without water, a person can survive only a few days.

teile.einleitung: **Interest on debts** is interest that you pay for borrowed money. In Switzerland, you may deduct private interest on debts from your income up to an upper limit. Interest that you receive yourself, on the other hand, is income.
wichtigste: You pay interest on debts for borrowed money, for example for a mortgage.
Private interest on debts may be deducted from income.
The deduction is limited.
For federal tax the rule is: investment income plus 50,000 francs.
Interest you receive, for example on a savings account, is income.
Interest on consumer loans is also interest on debts.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who borrows money pays a price for it: **interest**. For the person who has borrowed the money, this is **interest on debts**. The best-known kind in Switzerland is the **mortgage**. Many people use it to finance a house or a flat. Every year they pay mortgage interest to the bank for it.

In the tax return, you may deduct **private interest on debts**. This makes taxable income smaller. But the deduction is **limited**. For **direct federal tax**, you may deduct at most as much as you have in investment income, plus 50,000 francs. The cantons have similar rules.

Anyone who lives in their own house in Switzerland has to pay tax on an **imputed rental value** as income. This is an imagined amount that you would receive as rent. In return you may deduct mortgage interest and maintenance costs. The abolition of the imputed rental value was argued about in politics for a long time; opinions on it differ.

The difference is important: interest you **pay** can be deducted. Interest you **receive**, for example on a savings account or for bonds, is **income** and must be taxed. On larger amounts of interest, the bank often deducts **withholding tax** of 35 per cent. If you declare the interest in your tax return, you get this back.

gewusst: Withholding tax is meant to make sure that interest and other income are declared honestly in the tax return.
Companies' business interest on debts is treated differently from private interest on debts.

teile.einleitung: Direct federal tax is a tax that the Confederation charges on the income of people and the profits of companies. It is not collected by the Confederation itself, but by the cantons. After VAT, it is one of the Swiss Confederation's most important sources of income.
wichtigste: Direct federal tax is charged by the Confederation and collected by the cantons.
It taxes the income of private individuals and the profits of companies.
It is progressive: those who earn more pay a higher percentage.
For private individuals, the tax rate is at most 11.5 per cent.
Companies pay 8.5 per cent of their net profit to the Confederation.
The cantons may keep just over a fifth of the revenue.
The right to charge this tax is written into the Federal Constitution for a limited time.

abschnitte.text: Direct federal tax is the Confederation's only income tax. It is called **direct** because it is paid directly by the person who receives the income. By contrast, VAT is an **indirect tax**, hidden in the price of goods. Direct federal tax is governed by the Federal Act on Direct Federal Tax.

You do not fill in a separate tax return for direct federal tax. The details from the cantonal tax return are used for it as well. The cantonal **tax office** calculates the federal tax and sends the bill. The cantons may keep 21.2 per cent of the revenue and transfer the rest to the Confederation.

The tax is strongly **progressive**. People with a low income pay no direct federal tax at all. For middle incomes the amount is often small; only for high incomes does it rise significantly. The highest rate is 11.5 per cent of income; for companies a fixed rate of 8.5 per cent applies to **net profit**.

Originally there was no federal income tax; the cantons alone taxed income. During the Second World War, from 1941, the Confederation introduced a **defence tax** to pay for national defence. This tax remained after the war and has been called direct federal tax since 1983. To this day the Federal Constitution only allows it for a limited time, and the people and the cantons have to extend the time limit from time to time.

abschnitte.titel: What is the money used for?
abschnitte.text: The revenue goes into the general federal funds. With it, the Confederation pays, for example, for the army, the universities ETH and EPFL, contributions to the AVS and to rail transport. Part of it is passed on through **fiscal equalisation** to cantons with less money. In this way the tax helps to even out differences between the regions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tax that you pay yourself on your income or assets.
A tax that is included in the price of goods, such as VAT.
What a company has left after deducting all its costs.
The higher the income, the higher the tax rate.

gewusst: For almost 40 years, direct federal tax was called the defence tax.
Many families on low incomes pay no direct federal tax at all.
In a popular vote in 2018 it was decided that the Confederation may charge direct federal tax until the end of 2035.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has three levels of government: municipalities, cantons and the Confederation. At federal level, tasks are carried out that concern the whole country, for example the army.
wichtigste: The federal level is the highest of the three levels of government.
National defence is a matter for the Confederation.
The Confederation pays for the army with federal money.
Important sources of federal income are direct federal tax and VAT.
Whatever the cantons and municipalities can sort out themselves stays with them.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, tasks are divided between **three levels**. The **municipalities** look after local things, such as nursery school and water. The **cantons** are responsible, for example, for the police, hospitals and schools. At **federal level**, questions for the whole country are dealt with. This division is called **federalism**.

A clear example of a federal task is **national defence**. The **army** protects the whole of Switzerland and not just one canton. That is why the Confederation pays for it. It buys equipment, trains soldiers and maintains barracks. The money comes from the federal funds.

The Confederation has its own **income**. The most important sources are **VAT** and **direct federal tax** on income and profits. On top of that come withholding tax, taxes on mineral oil and tobacco, and customs duties. The Confederation pays for its tasks with this money. Municipalities and cantons, on the other hand, have their own taxes.

Besides the army, the Confederation looks after the **motorways** and **foreign policy**. It runs the AVS, regulates customs and is responsible for the national currency. The two Federal Institutes of Technology are also federal universities. Which tasks the Confederation has is set out in the **Federal Constitution**. A new federal task requires a popular vote.

gewusst: The Confederation may only take on new tasks if the people and the cantons agree to a change in the Federal Constitution.
In German, “Stände” is another word for the cantons.

teile.einleitung: Fiscal equalisation is a system with which money is redistributed in Switzerland between the Confederation and the cantons. Financially strong cantons and the Confederation use it to support financially weaker cantons. In this way all cantons should be able to carry out their tasks, such as schools, roads and hospitals, well.
wichtigste: Fiscal equalisation distributes money from financially strong to financially weak cantons.
It is paid for by the Confederation and the financially strong cantons.
Its current form has applied since 2008 and is called the NFA.
Resource equalisation helps cantons with little tax-raising power.
Burden equalisation helps cantons with special costs, for example because of mountains or big cities.
The paying cantons include, for example, Zug, Zurich, Geneva and Schwyz.
Fiscal equalisation strengthens the cohesion between the regions of Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland's 26 cantons differ greatly in how rich they are. Some are home to many well-paid people and large companies; others lie in mountain regions with less income. **Fiscal equalisation** partly evens out these differences. It is an important part of **federalism**, in which the cantons carry out many tasks themselves.

In 2004 the people and the cantons accepted a major reform, the **reorganisation of fiscal equalisation and the division of tasks**, NFA for short. It came into force on 1 January 2008. It also set out more clearly which tasks the Confederation pays for and which the cantons pay for. The system has been adjusted several times since then.

With **resource equalisation**, it is calculated how much tax a canton could take in per resident. Cantons with high potential pay into a common pot, and the Confederation also adds a lot of money. Cantons with little potential receive money from this pot. Per head, the canton of Zug has been the biggest paying canton for years.

Some cantons have particularly high costs that are not their fault. Mountain cantons such as the Grisons or Uri, for example, have to maintain many roads in steep terrain; this is called **geographical and topographical burdens**. Urban cantons such as Basel-Stadt or Geneva, on the other hand, have higher costs due to social tasks in big cities. Both kinds of burden are cushioned with money from the Confederation.

Without fiscal equalisation, poor cantons would have to charge much higher taxes or offer fewer services. Then even more people and companies would move to rich cantons. Equalisation makes sure that mountain valleys also have good schools and hospitals. Even so, there are arguments again and again, because paying cantons think they pay too much.

begriffe.erklaerung: A form of state in which the Confederation and the cantons share power and tasks.
The abbreviation for Switzerland's fiscal equalisation system since 2008.
A canton that pays more into fiscal equalisation than it receives.
A canton that receives money from fiscal equalisation.

gewusst: Measured in absolute francs, the canton of Bern has received particularly large amounts from fiscal equalisation for years.
The payments in fiscal equalisation are recalculated every year.
Many cantons also have a similar equalisation system between rich and poor municipalities.

teile.einleitung: At the railway station, in the park or in the old town there are **public toilets**. They are there for everyone who needs to go while out and about. Keeping them clean takes money, and this often comes from the municipality.
wichtigste: Public toilets, often simply called WCs, are there for everyone.
Many are built and cleaned by the municipality.
The money for this often comes from taxes.
Some toilets cost a small fee, for example at the railway station.
There are also toilets for wheelchair users.
Anyone who leaves a toilet clean helps everyone.

abschnitte.text: If you are out for a long time, at some point you need a toilet. That is why there are **public toilets** in many places: in parks, at railway stations, by playgrounds or on lake shores. They are especially important for children, older people and tourists. A sign with symbols shows where the nearest toilet is.

A public toilet has to be built, supplied with water and electricity and often **cleaned** several times a day. On top of that come paper, soap and repairs. That costs a lot of money. It is often paid for by the **municipality** with **tax money**. Sometimes railway stations, shops or restaurants also share the costs.

Many public toilets are free. At large **railway stations** you often have to pay a small **fee**. In return these toilets are usually supervised and especially clean. There are also **wheelchair-accessible** toilets with more space and grab rails. Some have a baby changing table.

There were already public toilets in **ancient Rome**. There many people sat side by side on long stone benches. A Roman emperor called **Vespasian** even had a tax charged on the urine from public latrines, because it was used for tanning leather. That is where the saying “money does not stink” comes from.

gewusst: In France and Italy, public urinals are still sometimes called “vespasiennes” or “vespasiani” after the Emperor Vespasian.
19 November is World Toilet Day. It is a reminder that many people in the world have no access to a clean toilet.

teile.einleitung: Children can own money too, for example in a savings account. This money is called **children's assets**. For tax purposes, however, it is not declared by the child but by the parents.
wichtigste: Children's assets include, for example, savings accounts, securities or inherited money.
The **parents** declare the assets of children under 18 in their tax return.
The interest on the child's savings account also goes in the parents' return.
A child under 18 does not need their own tax return for this.
Wages from their own work, such as an apprentice's wage, are taxed separately.

abschnitte.text: If grandparents pay money into a savings account for a birthday, this money belongs to the child. This is called **children's assets**. Until the child is 18, the parents manage this money. But they may not simply spend it on themselves, because it belongs to the child.

In Switzerland, the assets of children under 18 are counted as part of the parents' assets. That is why the parents enter the savings account in their **tax return**, in the schedule of accounts and securities. The **interest** belongs there too. The child does not have to fill anything in.

If a child earns money from work, for example as an **apprentice**, something else applies. This **earned income** is taxed separately from the parents. From their 18th birthday, everyone fills in their own tax return anyway, including for their assets.

gewusst: For children, there is a **child deduction** in the parents' tax return, which lowers the family's taxes.
Many banks offer special youth savings accounts with slightly better interest.

teile.einleitung: Every year the Confederation spends many billions of francs. Most of the money goes on social welfare, above all on the AVS and other social insurance schemes.
wichtigste: The Confederation's largest area of spending is social welfare.
This mainly includes contributions to the AVS and the IV.
Other large areas are transport, education and research, and the army.
The Confederation passes part of its income on to the cantons.
Every year Parliament decides on the federal budget.

abschnitte.titel: What the Confederation needs money for
abschnitte.text: The **Confederation** has many tasks for the whole country. For this it spends **billions of francs** every year. The money comes mainly from VAT and direct federal tax. Spending is divided into areas, for example social affairs, transport or education. That way you can see where the money goes.

The largest area is **social welfare**. This means above all contributions to the **AVS**, the old-age pension. The **IV**, the disability insurance for people with disabilities, and contributions to reduce health insurance premiums also belong to it. Because there are more and more older people, this spending is rising. About a third of all federal spending goes into this area.

The Confederation also needs a lot of money for **transport**, meaning for the railways and motorways. Another important area is **education and research**, for example the two Federal Institutes of Technology (ETH). On top of that come **national defence** with the army, and agriculture. Relations with other countries and development cooperation also cost money.

A large part flows back to the **cantons**. For example, they receive a share of direct federal tax. Through **fiscal equalisation**, cantons with little money get support. Every year **Parliament** decides on the budget. The **debt brake** makes sure that in the long run the Confederation does not spend more than it takes in.

gewusst: The AVS was introduced in 1948 and is one of Switzerland's most important social institutions.
Federal spending on the AVS is growing because people in Switzerland are living longer and longer.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who fills up with petrol or diesel at a petrol station also pays taxes in the price. One of them is the **mineral oil tax**. It belongs to the Confederation and helps to pay for roads and transport.
wichtigste: The **mineral oil tax** is a tax of the **Confederation** on fuels.
It is charged mainly on **petrol** and **diesel**.
It is included in every litre you fill up with.
On top of that comes **VAT**.
A large part of the money goes into **roads** and transport.
That is why the state accounts for a large part of the price of petrol.

abschnitte.text: The **mineral oil tax** is charged on fuels such as **petrol** and **diesel**. It is not added at the till but is already included in the price per litre. It is paid first by the companies that import or produce fuel in Switzerland. They pass the costs on to the customers through the price.

If Mr Rossi fills up with 40 litres of petrol, he pays the **mineral oil tax** and also **VAT**. VAT is even calculated on the price including the mineral oil tax. That is why a large part of the price of petrol goes to the state. The rest covers the fuel itself, transport and the petrol station.

An important part of the revenue is earmarked for **road transport**. It pays, for example, for building and maintaining motorways and for contributions to the cantons for their roads. Part goes into the **National Roads and Urban Transport Fund**, NAF for short. The rest goes into the Confederation's general funds.

gewusst: Besides the mineral oil tax, there is also a **mineral oil tax surcharge** on fuel, which goes entirely to road transport.
Electric cars pay no mineral oil tax, because they do not fill up with fuel.

teile.einleitung: The **municipality** is your village or your town. It is the level of the state that is closest to you. It looks after many things in your surroundings, for example the school, the playground and the fire service.
wichtigste: The municipality is the village or town where you live.
It looks after things nearby, such as the school building, the playground and local roads.
The fire service is usually a task of the municipality.
The municipality pays for its tasks mainly with taxes.
There are more than 2,000 municipalities in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Everyone in Switzerland lives in a **municipality**. Some are small villages with a few hundred inhabitants, others are big cities such as Zurich or Geneva. Several municipalities together form a **canton**. All the cantons together form the **Confederation**.

The municipality builds and looks after the **school building** and the nursery school. It looks after **playgrounds**, local streets, water and waste water. It organises rubbish collection and the **fire service**. When you move house, you register at the municipal office.

The municipality is run by the **municipal council**, headed by the mayor, called the municipal president. In many small municipalities, the voters decide at the **municipal assembly**. Larger municipalities and towns have their own **parliament** for this.

The municipality receives part of the **taxes** that people and companies in the area pay. On top of that come **fees**, for example for rubbish and waste water, and contributions from the canton. The fire service is often also paid for with a **fire service charge**. Every year a budget is drawn up showing what the money will be used for.

gewusst: Besides the place where they live, every Swiss citizen also has a place of origin, which is shown in their passport.
Because municipalities merge, there are far fewer municipalities today than fifty years ago.

teile.einleitung: Interest is something like the price of money. If you save money, you can receive interest. If you borrow money, you have to pay interest.
wichtigste: Interest is an amount paid for borrowed money.
The bank sometimes pays interest on money in a savings account.
Anyone who takes out a loan pays the bank interest.
Interest is usually given as a percentage per year.
Interest on savings accounts is often small.
There is no interest in a money box at home.
If the interest is lower than inflation, purchasing power falls.

abschnitte.text: When you put money into a **savings account**, the bank can work with this money. As a small thank you, it sometimes pays you **interest**. If Leonie has saved 100 francs and there are 101 francs in the account at the end of the year, the one franc is the interest. In a **money box** at home, on the other hand, the money stays exactly the same. Nobody works with your money there.

Anyone who borrows money from the bank takes out a **loan**. Later you have to pay the money back and pay interest on top. So interest is the price you pay for being allowed to use someone else's money. When buying a house, such a loan is called a **mortgage**. That is why borrowing always costs something.

Interest is usually given as an **interest rate** in **per cent** per year. One per cent is one hundredth. You calculate: amount times interest rate divided by 100. If Lia pays 3 per cent interest on a loan of 10,000 francs, that is 300 francs a year. At 1 per cent on 100 francs, it is 1 franc.

When prices rise, this is called **inflation**. If a savings account pays 1 per cent interest but prices rise by 2 per cent, in the end you can buy less than before. So **purchasing power** falls. That is why it is worth comparing interest and inflation. How high interest rates are in Switzerland depends strongly on the **key interest rate** of the Swiss National Bank.

gewusst: From 2015 to 2022, the Swiss National Bank even had a negative key interest rate. Some customers then had to pay the bank something for very large balances.
Small amounts of interest can add up to a noticeable sum over many years.

teile.einleitung: For school you need **school materials** such as books, exercise books and pens. In compulsory schooling, children get many of these things free. They are paid for by the municipality or the canton with tax money.
wichtigste: School materials include textbooks, exercise books, pens and other things.
In compulsory schooling, children receive many schoolbooks without buying them.
This is paid for by the municipality or the canton.
The reason is that compulsory schooling must be free of charge.
In Switzerland, many textbooks are produced by cantonal publishers.
Personal things such as gym shoes are usually bought by the parents.

abschnitte.text: **School materials** include many things: **textbooks** such as maths or language books, workbooks, pens, rulers and materials for crafts. In many schools today, **tablets** or laptops are added too. Without these materials, good lessons would hardly be possible.

The **Federal Constitution** requires primary schooling to be **free of charge**. That is why parents do not have to buy the most important textbooks for compulsory schooling. The **municipality** or the **canton** pays for them with **tax money**. Often the books belong to the school and are passed on to the next class after the school year.

In Switzerland, the schoolbooks are often developed by the cantons' **textbook publishers**. They work together with teachers and experts. The books follow **Lehrplan 21**, the curriculum that applies in the German-speaking cantons. In this way children in different cantons learn similar things.

Not everything is free. Personal things such as a **school bag**, **gym shoes** or clothes are usually bought by the parents. For school trips and camps, schools may only ask for a small contribution. In 2017 the **Federal Supreme Court** ruled that parents mainly have to pay for food, because they save on food at home at the same time.

gewusst: In many schools, a maths book is used by several year groups one after another.
Lehrplan 21 is called that because 21 German-speaking and multilingual cantons drew it up together.

teile.einleitung: **Net income** is an intermediate step in the tax return. You work it out by subtracting certain deductions from your total income. After the social deductions, this gives your taxable income.
wichtigste: You start with total income from wages, pensions and investment income.
From this you subtract work-related expenses, insurance premiums and other deductions.
The result is called net income.
From net income you subtract the social deductions, for example for children.
What is left is taxable income.
The tax is calculated on taxable income.

abschnitte.text: In the tax return, you first write down all your **earnings**. These include **wages**, pensions, interest and other income. Together they make up your **total income**. It is the starting point for the whole calculation. But not all of it is taxed.

People who work have costs, for example for **travelling to work** or eating away from home. These **work-related expenses** can be deducted. On top of that come other deductions, for example for **insurance premiums**, contributions to pillar 3a or **interest on debts**. If you subtract all this from total income, you get **net income**.

Next come the **social deductions**. They take personal circumstances into account, for example if someone has **children** or supports relatives. These deductions are fixed amounts set by law. They are meant to ease the burden on families and people with special responsibilities.

What is left after the social deductions is **taxable income**. The **tax scale** is applied to this amount. So the difference is this: with taxable income, the social deductions have also been subtracted. The Confederation and the cantons partly have different deductions, which is why the amounts can differ slightly.

gewusst: Net income is often used as the basis for further limits, for example for deducting donations.
Tax programs work out the individual steps from total income to taxable income automatically.

teile.einleitung: **Bracket creep**, known in German as “cold progression”, is a hidden tax increase. It happens when wages rise only because of **inflation** and you pay more tax as a result, even though you cannot afford any more. That is why the Confederation and the cantons offset it.
wichtigste: Bracket creep means higher taxes only because of inflation, without more purchasing power.
It happens because income tax is progressive.
If your wage rises only because of inflation, you slip into a higher band.
That is why the Confederation and the cantons adjust their tax scales to inflation.
Inflation should not secretly bring in more taxes.

abschnitte.text: **Inflation** means that prices rise. With the same money, you can then buy less. So that people do not become poorer, many companies raise wages in line with inflation. So you have more francs, but you cannot afford more than before. Your **purchasing power** stays the same.

Income tax is **progressive**: the higher the income, the higher the tax rate. If your wage rises because of inflation, you slip into a **higher band**. Then you pay a bigger share of your wage in tax. In the end you are left with less purchasing power than before, even though in real terms you do not earn any more.

To prevent this, the **Confederation and the cantons** regularly adjust their tax scales and deductions to inflation. So the bands are shifted along with prices. At federal level, this adjustment is required by law. In the cantons the rules vary.

gewusst: The German name “cold” means that the tax rises without anyone changing the law.

teile.einleitung: **World Savings Day** takes place every year at the end of October. On this day, many banks especially invite children to bring in their savings. The day is meant to remind people how important saving is.
wichtigste: World Savings Day is every year at the end of October, usually on 30 or 31 October.
Many banks invite children to empty their money box and pay the money in.
There is often a small present for doing so.
The day was agreed in 1924 at an international congress of savings banks.
It is meant to encourage people to save.

abschnitte.text: In October 1924, representatives of **savings banks** from many countries met at a congress in Milan. There they decided to introduce a common savings day. After the First World War, many people had lost their savings. With World Savings Day, the aim was to strengthen **trust** in saving. Since then it has been celebrated in many countries.

In Switzerland, many people know World Savings Day above all as a **children's day**. Children take their money box to the bank, where the money is counted and paid into their account. Many banks hand out small presents. Some also offer games or competitions. In this way children experience how their savings keep growing at the bank.

World Savings Day is meant to show that **saving regularly** pays off. If you practise putting money aside as a child, you often find it easier later on. Today it is not only about the money box. Many banks also use the day to give information about handling money.

gewusst: Because 31 October is a public holiday in some countries, banks there often celebrate World Savings Day on the last working day before it.
A similar idea lies behind the savings book that many children used to bring with them on World Savings Day.

teile.einleitung: The average tax rate shows what share of your whole income goes in tax. It is important for understanding how heavily someone is really taxed.
wichtigste: The average tax rate is the total tax divided by taxable income.
It is usually given as a percentage.
The marginal tax rate applies only to each additional franc.
Because of progression, the average rate is lower than the marginal tax rate.
In Switzerland, the rate also depends on where you live.

abschnitte.text: For the **average tax rate**, you divide the **total tax** by the **taxable income**. An example: someone has a taxable income of 50,000 francs and pays 5,000 francs in taxes. Then the average tax rate is 10 per cent. So it shows how much of each franc goes to the state on average. The numbers here are only an example.

In Switzerland, income taxes are **progressive**. This means: the higher the income, the higher the tax rate. The first francs are not taxed at all or only lightly. For higher parts of income, the rate rises. In this way people with a lot of income pay proportionally more.

The **marginal tax rate** shows how much tax is due on the **next additional franc**. Because of progression, it is higher than the average rate. After all, the lower parts of income are taxed at a lower rate. If you get a pay rise, you pay the marginal tax rate on that part. Even so, after a pay rise you always have more money left than before.

In Switzerland you pay taxes to the **Confederation**, the **canton** and the **municipality**. Cantons and municipalities set their rates themselves. That is why the average tax rate on the same income varies depending on **where you live**. Comparisons often show big differences between the cantons. This is called **tax competition**.

gewusst: With progression, a pay rise never means that you are left with less money overall.
Two people with exactly the same wage can pay very different amounts of tax in different municipalities.

teile.einleitung: **Debts** are money you have to pay back to someone. They play an important part in wealth tax: they are subtracted from your assets. Only net wealth is taxed.
wichtigste: Debts are money that you owe someone.
Wealth tax is charged only by cantons and municipalities, not by the Confederation.
Net wealth is what is taxed.
Net wealth is assets minus debts.
A mortgage is a typical debt for a house.
There is a deduction from income for private interest on debts.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who borrows money has **debts**. This can be a loan from the **bank**, an unpaid bill or a loan from people you know. Usually you also have to pay **interest** on borrowed money. Debts are not always bad, for example when buying a house. They become dangerous when you can no longer pay them back.

In Switzerland, you pay a tax on your **assets**. These include money in your account, securities, houses or land. This **wealth tax** is charged only by the **cantons** and **municipalities**. The Confederation has no wealth tax. What usually counts is the situation at the end of the year.

For wealth tax, what counts is **net wealth**. You calculate: assets minus debts. Anyone who owns a house worth one million francs and has a **mortgage** of 600,000 francs has only 400,000 francs of net wealth from this house. Many cantons also have a **tax-free allowance** up to which no wealth is taxed.

Young people sometimes get into debt through mobile phone contracts, online shopping or **small loans**. It is important only to spend what you really have. A **budget** helps you keep track. Anyone who does not know what to do can find help at a **debt advice service**, which exists in many cantons.

gewusst: Debts that are not paid can lead to debt enforcement proceedings and are then recorded in the debt enforcement register.
Tax debts themselves can also be declared as debts for wealth tax.

teile.einleitung: In museums you can marvel at art, look at dinosaur bones or discover the history of Switzerland. Many museums could not survive on entrance fees alone. That is why they receive money from municipalities, cantons or the Confederation, and this money comes from **taxes**.
wichtigste: Museums show **art**, **history**, **nature** and **technology** for everyone.
Many museums are supported by **municipalities** and **cantons**.
The money for this comes from **taxes**.
The Confederation also runs museums, for example the National Museum in Zurich.
Entrance fees usually cover only part of the costs.
In many museums, children get in cheaply or for free.

abschnitte.text: A **museum** collects valuable things, preserves them and shows them to the public. Experts research the collection and prepare **exhibitions**. Many museums also offer guided tours and workshops for school classes. In this way knowledge from art, history and nature becomes accessible to everyone.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the money come from?
abschnitte.text: A museum needs money for staff, buildings, heating, security and looking after the collection. **Entrance fees** are usually not enough for this. That is why **municipalities** and **cantons** support many museums with **tax money**. On top of that there are often contributions from foundations, companies and patrons.

The **Confederation** also supports museums. The **Swiss National Museum** includes the National Museum in Zurich, the Château de Prangins in the canton of Vaud and the Forum of Swiss History in Schwyz. There you can learn a lot about the history and culture of Switzerland.

Because the general public helps to fund museums, they should be open to as many people as possible. That is why many museums have low prices for families, schools and young people. In some cities there is a **Museum Night**, when you can visit many museums in one evening.

gewusst: There are more than a thousand museums in Switzerland, which is a very large number in relation to the population.
**International Museum Day** takes place every year in May.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who uses a bank card or online banking must handle it with care. This **duty of care** is written in the banks' terms and conditions. If you break it, you often have to bear any damage yourself.
wichtigste: Duty of care means handling your card, PIN and passwords carefully.
You must not write your PIN on the card or keep it together with the card.
You do not pass on your PIN or passwords to anyone.
A lost or stolen card must be blocked straight away.
You should check your bank statements regularly.
If you break these duties, you often have to pay for any damage yourself.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who gets a card accepts the bank's **terms and conditions**. They state how you must handle your card and log-in details. In return, the bank promises to cover the damage in certain circumstances if there is fraud. But this only applies if you yourself were careful. That is why it is worth knowing these rules.

The **PIN** is a secret number that belongs to the card. You should learn it by heart and not write it down. If you do note it down and leave it with the card, you are breaking the duty of care. If the card is then stolen and money is withdrawn, the bank often does not pay. When typing it in, you cover the keypad with your hand. Simple numbers such as a date of birth are not suitable as a PIN.

If your card is gone, you must have it **blocked straight away**. Every minute counts, because in that time someone could pay with it. If you have been robbed, you also report it to the police. The same applies to online banking: if you notice anything suspicious, you inform the bank immediately. If you wait a long time, you risk having to bear the damage yourself.

Taking care also includes regularly looking at your **bank statements** or the transactions in the app. That way you discover unknown debits early. You report mistakes or unknown payments to the bank within the time limit stated in the terms and conditions. The faster you act, the better a fraud can be cleared up.

gewusst: Many banks let you change your PIN at the cash machine to a number that is easy to remember but hard to guess.
In the banking app you can often block cards temporarily yourself and unblock them again.

teile.einleitung: There is a **deadline** for the tax return. Anyone who misses it and does not ask for an extension receives a **reminder** from the tax office. It gives a new, short deadline.
wichtigste: A deadline applies to the tax return, in many cantons the end of March.
You can ask for an **extension** beforehand.
Anyone who misses the deadline without an extension receives a **reminder** with a further deadline.
The reminder often costs a fee.
Anyone who still does not react is assessed **at the tax office's discretion**.
A **fine** may also be imposed.

abschnitte.text: Every year the tax office sends out the documents for the **tax return**. You must return them filled in by a certain date. In many cantons this is the end of March, but the cantons set it themselves. If you need more time, you can ask for an **extension** before it runs out, often easily online.

Anyone who misses the deadline and has no extension receives a **reminder**. In it, the tax office asks you to submit the return within a short **further deadline**. In many cantons this reminder costs a **fee**. By now at the latest, you should fill in the return.

If you still do not submit the return after the reminder, the tax office estimates your income and assets itself. This is called a **discretionary assessment**. The office tends to estimate on the high side, so you usually pay more. A **fine** can also be imposed, because you have not fulfilled your obligations.

gewusst: The German word “mahnen” means roughly to remind someone of something.

teile.einleitung: Taxes can be paid in different ways. With a **direct tax**, you get your own bill from the tax office and pay the tax yourself. The most important example is income tax.
wichtigste: Direct taxes are charged directly on the person or company.
You get your own tax bill from the tax office for them.
Income tax is the most important example of a direct tax.
Wealth tax and companies' profit tax are also direct taxes.
How much you pay depends on how much you earn or own.
In Switzerland, the Confederation, cantons and municipalities charge direct taxes.

abschnitte.text: With a **direct tax**, it is clear who has to pay it: the person who has the income. The tax office calculates the amount and sends a **tax bill**. The basis for this is the **tax return**, in which you state your income and assets. That way the office knows how much someone has earned.

The best-known direct tax is **income tax**. People who have assets also pay a **wealth tax**. Companies pay a **profit tax** on their profits. Another example is **inheritance tax**, which many cantons have.

In Switzerland, adults pay direct taxes in three places: to the **Confederation**, to the **canton** and to the **municipality**. The tax paid to the Confederation is called **direct federal tax**. Cantons and municipalities set their taxes themselves. That is why you pay different amounts depending on where you live.

Direct taxes are based on **economic ability to pay**. Those who earn more pay more. Often the percentage even rises with income. This is called **progression**. People who earn very little often pay no income tax at all.

The opposite are **indirect taxes** such as **VAT**. It is included in the price of goods, and you do not get a separate bill for it. With direct taxes, on the other hand, you can see exactly how much you pay. Together, both kinds pay for schools, roads and much more.

gewusst: Switzerland is one of the few countries where taxes also differ from canton to canton and from municipality to municipality.
Direct federal tax is time-limited by law and has to be extended by the people again and again.

teile.einleitung: Education costs money, for example for courses, books or school fees. Whether you can deduct these costs from your taxes depends on whether it is your first education or a later one.
wichtigste: The costs of a first education are normally not deductible.
A first education includes, for example, an apprenticeship or upper secondary school (Gymnasium).
These costs count as living costs.
Education and further training after the first qualification are deductible.
From the age of 20, other education costs can also be deductible.

abschnitte.text: A **first education** is the first course of education after compulsory schooling. Typical examples are an **apprenticeship** or the **Gymnasium**, the academic upper secondary school. A specialised upper secondary school also counts. When you finish, you have your first qualification at what is known as **upper secondary level**. Further education often follows after that.

The costs of a first education count as **living costs**. These are costs that are part of normal life, such as food or housing. Such costs cannot be deducted from taxes. In most cases the **parents** pay for the first education anyway. They often get a **child deduction** or an education deduction for it in their tax return.

It is different with **education and further training** after the first qualification. If, for example, you attend a course or a college of higher education after your apprenticeship, you may deduct the costs.
