People who do a course of education **from the age of 20** can also often claim a deduction. The deduction is limited to a **maximum amount** per year. You need receipts for it.

Since 2016, new rules on this have applied at federal level and in the cantons. The aim: people who **continue their training** should get tax support. Further training helps you stay up to date in your job. This benefits the people themselves and the economy too. Exactly how much you may deduct is set out in federal and cantonal law.

gewusst: A course after an apprenticeship can be deductible, but the apprenticeship itself is not.
Parents can often claim a child deduction for children in education, even if the children are already adults.

teile.einleitung: When you grow up, at some point you fill in a **tax return** yourself for the first time. That seems complicated at first, but it is quite manageable. Help is available from your parents, from the tax office and from advice centres.
wichtigste: In the tax return you state how much you earn and own.
Your first own tax return usually comes in the year after your 18th birthday.
The tax office sends the documents or access details for the online return.
Important documents are the salary statement and bank statements.
Many tax offices offer leaflets and information.
If you need more time, you can ask for an extension.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland you come of age at 18. From then on you are normally **liable to tax** yourself. Your first own tax return usually comes in the year after your 18th birthday. The tax office of your municipality or canton sends you a letter about it. It also says by when you must submit the return.

If you work or do an apprenticeship, you get a **salary statement** from your employer. It shows how much you earned in the year. On top of that come statements from your bank account, which show your assets at the end of the year. Receipts for **deductions** such as travel costs to work are also important. It is worth collecting all your documents in a folder throughout the year.

Many cantons offer an **online program** that guides you through the return step by step. It calculates a lot by itself and shows what is still missing. It is important to be honest and complete. Anyone who deliberately hides something can be fined.

The first time, **parents** often help, as they have done many tax returns themselves. The **tax office** also gives information by phone or at the counter and has **leaflets** for young adults. Some municipalities, youth advice services or associations offer courses. Asking is allowed and makes sense.

The tax return must be submitted by a certain **deadline**. If you cannot manage it, you can usually ask for an **extension**. Anyone who submits nothing at all is sent a reminder and their tax is estimated by the office. This estimate is often on the high side, which is why it pays to fill in the return on time.

gewusst: Young people in education often have so little income that they pay little or no income tax.
Even if you earn nothing, you still have to fill in the tax return if the tax office asks for it.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has two Federal Institutes of Technology: ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne. They belong to the Confederation and are mostly paid for with federal money.
wichtigste: ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne are universities of the Confederation.
They are mostly financed with federal money.
ETH Zurich opened in 1855.
Several research institutes also belong to the ETH Domain.
Both universities are among the best known in the world.

abschnitte.text: **ETH** stands for **Eidgenössische Technische Hochschule**, the Federal Institute of Technology. There are two of them: **ETH Zurich** and **EPFL** in Lausanne. EPFL is the French abbreviation. Most universities in Switzerland belong to the cantons. The two Federal Institutes of Technology, by contrast, are a matter for the **Confederation**.

Most of the money comes from the **Confederation**, meaning money from federal taxes. On top of that come contributions from research projects, from companies and from foundations. Students' tuition fees cover only a small part. In this way the Confederation wants to strengthen **education and research**. Good research brings new ideas, companies and jobs.

**ETH Zurich** opened in **1855**, a few years after the federal state was founded. The school in Lausanne was at first a school of the canton of Vaud. In **1969** the Confederation took it over, and it became EPFL. Since then Switzerland has had two federal institutes of technology. One is in German-speaking Switzerland, one in French-speaking Switzerland.

Besides the two universities, four **research institutes** also belong to the **ETH Domain**. These are the Paul Scherrer Institute, the WSL for forest, snow and landscape, Empa and Eawag for water research. There, experts carry out research on topics such as energy, materials and the environment. **Albert Einstein** also studied at ETH Zurich. Many Nobel Prize winners have studied or done research there.

gewusst: Albert Einstein completed his studies at ETH Zurich in 1900.
The WSL includes the Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research in Davos, which issues avalanche warnings.

teile.einleitung: TWINT is a Swiss app for paying with your mobile phone. With it you can send money in shops, on the internet, at the kiosk or simply between friends. TWINT is the most popular mobile payment method in Switzerland.
wichtigste: TWINT is a Swiss app that lets you pay with your mobile phone.
With TWINT you can also send money directly to friends and family.
In a shop you pay by scanning a QR code.
The app is offered by many Swiss banks and PostFinance.
The payment is taken directly from the linked bank account.
More than five million people in Switzerland use TWINT (as of about 2024).
The app is protected with a PIN, fingerprint or face recognition.

abschnitte.text: **TWINT** is a payment app that was developed in Switzerland. You download your own bank's app and link it to your **bank account**. After that you can pay with your mobile phone, without cash or a card. The money goes directly from your account to the recipient.

In a shop or at a machine, you scan a **QR code** and confirm the amount in the app. Online, you choose TWINT when paying and confirm the payment on your phone. Between friends, you can simply send money to a **mobile number**, for example to share the cost of a pizza. Parking, tickets, donations and farm shops can often be paid with TWINT too.

TWINT was developed by PostFinance and came onto the market in 2015. At the same time there was the payment app Paymit, run by several banks. In 2016 the two decided to merge, and since then the big Swiss banks have run TWINT together. The name TWINT is a **made-up word** and not an abbreviation.

The app is protected with a **PIN**, a fingerprint or face recognition. You must not tell anyone these log-in details. You should be careful with money requests from strangers, because fraudsters also try to get money through TWINT. If your phone is lost, you should have TWINT blocked through your bank straight away.

TWINT is the most widely used **mobile payment method** in Switzerland. More than five million people use the app (as of about 2024), and many shops, clubs and market stalls accept it. TWINT is especially practical for small amounts, which used to be paid mostly in cash. In principle, TWINT only works with Swiss francs and an account at a Swiss bank.

begriffe.erklaerung: A program for a mobile phone or tablet.
A square code that you scan with your phone camera.
Paying with your mobile phone instead of cash or a card.
A request in the app asking someone to send you money.

gewusst: Many Swiss people say “I'll TWINT you the money”, so TWINT has almost become a verb of its own.
With TWINT you can often manage loyalty cards and vouchers too.
Street musicians and charity collectors today often display a TWINT code as well.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who is in trouble and needs the police dials **117**. The call is free, and you do not have to pay for the help either. That is because the police are financed with **tax money**.
wichtigste: The emergency number for the **police** is **117**.
You can reach the fire service on **118** and the ambulance service on **144**.
The European emergency number **112** also works in Switzerland.
Emergency calls are free from any phone, including mobiles.
The police are paid for with **tax money**.
Anyone in trouble may always call, children too.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are several **emergency numbers**. On **117** you reach the police, on **118** the fire service and on **144** the ambulance service. The number **112** also puts you through to the police. **Rega**, the helicopter rescue service, has the number 1414.

Stay calm and first say your **name**. Then explain **where** you are and **what** has happened. Listen carefully and answer the questions. Only hang up when the person on the phone tells you to. Emergency numbers may only be dialled in an emergency, so that the lines stay free for real help.

In Switzerland, the **police** belong mainly to the **cantons**; many cities also have their own city police. Their wages, cars and equipment are paid for with **tax money**. That is why nobody who calls the police in an emergency has to worry about a bill. In this way everyone can get help, no matter how much money they have.

gewusst: You can call emergency numbers even from a mobile phone with no credit.
On the number 145 you can get help with poisoning, for example if a child has swallowed something dangerous.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who is not yet 18 is considered a **minor**. Special tax rules apply to minors. Usually their income and assets are declared by their parents, but not their wages from work.
wichtigste: A minor is anyone who is not yet **18 years** old.
The income and assets of minors are in principle taxed together with those of their **parents**.
**Earned income**, for example an apprentice's wage, is taxed separately.
That is why, depending on the canton, apprentices get their own tax form early on.
From 18, everyone fills in their own tax return.

abschnitte.text: If a child has a savings account or inherits money, these **assets** are declared in the parents' tax return. The **interest** on them belongs there too. The child does not have to fill in a return of their own. The parents can also make a **child deduction** for each child.

abschnitte.titel: Your own wages are taxed separately
abschnitte.text: Something different applies to money that minors earn with their own work. This **earned income** is taxed **separately**, meaning it is not counted as part of the parents' income. This mainly concerns the **apprentice's wage**. A 16-year-old apprentice therefore pays the tax on her wage herself.

On your 18th birthday you come **of age**. From then on you fill in a completely separate **tax return** for all your income and assets. How early young people with an apprentice's wage get their own form is regulated slightly differently by each canton.

gewusst: At 18 you may also vote and elect in Switzerland.
In the canton of Glarus, young people may vote on cantonal and municipal questions from the age of 16.

teile.einleitung: The salary statement shows various amounts. For the tax return one is particularly important: the **net wage**. It is entered as income from employment.
wichtigste: The **gross wage** is the full wage before deductions.
The **net wage** is the gross wage minus contributions to social insurance and the pension fund.
These contributions include **AVS, IV, EO, unemployment insurance** and occupational pension provision.
In the tax return, you enter the net wage as shown on the **salary statement**.
The contributions are therefore already taken into account and are not deducted again.

abschnitte.text: The **gross wage** is the wage you earn according to your contract. The employer deducts contributions from it, for example for the **AVS**, the IV, the EO, unemployment insurance and the **pension fund**. What is left is the **net wage**. It is shown on the salary statement.

In the tax return, you state your **income from employment**. For this, you copy the **net wage** from the salary statement. Employment means you are employed by a company or an authority. Anyone who has had several jobs adds up the net wages from all their salary statements.

Because the contributions to the AVS and the pension fund have already been taken off the net wage, you may not deduct them again. But other deductions are still possible, for example for **travelling to work**, **meals** or voluntary payments into **pillar 3a**. Only after that do you arrive at your taxable income.

gewusst: The net wage in the tax return is not always the same as the amount in the bank account, because, for example, contributions to accident insurance may be treated differently.

teile.einleitung: In a popular vote, the people entitled to vote decide on a question themselves. In Switzerland they can often have a say, including on what tax money is spent on.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, those entitled to vote vote several times a year.
Votes are held in the municipality, in the canton and at federal level.
In the municipality, a vote might be about whether a new swimming pool should be built.
Swiss citizens aged 18 and over are entitled to vote.
In the canton of Glarus you may vote on cantonal and municipal matters from the age of 16.
With the initiative and the referendum, the people can trigger votes themselves.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland is a **direct democracy**. This means that citizens do not only elect the parliament but also decide on questions themselves. This is called a **popular vote**. At federal level there are usually four voting dates a year. You can vote at the polling station, by post and, in some cantons on a trial basis, electronically.

In the **municipality**, votes are often about things close to home. Should a new **swimming pool** or school building be built? How high should the **tax rate** be? In smaller municipalities this is decided at the **municipal assembly**, in larger ones at the ballot box. In this way the voters have a say in what **tax money** is spent on.

With a **popular initiative**, people can demand a change to the Federal Constitution. For this, 100,000 signatures are needed within 18 months. With a **referendum**, people can demand a vote on a new law. For this, 50,000 signatures are needed within 100 days. Changes to the Constitution need a **popular majority** and a **majority of the cantons**, meaning a majority of the votes and of the cantons.

At federal level, Swiss citizens aged **18** and over may vote. In the canton of **Glarus**, the voting age is 16 for cantonal and municipal matters. In some cantons and municipalities, foreign residents may also have a say. In Appenzell Innerrhoden and Glarus there is still the **Landsgemeinde**. There the voters vote in the open air by raising their hands.

gewusst: Switzerland has held more national popular votes than any other country in the world.
Women's right to vote at federal level was only introduced in Switzerland in 1971.

teile.einleitung: If you travel to work, you have costs for tickets, a bike or a car. In Switzerland you may deduct part of these **travel costs** in your tax return. That way you pay a little less tax.
wichtigste: The costs of getting between home and work are deductible.
What usually counts is the cost of public transport.
Car costs only count if public transport is not a reasonable option.
Private journeys in your free time cannot be deducted.
At federal level and in many cantons there is an upper limit on the deduction.

abschnitte.text: A **deduction** is an amount that you may subtract from your income before the tax is calculated. The idea: if you have to spend money just to be able to work, you should not pay tax on it. That is why such costs are called **work-related expenses**. Travel costs are part of them.

In principle, the tax office calculates with the cost of **buses, trams and trains**, for example a season ticket. If you travel by bike or a small motorbike, you can often deduct a fixed **flat rate**. The exact rules are in the canton's guidance notes.

The higher **car costs** are only accepted if public transport is **not a reasonable option**. This may be the case if there is no connection, if someone works at night or in **shifts**, or if you save a great deal of time by car. Health reasons can also count. You must give your reasons in the tax return.

For **direct federal tax** there is a maximum amount for the travel cost deduction. Many cantons also have an upper limit, but the amounts vary. So anyone who commutes a very long way cannot deduct all their costs. In this way the tax system is not meant to reward long journeys to work.

gewusst: The upper limit at federal level was introduced in connection with the expansion of the railway infrastructure.
For eating lunch away from home there is often a separate deduction, not under travel costs.

teile.einleitung: The **fire service** puts out fires and helps with accidents, storms and floods. In Switzerland you can reach it on the number **118**. It is usually organised by the municipality.
wichtigste: The emergency number for the fire service is 118.
The municipality usually organises the fire service.
It is paid for largely with taxes and charges.
Many firefighters do it alongside their job; this is called a volunteer fire service.
Large cities also have a professional fire service.

abschnitte.text: If there is a fire, you dial **118**. Say calmly **where** the fire is, **what** has happened and **who** is calling. Stay on the phone until the person at the control centre has finished asking questions. The European emergency number **112** also works in Switzerland.

The fire service does not only put out fires. It rescues people from cars after accidents, pumps water out of cellars and helps during **storms** and **floods**. It also deals with spilt oil or dangerous substances. That is why it has many different vehicles and pieces of equipment.

Every **municipality** makes sure that a fire service is ready. Small municipalities often join together and have a shared fire service. Most fire services are made up of **volunteers** from the village who have another job. They practise regularly and turn out when the alarm goes.

The money comes from **municipal taxes** and, in many cantons, from a **fire service exemption charge**. This is paid by adults who do not serve in the fire service. In many cantons, the cantonal **building insurance** also supports the fire services, for example when buying vehicles.

gewusst: Most firefighters in Switzerland are not professionals but volunteers.
Many fire services have a youth fire service, in which even children and teenagers can take part.

teile.einleitung: We often come across the word **public**: public playground, public school, public transport. It means that something is **there for everyone**. It is often paid for with taxes.
wichtigste: Public means: there for everyone.
The opposite of public is private.
Many public things belong to the municipality, the canton or the Confederation.
They are often built and maintained with tax money.
Examples are playgrounds, roads, schools and libraries.
Because public things belong to everyone, we look after them together.

abschnitte.text: A **public playground** may be used by all children, without paying to get in. The same applies to parks, streets, fountains and many footpaths. Public means that everyone has access. Sometimes there are rules, for example opening times, but nobody is shut out.

The opposite of public is **private**. A private garden belongs to a family, and only they may decide who can come in. A public park belongs to the general public. With schools there are both: the **public school** is free, a private school charges school fees.

Public things are not free. Someone has to build, clean and repair them. This is usually done by the **municipality**, the **canton** or the **Confederation**. People also speak of the **public sector**. The money for it comes largely from the **taxes** that people and companies pay.

Because public things belong to everyone, everyone should treat them well. Anyone who leaves rubbish lying around or breaks something harms everyone. In the end, everyone pays for the repair again with their taxes. That is why rubbish belongs in the bin, and graffiti on walls is forbidden.

gewusst: According to the Federal Constitution, attending public compulsory school in Switzerland is free of charge.
In Switzerland, authorities are also meant to be as open as possible: under the principle of transparency, you may look at many official documents.

teile.einleitung: The **Swiss National Bank** (SNB) is the central bank of Switzerland. It looks after the franc and conducts the country's monetary policy. Its most important aim is to keep prices stable.
wichtigste: The SNB is the central bank of Switzerland and has head offices in Bern and Zurich.
Its main aim is price stability, while also keeping an eye on the economy.
For the SNB, price stability means that consumer prices rise by less than 2% a year.
The SNB also wants to avoid falling prices, known as deflation.
The SNB issues the banknotes; the coins are minted by the Confederation.
Of its profit distributions, one third goes to the Confederation and two thirds to the cantons.

abschnitte.text: The SNB is not an ordinary bank. Private individuals cannot open an account there. Instead it is the **bank of the banks** and the guardian of the franc. It was founded in 1907. The Federal Constitution gives it the task of conducting a monetary policy that serves the interests of the country as a whole. In doing so it is independent and takes no instructions from the government.

When prices rise sharply, this is called **inflation**. Then you can buy less with the same money. The SNB speaks of price stability when consumer prices rise by less than 2% a year. If prices fall over a long time, this is called **deflation**. That can also harm the economy, which is why the SNB wants to avoid both.

The most important tool is the **SNB policy rate**. If the SNB raises it, borrowing money becomes more expensive and inflation is slowed down. If it lowers it, loans become cheaper and the economy is given a boost. The SNB can also buy or sell foreign currencies to influence the value of the franc. In addition, it manages Switzerland's currency reserves, including a lot of gold.

The SNB issues the **banknotes** and makes sure there is enough cash. The current series of notes is the ninth and was introduced from 2016. The coins, on the other hand, are minted by the Federal Mint **Swissmint** on behalf of the Confederation. But the SNB also puts them into circulation.

abschnitte.titel: Profits for the Confederation and cantons
abschnitte.text: The SNB can make profits or losses, mainly with its foreign currencies and its gold. When there is enough profit, it pays part of it out to the **public sector**. By law, one third goes to the Confederation and two thirds to the cantons. In years with big losses, there may be no payout at all.

gewusst: The SNB is a public limited company whose shares are traded on the stock exchange. Most of the shares belong to cantons and cantonal banks.
From 2011 to 2015 the SNB set a minimum exchange rate of 1.20 francs to the euro.
Part of the SNB's gold reserves is stored in Switzerland and part abroad.

teile.einleitung: You should be careful with money, cards and games on a tablet. A few simple rules help you to protect your money. The most important rule: if something seems strange, tell an adult straight away.
wichtigste: If your wallet is gone, tell your parents straight away so that cards can be blocked.
A real bank never asks for your PIN.
If you find a wallet, you hand it in at the lost property office or to the police.
On the bus, you carry your wallet in a closed bag close to your body.
Before you spend money in a game, you ask your parents.
If a cash machine looks strange, you do not put your card in.

abschnitte.text: If your wallet is gone, tell your parents **straight away**. Maybe there was a card in it that needs to be **blocked** quickly. Then nobody else can pay with it. After that you can ask at the lost property office whether someone has handed it in. Many municipalities have a lost property office, and the railways often have one too.

Sometimes fraudsters call and say they are from the bank. They ask for your **PIN** or a code. A real bank never does that. Do not give anything away, hang up and tell your parents. The same goes for messages on your mobile phone that ask for passwords.

A wallet you find belongs to someone else. Hand it in together with an adult at the **lost property office** or to the **police**. That way it can get back to its owner. Under Swiss law, anyone who hands in something valuable can receive a fair **finder's reward**. You may not simply keep things you find.

abschnitte.titel: Out and about and at the cash machine
abschnitte.text: In a crowd, for example on the bus, someone can reach into open bags without being noticed. So carry your wallet in a **closed bag** close to your body. Fraudsters sometimes attach devices to cash machines to steal card details. This is called **skimming**. If something looks loose, stuck on or unusual, do not use the cash machine and tell an adult.

Many games on tablets and mobile phones are free, but they sell extras. These **in-app purchases** cost real money, even if they look like game coins. Sometimes it takes just a single tap. So always ask your parents first. They can set the device so that purchases need a password.

gewusst: Cards can be blocked around the clock; the number is often on the back of the card or in the banking app.
You never write your PIN on the card and never tell it to anyone, not even your friends.

teile.einleitung: **Withholding tax** is a federal tax on certain kinds of income, such as dividends and interest. It is 35% and is deducted directly at source. If you declare the income correctly in your tax return, you get it back.
wichtigste: Withholding tax is 35%.
It is deducted from dividends of Swiss companies and from larger interest income.
The deduction is made directly, before the money reaches the recipient.
If you declare the income in your tax return, you get the tax back.
It is meant to ensure that wealth and income are taxed honestly.
Small amounts of interest on bank accounts are exempt up to a limit.

abschnitte.text: When a Swiss company pays its shareholders a **dividend**, it first deducts 35%. It transfers this amount to the **Federal Tax Administration**. The recipient gets only the remaining 65%. The same happens with interest on bank accounts, but only above a certain amount per year. That is why it is called a tax at source.

abschnitte.titel: Getting it back with your tax return
abschnitte.text: Anyone who lives in Switzerland can **reclaim** the withholding tax. To do this, you list your securities and income in the **schedule of securities** in your tax return. The tax that was deducted is then offset against your taxes or paid back. That is also where its German name, which means “offsetting tax”, comes from. If you hide the income, you lose the 35%.

Withholding tax is above all a **safeguard tax**. It is meant to stop people hiding their wealth and income from the tax authorities. Anyone who does not declare simply pays the 35%, and that is usually more than the normal tax. So it pays to be honest. For the Confederation, it is also an important source of income.

Withholding tax does not only apply to dividends and interest. It is also charged, for example, on large **lottery winnings** and on certain insurance payments. People who live abroad can reclaim part of it, depending on the **double taxation agreement**. The exact rules are set out in the Federal Act on Withholding Tax.

gewusst: Withholding tax was introduced during the Second World War, in 1944.
Interest on normal bank accounts is exempt from the tax as long as it is not more than 200 francs a year.

teile.einleitung: Taxes are a way of **sharing** costs **fairly** among everyone. Everyone helps, but not everyone pays the same amount. Those who earn more give more; those who have little give less.
wichtigste: With taxes, everyone together pays for schools, roads and help for people in need.
In Switzerland, people who earn a lot pay more tax than people on low wages.
People who earn little need most of their money for food and housing.
Fair means: each person gives according to what they can afford.
This idea is also written in the Federal Constitution.

abschnitte.text: Imagine everyone had to pay the same amount. For a family on a low wage that would be very hard; for a rich person it would hardly be noticeable. That is why Switzerland follows the principle of **economic ability to pay**. This means: those who can carry more, carry more.

With income tax, the tax rate rises with income. This is called **progression**. So someone who earns twice as much pays more than twice as much tax. Very small incomes are often completely tax-free, so that the money for the basics remains.

Every person needs money for **food, housing and clothes**. People who earn little spend almost everything on these. If these people had a lot of tax taken from them, they would no longer have enough to live on. **Deductions**, for example for children, also help families.

Even so, almost everyone makes a contribution, for example through **VAT** when shopping. How high taxes should be is often argued about in politics. Some think the rich should pay even more; others think taxes are already high enough. In Switzerland, the voters often decide on this.

gewusst: The Federal Constitution states that taxes are charged according to economic ability to pay.
A small share of taxpayers pays a large share of direct federal tax.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Tax Administration, FTA for short (ESTV in German), is the tax authority of the Confederation. Among other things, it deals with VAT and direct federal tax.
wichtigste: ESTV is the German abbreviation for the Federal Tax Administration.
It is the tax authority of the Confederation.
It is responsible for VAT.
For direct federal tax, it supervises the cantons.
The FTA belongs to the Federal Department of Finance.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Tax Administration** is a federal office. It belongs to the **Federal Department of Finance**. Its head office is in **Bern**. Its task is to make sure that federal taxes are charged correctly. That way the Confederation gets the money for its tasks.

One of its main tasks is **value added tax**, VAT for short. Companies that are liable for VAT regularly settle their accounts with the FTA. They report how much tax they have taken in. The FTA checks these returns and inspects companies. VAT on goods from abroad, on the other hand, is the responsibility of the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security.

**Direct federal tax** is collected by the cantons. The FTA **supervises** them in doing so, so that the same rules apply everywhere. The FTA is also responsible for **withholding tax**. This 35 per cent tax is deducted, for example, from interest and dividends. If you declare it correctly in your tax return, you get it back.

The FTA also produces **statistics** and comparisons of taxes in the cantons. It publishes leaflets that explain how taxes work. For schools it offers learning materials on the subject of taxes. In this way it helps people understand the tax system better. For your own tax return, however, the cantonal tax office is usually the right place.

gewusst: Withholding tax is meant to prevent people from hiding interest or assets in their tax return.
Private individuals' tax returns are dealt with not by the FTA but by the cantonal tax office.

teile.einleitung: Two-factor authentication is a security method in which you have to provide two different proofs, when logging in, that you really are the right person. In online banking this is usually a password plus a confirmation on your mobile phone. That way your account stays protected even if someone has found out your password.
wichtigste: With two-factor authentication, you need two different proofs to log in.
One factor is something you know, for example a password or a PIN.
Another factor is something you have, for example a mobile phone or a small device from the bank.
Body features such as a fingerprint or your face can also serve as a factor.
A second factor makes it much harder for fraudsters to log into someone else's account.
All Swiss banks today require this kind of double log-in for online banking.
You must never pass on codes and confirmations to other people.

abschnitte.text: The word **authentication** means proving who you are. With two-factor authentication, **2FA** for short, you need two proofs from different areas to do this. You can compare it to a front door with two locks. A burglar would then have to steal two different keys.

Experts distinguish three groups of factors. **Knowledge** is something only you have in your head, such as a password. **Possession** is an object only you have, for example your smartphone or a bank card. **Biometrics** are features of your body, such as your fingerprint or face.

abschnitte.titel: How it works in online banking
abschnitte.text: First you enter your contract number and password. Then a message appears on your mobile phone in the bank's app, which you have to confirm. Some banks instead send a code by text message or show a coloured graphic that you scan with your phone. Only when both steps work does the account open.

Fraudsters often try to get passwords with fake emails, known as **phishing**. But thanks to 2FA, a stolen password alone gets them nowhere. That is why some try to talk people into giving away a code or confirming a message over the phone. But a real bank never asks for passwords or confirmation codes.

Switch on two-factor authentication for email, gaming accounts and social networks too. Never confirm a log-in on your phone that you did not start yourself. Protect your phone with a lock so that a thief cannot simply use it. Keep **recovery codes** in a safe place in case your phone gets lost.

begriffe.erklaerung: Proving that you really are the person you claim to be.
A piece of proof when logging in, for example a password or your mobile phone.
Fraud using fake messages to steal passwords or codes.
Recognising a person by body features such as a fingerprint or face.

gewusst: Two passwords one after the other do not count as real two-factor authentication, because both are knowledge.
In the past, banks sent out paper lists of codes that you had to type in one after another when logging in.
When you pay by card in a shop, you also use two factors: the card as possession and the PIN as knowledge.

teile.einleitung: In many municipalities, there are green boxes with little bags for **dog mess** at the side of paths. Dog owners can use them to pick up their dog's mess cleanly and dispose of it. That way paths, meadows and playgrounds stay clean.
wichtigste: The boxes at the side of paths are for dog mess.
You pick up the mess with a little bag and throw it into the box.
The municipality puts up the boxes and empties them.
This is often paid for with the dog tax.
In many places, anyone who leaves the mess lying around can be fined.

abschnitte.text: Dog mess on paths is unpleasant if you step in it. On **meadows and fields** it is also a problem for cows and other animals, because it can get into their feed. It can also contain **germs**. That is why it belongs in the rubbish and not on the ground.

The **municipality** puts up the boxes, refills the bags and empties the containers regularly. In Switzerland they are often known by the name **Robidog**. Dog owners can pick up the mess with the bag, tie it up and throw it straight into the box. You can also put the bag in your ordinary rubbish at home.

Anyone who keeps a dog pays a **dog tax** in most municipalities. The amount varies from municipality to municipality. Among other things, the money pays for the boxes and bags. Anyone who leaves the mess lying around risks a **fine** in many municipalities.

gewusst: Dog mess does not belong in the compost or the green waste, but in the general rubbish.

teile.einleitung: Companies such as public limited companies and limited liability companies pay **profit tax** on their profits. It goes to the Confederation, canton and municipality. For the state it is an important source of income.
wichtigste: Companies pay profit tax on their profits.
It goes to the Confederation, canton and municipality.
At federal level, the rate is 8.5 per cent of the profit.
The cantons set their rates themselves, which is why they differ.
Since 2024, a minimum tax has applied to very large international corporations.

abschnitte.text: Profit tax is paid by **legal entities**. These are companies that are legally independent, for example an **AG**, a **GmbH** or a cooperative. With a **sole proprietorship**, on the other hand, the owner pays ordinary income tax on the profit.

The **Confederation** charges a fixed rate of **8.5 per cent** on profits. On top of that come the taxes of the **canton** and **municipality**. These are different in every canton. That is why the total tax burden for companies is not equally high everywhere.

In the past, some companies had special tax advantages in some cantons. With the **Tax Reform and AHV Financing**, which the people accepted in 2019, these were abolished. Afterwards many cantons lowered their profit taxes for all companies. At the same time, the **AVS** received additional money.

Many countries have agreed on a worldwide **minimum tax** for very large corporations. Switzerland accepted this rule in a vote in 2023. Since 2024, such corporations have had to pay at least **15 per cent** tax on their profits. For small companies such as the village bakery, nothing changes as a result.

gewusst: Profit tax itself can be deducted as an expense when calculating taxable profit.
Companies that make a loss pay no profit tax, but still have to submit a tax return.

teile.einleitung: With almost every purchase you pay a tax without noticing. It is called **value added tax**, **VAT** for short (MWST in German). It is already included in the price, whether you buy an ice cream, a comic or a T-shirt.
wichtigste: **VAT** is included in the price of many goods and services.
It is a tax of the **Confederation** and one of its most important sources of income.
Everyone who buys something pays it, children too.
Shops collect it and transfer it to the **Federal Tax Administration**.
Since 2024 the standard rate has been **8.1 per cent**.
A lower rate applies to food and books.
Companies with a turnover of less than 100,000 francs a year do not have to account for VAT.

abschnitte.text: When Lea buys an ice cream, a tax is already included in the price: **VAT**. On many till receipts it appears with the German abbreviation **MWST**. Because all customers pay it when shopping, children pay it too. That is why it is called a tax on **consumption**.

The shop takes in the VAT when it sells. But it does not keep it; it passes it on to the **Federal Tax Administration**. So the money goes to the **Confederation**. Companies may deduct the VAT they themselves paid when buying their goods.

Since 2024 the **standard rate** has been 8.1 per cent. If a T-shirt costs 100 francs without VAT, 8.10 francs are added. So it costs 108.10 francs. For food, books, comics and medicines, a **reduced rate** of 2.6 per cent applies. For overnight stays in hotels there is a special rate of 3.8 per cent.

VAT is one of the Confederation's biggest sources of income. With the money it pays, for example, for education, transport and the army. Part of it also goes to the **AVS**. Very small companies with an annual turnover of less than **100,000 francs** do not have to account for VAT. This saves them a lot of work.

gewusst: VAT has existed in Switzerland since 1995. Before that there was the **turnover tax on goods**.
Compared with EU countries, the Swiss VAT rate is very low; there it is usually around 20 per cent.

teile.einleitung: Many people travel to work every day, by train, bike or car. You can often deduct the cost of this commute in your tax return.
wichtigste: The cost of commuting counts as a work-related expense.
You may deduct it in your tax return within certain limits.
Holidays or presents cannot be deducted.
At federal level there has been an upper limit on the travel cost deduction since 2016.
The cantons also have their own rules for the deduction.
People who travel back and forth between home and work every day are called commuters.

abschnitte.text: Many people do not live in the same place where they work. They travel there and back every day; they are called **commuters**. In Switzerland, a large share of working people commute to another municipality. Many use **public transport** for this, with trains, trams and buses. Others go by bike or by car.

The cost of the **commute** counts as a **work-related expense**. You only have it because you work. That is why you may deduct it from your income in your **tax return**. Usually you deduct the cost of public transport, for example for a season ticket. A car can often only be deducted if public transport is not a reasonable option.

The deduction is not unlimited. At **federal** level there has been an upper limit on travel costs since **2016**. It was introduced after the voters had accepted the proposal on financing the railway infrastructure. Many **cantons** also have their own upper limits, which vary in size. For a bike there is often a fixed **flat rate**.

You may only deduct what the law allows. Spending on **holidays**, hobbies or **presents** belongs to private life and cannot be deducted. Journeys in your free time do not count as commuting either. If you deduct too much, you can expect the tax office to ask questions. That is why you keep receipts such as your season ticket safe.

gewusst: With the GA travelcard, the general season ticket, you can use almost all trains, buses and boats in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: When people in Switzerland talk about the “Bund”, the Confederation, they mean the state of the whole of Switzerland. It is responsible for tasks that concern the whole country, for example motorways and the army.
wichtigste: The “Bund” means the state of the whole of Switzerland, the Confederation.
Switzerland has three levels: Confederation, cantons and municipalities.
The Confederation looks after tasks for the whole country.
These include, for example, the army, motorways and foreign policy.
The Confederation pays for its tasks with taxes such as VAT.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland is a **federal state**. This means that several cantons have joined together to form a common state. This common state is called the **Confederation**. Its basis is the **Federal Constitution**; the first one dates from 1848. That is why the country is also called the “Swiss Confederation”.

In Switzerland there are three **levels of government**. Closest to the people are the **municipalities**. Above them are the **26 cantons**. At the very top is the **Confederation**. Each level has its own tasks and charges its own taxes. Whatever the municipality or the canton can sort out well on its own should be dealt with there.

The Confederation takes on tasks that are important for the **whole country**. It is responsible for the **army**, which protects the whole country. It owns the **motorways**, which connect all parts of the country. It manages relations with other countries and the **AVS**. Customs, the railway network and the national currency, the franc, are also matters for the Confederation.

The government of the Confederation is the **Federal Council**, with seven members. The laws are made by Parliament, the **Federal Assembly**. It consists of the **National Council** with 200 members and the **Council of States** with 46 members. On important questions, the **people** decide in popular votes. The government and Parliament are based in Bern.

gewusst: The abbreviation CH on cars stands for “Confoederatio Helvetica”, the Latin name of Switzerland.
Although Switzerland is a federal state, it still calls itself a “Confederation” today.

teile.einleitung: The **SMI** is the best-known share index in Switzerland. The abbreviation stands for Swiss Market Index. In a single number, it shows how the largest Swiss companies are doing on the stock exchange.
wichtigste: SMI stands for Swiss Market Index.
It includes the 20 largest and most traded shares on the Swiss stock exchange.
The SMI is calculated by the Swiss stock exchange SIX in Zurich.
If the SMI rises, the shares of these companies have on average become worth more.
Large companies carry more weight in the index than smaller ones.
The SMI was introduced in 1988.

abschnitte.text: An **index** combines many individual values into one number. With the SMI, these are the prices of 20 shares. Instead of looking at each company separately, you can see from the index whether the stock exchange as a whole is going up or down. That is why the SMI is also called the thermometer of the Swiss stock exchange. It is mentioned in the news almost every day.

The SMI contains the largest companies whose shares are traded on the **SIX Swiss Exchange**. These include well-known names such as Nestlé, Novartis and Roche. Exactly which companies are included is reviewed regularly. If a company becomes smaller or its shares are traded less often, it can drop out of the index. Another company then takes its place.

The shares do not all count the same. What matters is the **market capitalisation**, meaning the value of all the freely tradable shares of a company. The bigger a company, the more strongly it affects the index. So that a single company does not get too much weight, there is an upper limit. The SMI started with a value of 1500 points.

abschnitte.titel: What the SMI is used for
abschnitte.text: Investors like to compare their investments with the SMI. There are also **index funds** that simply buy all the SMI shares in the same proportions. Anyone who owns such a fund goes through roughly the same ups and downs as the index. Besides the SMI there are other indices, for example the SPI, which includes many more Swiss companies.

gewusst: The SMI is a price index: dividends that are paid out are not added to it.
Just a few companies make up a large part of the SMI, which is why Nestlé, Novartis and Roche move the index especially strongly.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who drives a car on Swiss motorways needs a vignette. Since 2023 it has been available not only as a sticker but also electronically: the e-vignette.
wichtigste: The e-vignette is an electronic vignette.
It is linked to the vehicle's number plate.
It has existed since 2023.
The sticker for the windscreen is still available.
The money goes towards building and maintaining the national roads.

abschnitte.text: The **vignette** is a charge for using the **motorways** and expressways. Anyone who drives a car or rides a motorbike on these roads must have one. It is valid for one calendar year at a time. The vignette has existed in Switzerland since 1985. The people had voted in favour of introducing it.

Since 2023 you can also buy the vignette **electronically**. Then there is no sticker any more. The e-vignette is linked to the **number plate**, meaning the vehicle's registration number. You buy it online from the Confederation. At a check, the number plate is checked.

The **sticker** is still available, for example at petrol stations and post offices. It is stuck to the windscreen and is only valid for that vehicle. The e-vignette has one advantage: you do not have to stick anything on or scrape anything off if the windscreen is replaced. One disadvantage: it is tied to the number plate, not to a windscreen. Anyone who changes their number plate needs to bear this in mind.

The vignette costs a fixed amount, which has been 40 francs for many years. The money goes into a special **federal** fund for the **national roads** and urban transport. It is used to build, maintain and repair motorways. Anyone who drives without a valid vignette risks a **fine**. On top of that, you still have to buy the vignette.

gewusst: The annual vignette is already valid from 1 December of the previous year and remains valid until the end of January of the following year.
Lorries do not pay for a vignette but a separate charge, which is calculated according to the kilometres driven.

teile.einleitung: Interest is an important part of a bank's business. It pays interest on savings and charges interest on loans. It lives on the difference between the two.
wichtigste: Interest is the price of borrowed money.
Anyone who takes out a loan from the bank pays interest.
The bank pays interest on savings because it can lend them on.
Loan interest is usually higher than savings interest.
One per cent interest is one hundredth of the amount.
The National Bank's key interest rate affects all other interest rates.

abschnitte.text: Many people take their money to the bank. The bank does not keep it all in the vault. It lends part of it to others, for example to families buying a house, or to companies. For these **loans** it receives **interest**. It passes part of this on to savers as interest.

**Savings interest** is the interest the bank pays you on your balance. **Loan interest** is the interest you pay when you borrow money. Loan interest is almost always higher. With the difference, the bank covers its costs, for example for staff and buildings. It also carries the **risk** that someone will not pay back a loan.

Interest is given as a **percentage per year**. If Tim has 500 francs in his savings account and the bank pays 1 per cent, you calculate 500 divided by 100. That gives 5 francs interest after one year. At 2 per cent it would be 10 francs. The higher the amount and the interest rate, the more interest.

abschnitte.titel: The role of the National Bank
abschnitte.text: The **Swiss National Bank**, SNB for short, sets the **key interest rate**. It affects how much interest banks charge for loans and pay on savings. If the SNB lowers the key rate, loans usually become cheaper. If it raises it, interest rates often rise. In this way the SNB tries to keep prices in Switzerland stable.

gewusst: Mortgages for houses are especially common in Switzerland. Many homeowners pay interest on them for decades.
Even very old legal texts from Mesopotamia contained rules about interest.

teile.einleitung: A discretionary assessment is an estimate of taxes made by the tax office. It happens when someone does not submit their tax return despite a reminder, or when important documents are missing. Then the office sets the income and assets itself, and this is often more expensive than expected.
wichtigste: A discretionary assessment is an estimate of income and assets by the tax office.
It is made when the tax return is not submitted despite a reminder.
The tax office can also estimate if documents are missing or incomplete.
On top of that there is the threat of a fine for breaching procedural obligations.
The estimate tends to be high, so that not submitting does not pay.
You can only challenge a discretionary assessment with good evidence.
If you need more time, you can ask for an extension in good time.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, every person liable to tax must submit a tax return once a year. From it, the tax office calculates the taxes; this is called the **assessment**. If the necessary details are missing, the office may set the figures itself. Because it decides according to its own, but dutiful, **discretion**, this is called a discretionary assessment.

First the tax return arrives with a deadline, in many cantons the end of March. If you do not submit it, you receive a **reminder** with a new deadline. If you do not react to that either, the tax office makes an estimate. The same can happen if you do submit a form but leave out important documents such as the salary statement.

The tax office relies on all the information it has, for example earlier tax returns or wage reports. It often puts the income somewhat higher than in the previous year. Deductions that you have not proved are usually not taken into account. That is why with a discretionary assessment you often pay **more tax** than necessary.

Anyone who does not submit their tax return is breaching their **procedural obligations**. For this there is a fine: for direct federal tax up to 1,000 francs and in serious cases up to 10,000 francs. You still have to pay the estimated taxes. If these are not paid either, **debt enforcement proceedings** follow in the end.

You can lodge an **objection** against any assessment within 30 days. With a discretionary assessment, however, you must then prove that the estimate is obviously wrong. Usually you have to submit the missing tax return with the documents to do so. The easiest thing is to hand in the return on time or to apply for an extension early.

begriffe.erklaerung: The calculation of taxes by the tax office.
The freedom an authority has to make a sensible decision itself.
A written challenge to a decision made by an authority.
An official procedure for collecting unpaid debts.

gewusst: In many cantons you can apply for an extension for your tax return quite easily online.
Anyone who does not submit their tax return does not save tax, but usually pays more.
Young adults aged 18 and over can also receive a discretionary assessment if they forget their first tax return.

teile.einleitung: Anyone doing an apprenticeship receives an **apprentice's wage** from their training company. This wage is also income and belongs in the tax return. For this, apprentices receive a **salary statement** every year.
wichtigste: The apprentice's wage is set in the **apprenticeship contract**.
It usually rises with each year of the apprenticeship.
Contributions are deducted from the wage, for example for insurance.
The training company issues a **salary statement** every year.
The apprentice's wage is taxable income.
Because of deductions, many apprentices pay little or no tax.

abschnitte.text: Apprentices work in the company and also attend **vocational school**. For this they receive a wage. How high it is is stated in the **apprenticeship contract**. It depends on the occupation, the industry and the year of the apprenticeship and is usually much lower than the wage of qualified professionals.

At the end of the year, apprentices also receive a **salary statement**. It shows how much you earned in the whole year and which contributions were deducted. You need these figures for the **tax return**. That is why you should keep the salary statement safe.

The apprentice's wage is **taxable income**. Even for those under 18, it is taxed separately, meaning it is not added to the parents' income. Because you can make deductions, for example for travelling to work, often only a little is left. That is why many apprentices pay hardly any tax, but still have to fill in a return.

gewusst: From 1 January after their 17th birthday, apprentices also pay contributions to the **AVS**.
In Switzerland, a large share of young people do a vocational apprenticeship after compulsory schooling.

teile.einleitung: With **social engineering**, fraudsters do not mainly attack computers, but people. They exploit trust, helpfulness, fear or time pressure. In this way they try to get passwords, codes or money directly.
wichtigste: Social engineering means manipulating people to get data or money.
Fraudsters often pretend to be the bank, the police or a support service.
Real bank staff never ask for passwords or confirmation codes.
With spoofing, a real telephone number can be faked on the display.
Time pressure is a clear warning sign.
Anyone who passes on money through their account for strangers can be committing the crime of money laundering.

abschnitte.text: Fraudsters play a **role**. They claim to be the bank, the police, a parcel service or technical support. They seem friendly and competent. Sometimes they even know some real details about their victim. Then they ask for a code, a payment or access to the computer. Because everything sounds believable, people often notice the fraud too late.

abschnitte.titel: Time pressure as a warning sign
abschnitte.text: It is typical that you are told to act **immediately**. Your account is in danger, the money must be put somewhere safe at once. With this pressure, fraudsters want to stop you from thinking calmly or asking someone. That is exactly when someone under pressure should take a break. A genuine matter can wait until you have checked it.

With **spoofing**, fraudsters make another, real number appear on your display, for example the bank's number. So the number shown is no proof. The safest thing is to hang up and call the bank yourself on the number you know, for example from your card or the official website. You never pass on a code from the banking app, because the fraudster can use it to confirm a payment.

Some fraudsters look for people who will **pass on** money through their account in return for payment. These so-called **money mules** help to hide money from frauds. This can be punishable as **money laundering**. On top of that, you often have to pay for the damage. Offers of quick, easy money are therefore a warning sign.

gewusst: Many attacks on companies do not start with hacking but with a clever phone call or a fake email.
A good protection is a simple rule: never decide under pressure and always call back yourself.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who wins the lottery is overjoyed. But do you have to pay tax on the winnings? In Switzerland, winnings from licensed lotteries are **tax-free** up to a high limit.
wichtigste: Winnings from lotteries licensed in Switzerland are tax-free up to about **1 million francs**.
So a win of 50,000 francs in the Swiss lottery is tax-free.
Only the part above the limit is taxed as income.
With large winnings, **withholding tax** is deducted first.
Winnings in Swiss casinos are tax-free.
Tax-free winnings still count as part of your assets afterwards.

abschnitte.text: Since the **Gambling Act**, which came into force in 2019, winnings from Swiss lotteries have been tax-free up to about **1 million francs**. This applies to licensed lotteries and sports betting, for example from Swisslos or the Loterie Romande. So anyone who wins 50,000 francs may keep the whole amount.

If a win is above the limit, the part above it is taxed as **income**. The lottery company first deducts **withholding tax** of 35 per cent. If you declare the winnings correctly in your tax return, you get this withholding tax back. Then you pay the normal income tax.

Even tax-free winnings do not disappear from the tax return. The money won then becomes part of your **assets**. You pay **wealth tax** on it every year to the canton and municipality. The interest on the winnings is also taxable income.

gewusst: In Switzerland, part of the money that lotteries take in goes to charitable purposes such as sport, culture and social causes.
The chance of winning the jackpot in the Swiss number lottery is less than one in thirty million.

teile.einleitung: Heavy lorries put more strain on roads and the environment than cars. That is why in Switzerland, instead of the vignette, they pay the **performance-related heavy vehicle fee**, HVF for short (LSVA in German). It depends on how far, how heavy and how clean a lorry is.
wichtigste: The HVF applies to vehicles over **3.5 tonnes** that transport goods.
It depends on the **kilometres** driven in Switzerland.
The **weight** and **pollutant emissions** also count.
The HVF has existed since 2001.
A large part of the money goes to the railways.
Lighter vehicles need a vignette for the motorway instead.

abschnitte.text: The **HVF** is a federal charge for heavy lorries. It applies on all roads in Switzerland, not only on the motorway. The more kilometres a lorry drives, the more it has to pay. That is the difference from the **vignette**, which has a fixed price per year.

Three things determine the amount: the **kilometres** driven, the permitted **total weight** and the **emissions category**. A lorry that gives off a lot of pollutants pays more per kilometre than a modern, clean one. In Swiss lorries, a device measures the kilometres driven automatically.
The voters approved the HVF in a popular vote in **1998**. It was introduced in 2001. The aim was to move more goods from road to **rail**. This idea is called **modal shift policy**.

About two thirds of the revenue goes to the **Confederation**. It uses it mainly to expand the railways, for example for the New Rail Link through the Alps with the Gotthard Base Tunnel. About one third goes to the **cantons**. They often use the money for the costs of road traffic.

gewusst: Foreign lorries also pay the HVF for the kilometres they drive in Switzerland.
At 57 kilometres, the Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world.

teile.einleitung: Income tax is a tax on income, meaning above all on wages. It is one of the most important sources of income for the Confederation, cantons and municipalities.
wichtigste: Income tax is calculated according to income.
This includes wages, pensions and interest.
The Confederation, the canton and the municipality each charge an income tax.
The tax is progressive.
Every year you fill in a tax return for it.

abschnitte.text: You pay **income tax** on your **income**. This is above all your **wages**. But **pensions**, for example from the AVS, and **interest** also count. Self-employed people pay it on what they earn from their own business. Companies do not pay income tax but a profit tax.

In Switzerland, income tax exists on **three levels**. The **Confederation** charges direct federal tax. The **canton** and the **municipality** charge their own income taxes. Cantons and municipalities set their tax rates themselves. That is why you pay different amounts depending on where you live.

Income tax is **progressive**. This means: those who earn more pay not only more francs but also a higher **percentage**. Small incomes are taxed little or not at all. In this way everyone should contribute according to their **economic ability to pay**. This principle is written in the Federal Constitution.

Every year you fill in a **tax return**. In it you state your income and your assets. You may also make **deductions**, for example for travelling to work or for children. The tax office then calculates the tax. For people without a Swiss permanent residence permit, the tax is often deducted directly from their wages; this is called **tax at source**.

gewusst: In Switzerland you fill in a single tax return for the municipality, canton and Confederation.
Many cantons now offer the tax return online, entirely without paper.

teile.einleitung: With compound interest, not only the money you have saved grows, but the interest itself grows too. That sounds small, but over many years it makes a big difference. Those who start early benefit most.
wichtigste: With compound interest, interest is also calculated on earlier interest.
For this, the interest is not withdrawn but added to the capital.
This way the money grows a little faster every year.
1000 francs at 5 per cent become 1102.50 francs in two years.
Starting early and leaving the money for a long time helps most.
With the rule of 72 you can estimate when money will double.

abschnitte.text: The money you have saved is called **capital**. If you receive interest and do not withdraw it, it is added to the capital. The next year, the interest is then calculated on the larger amount. So you get interest on the interest. This is called **compound interest**. In this way the money does not grow evenly, but faster and faster.

You invest 1000 francs at 5 per cent interest. After one year you have 1050 francs. In the second year you get 5 per cent on 1050 francs, which is 52.50 francs. Together that makes **1102.50 francs**. Without compound interest it would be only 1100 francs. The difference is small at first, but grows bigger every year.

With the **rule of 72**, you can quickly estimate when money will double. You divide 72 by the interest rate. At 6 per cent, that gives 72 divided by 6, so about **12 years**. At 3 per cent it would be about 24 years. The rule is only an estimate, but very practical for rough calculations.

abschnitte.titel: Time is the most important helper
abschnitte.text: Compound interest needs above all **time**. Someone who saves small amounts while young can end up with more than someone who saves larger amounts later. That is why people are often advised to start saving early. But compound interest also works with **debts**: if interest is not paid, debts can also grow faster and faster.

gewusst: With very low interest rates, compound interest has only a weak effect. At 1 per cent, according to the rule of 72, it takes about 72 years for the money to double.
Compound interest shows exponential growth. The same principle also exists in nature, for example when bacteria multiply.
